#7399. Court to hear argument in religious discrimination challenge brought by Catholic preschools in Colorado

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

The Supreme Court will hear oral argument on Nov. 3 in a challenge brought by Catholic preschools in Colorado, which argue that their exclusion from Colorado’s universal preschool program is a form of religious discrimination in violation of the First Amendment, because Colorado will not provide them with an exemption from rules that would require them to admit everyone – including LGBTQ children and children with LGBTQ parents.

The Catholic preschools say that they “have no objection to Colorado’s decision to allow over 1,000 … preschools to selectively serve the communities they are designed to serve.” Instead, the preschools emphasize, they “simply want the same accommodation extended to them.”

Colorado counters that the Catholic preschools “remain welcome to participate in” the universal preschool program. However, the state writes, if they do, they must be “subject to the same equal-opportunity requirements that apply to all other publicly funded preschools—public and private, secular and religious.”

Under the universal preschool program, families in Colorado can receive up to 15 hours of free preschool per week at participating schools. To be part of the program, preschools must meet state standards in areas such as employee training; they are also required to sign a nondiscrimination agreement, in which they consent to “provide eligible children an equal opportunity to enroll and receive preschool services regardless of race, ethnicity, religious affiliation, sexual orientation, gender identity, lack of housing, income level, or disability.” Colorado does not allow them to refuse to serve LGBTQ families, because it believes such refusals would violate the nondiscrimination agreement.

The plaintiffs in the case are the Archdiocese of Denver, two Catholic parishes with preschools (one of which has since closed), and two parents of preschool-aged children. They went to federal court to challenge the state’s policy, arguing that making Catholic preschools’ participation in the universal preschool program contingent on accepting the agreement amounts to unlawful religious discrimination and that the First Amendment requires Colorado to create a religious exemption to allow them to participate in the program.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the 10th Circuit ruled for the state. It acknowledged that in a line of decisions, the Supreme Court has held that “when a state offers subsidies for private education, it cannot categorically withhold those funds from religious institutions.” In the 10th Circuit’s view, however, those cases do not apply to the preschools’ challenge because Colorado “did not exclude” religious preschools from the universal preschool program. To the contrary, the court of appeals wrote, it “welcomed and actively solicited their participation” and it is not seeking “to prohibit funds from being used for religious purposes.” “The restrictions imposed by the nondiscrimination requirement universally cover enrollment policies and conduct, but they are not a targeted burden on religious use.”

The court of appeals also rejected the challengers’ contention that the nondiscrimination requirement is unconstitutional because it burdens their right to freely exercise their religious beliefs. In the court’s view, Colorado’s conditions were neutral and generally applied to every preschool, regardless of religion – the kind of government actions, the Supreme Court held in 1990 in Employment Division v. Smith, that normally do not violate the Constitution.

Although a regulation issued by the Colorado Department of Early Childhood contains a series of preferences to facilitate the matching of families to preschools, including a “catchall” preference that allows preschools to request (and the state to grant) a preference not listed in the regulation, the court of appeals said that preference is not the kind of individualized exemption that would render the law not generally applicable, because the preschools are still required to comply with the nondiscrimination requirement.

The court of appeals also rebuffed the challengers’ argument that the nondiscrimination requirement is not generally applicable because the program permits schools to give preferences to low-income families and children with disabilities. As an initial matter, the court of appeals suggested, it was “not persuaded” that such preferences actually are exceptions to the nondiscrimination requirement because they were intended to protect such children and families and do not discriminate against wealthier families or children without disabilities. But in any event, it continued, the nondiscrimination agreement is still generally applicable because the Supreme Court’s cases only prohibit the state from treating religious activity less favorably than comparable secular activity. And the preferences for low-income families and children with disabilities are not comparable, the court of appeals concluded, because – unlike the exemption that the challengers in this case seek – they do not “undermine[] the government’s asserted interest in ensuring equal access to preschools.”

The challengers came to the Supreme Court in November 2025, asking the justices to weigh in – which they agreed in April 2026 to do.

At the Supreme Court, the justices will review two main questions. The first is the scope of the court’s 2022 decision in Carson v. Makin, in which the court struck down a Maine law that allowed public funding to be used for private schools, but not for schools that provide religious instruction.

The challengers contend that under Carson, this case should be “an uncomplicated one.” Colorado, the challengers say, “knowingly excluded Catholic preschools solely on account of their religious exercise” – specifically, “their religious practices of ensuring that all enrolling families are supportive of the Catholic Church’s teachings on sex and marriage and of treating enrolled four-year-olds in accordance with their biological sex.” That exclusion, the challengers argue, places a burden on their ability to exercise their religion, in violation of the Constitution.

Colorado counters that Carson “applied the settled principle that government may not target religion for disfavored treatment.” What the preschools are seeking instead, it says, is a “new rule that would trigger strict scrutiny whenever public-benefits conditions incidentally burden religiously motivated conduct.”

The second question before the justices centers on what a challenger has to show to prevail on a claim that a law is not generally applicable for purposes of Smith.

In Tandon v. Newsom, the challengers contend, the Supreme Court made clear that, for purposes of Smith, “[a] law is not generally applicable if it ‘treat[s] any comparable secular activity more favorably than religious exercise’” – a test that the universal preschool program fails. Colorado created the universal-preschool program to ensure equal access for all preschool-aged children, they emphasize. Because the exemptions for low-income families and children with disabilities allow preschools “to provide families with unequal access based on protected characteristics,” the challengers argue, “they undermine Colorado’s asserted interest in equal access ‘in a similar way’ to” the religious accommodation that the challengers seek. Moreover, the challengers add, the program also fails the “general applicability” test under Smith because it gives Colorado discretion, through the preference system, to allow participating preschools “to discriminate in favor of LGBTQ families and other groups,” such as “‘gender-nonconforming children,’ ‘children of color,’ or members of ‘the LGBTQ community.’”

Colorado pushes back, telling the justices that the law creating the universal preschool program “expressly prioritizes specialized services for” children from low-income families and children with disabilities, based on the state’s “longstanding awareness that ensuring equal opportunity for these children often requires providing them with additional support.” But “allowing publicly funded preschools to provide” such services does not “allow any secular conduct that undermines Colorado’s equal-opportunity interests”; therefore, it says, the law is generally applicable for purposes of Smith.

Similarly, Colorado continues, the system of preferences, used to match preschools with families, that are “unrelated to the characteristics protected by the equal-opportunity requirements, by definition, are not exceptions from those requirements.” It is clear, the state stressed, that such preferences can be implemented “only when” they “do not violate the equal-opportunity requirements.”

Correction (Oct. 30 at 11:40 a.m.): A prior version of this article stated that “a participating faith-based preschool may prioritize the enrollment of families that belong to the same faith as that school.”

Amy Howe is the co-founder of SCOTUSblog and its primary reporter.

Leo is an avid Chicago White Sox fan, and has been known to follow basketball, too.

Asked about the upcoming games on the papal plane during a recent trip to France, Leo said, âThey tell me that the people coming to the match, 90% are Villanova and 10% Notre Dame, so the voice of the people of God will be very strong on the Villanova side.â

#7394. Groups ask Supreme Court to leave lower court order in place halting border wall construction in southwestern Texas

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

The plaintiffs challenging the Trump administration’s efforts to build a border wall in the Big Bend region of southwestern Texas urged the Supreme Court on Thursday to leave in place an order by a federal trial judge in El Paso temporarily halting the construction. Eric Glitzenstein, a lawyer representing the plaintiffs, told the justices in a 40-page filing that granting the federal government’s request to lift that order would allow the Trump administration to “immediately resume blasting, bulldozing, road construction, and other border barrier-related construction across one of the most remote and ecologically and culturally significant landscapes in the United States.”

The dispute centers on three waivers of various environmental and conservation laws that then-Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem and her successor, Markwayne Mullin, issued earlier this year to authorize construction of the border wall in the Big Bend region, including areas in Big Bend National Park. Noem and Mullin relied on a provision of the Illegal Immigration Reform and Immigrant Responsibility Act of 1996 that gives the Secretary of Homeland Security the power to “waive all legal requirements” necessary “to ensure expeditious construction” of border walls and roads. With the waivers, Noem and Mullin determined that additional border barriers are required in the Big Bend area because it “is an area of high illegal entry.”

The plaintiffs in this case – an environmental group, a local landowner, and a group formed to preserve a church – went to federal court to challenge the waivers’ legality. On Oct. 2, U.S. District Judge Kathleen Cardone temporarily barred the Department of Homeland Security from continuing construction on the border wall in the Big Bend region “until and unless” the government complies with environmental and other applicable laws.

In a written opinion issued on Oct. 14 to explain her reasoning, Cardone concluded that the challengers were likely to prevail on their claim that under the major questions doctrine – the idea that if Congress intends to give a federal agency the power to make decisions of vast economic or political significance, it must say so explicitly – the DHS secretary did not have the authority to issue the waivers.

As an initial matter, Cardone rejected the government’s contention that she did not have the power to consider the challengers’ claims because they arose from a statute, while IIRIRA only allows federal courts to hear challenges to waiver decisions if they involve the Constitution. The major questions doctrine, she said, is a “constitutional … rule” based on the idea that “courts should expect Congress to speak clearly when it delegates major lawmaking authority to the executive.”

Turning to the question of whether the major questions doctrine barred the waivers, she observed that both the government and the challengers “appear to agree that the waiver of all legal requirements to construct a border wall in the Big Bend Sector is of ‘major economic and political significance.’” The key issue, she continued, is thus whether Congress clearly gave the DHS secretary the power to issue the Big Bend waivers. It did not, she wrote. She emphasized that another provision of IIRIRA authorizes the DHS secretary to “take such actions as may be necessary to install additional physical barriers and roads … in the vicinity of the United States border to deter illegal crossings in areas of high illegal entry into the United States.” When that provision is read together with the waiver provision, she said, it means that the DHS secretary can only waive legal requirements for “construction ‘to deter illegal crossings in areas of high illegal entry.’”

But the Big Bend region is not, she contended, such an area: although it “comprises over 25% of the U.S.-Mexico border,” it accounts for only a tiny percentage (“between 0.3% and 2.2%”) of all of the people apprehended crossing the border. This means, she said, that “if the Big Bend Sector is an area of high illegal entry, so is every other sector, and the waiver authority would apply to the entire U.S.-Mexico border. If that were the case, Congress could have simply authorized construction ‘to deter illegal crossings.’” The major questions doctrine instructs courts to avoid “interpretations that would render limiting language meaningless,” Cardone concluded.

The Trump administration came to the Supreme Court on Oct. 21, asking the justices to pause Cardone’s order and to grant review and summarily reverse it. First, U.S. Solicitor General D. John Sauer argued, the district court did not have the power to consider the challengers’ claim based on the major questions doctrine because their complaint specifically alleged that the DHS secretary “lacked ‘clear congressional authorization’ … to issue the waivers” under the IIRIRA – a statutory claim that “Congress denied district courts” the authority “to entertain.” But in any event, Sauer continued, “[e]ven assuming that the Secretary’s waiver authority implicates a question of ‘vast economic and political significance,’ Congress did clearly authorize the Secretary both to build border barriers and to waive legal requirements in order to facilitate their expeditious construction.”

In their brief on Thursday, the challengers insisted that the major questions doctrine applied to their claim, stressing that “the decision to waive myriad federal, state, local, and tribal laws across vast geography for the purpose of building border infrastructure, even through national and state parks where border crossings are miniscule, is a truly ‘extraordinary’ assertion of power.” “Whatever authority Congress delegated, it did not clearly authorize the sweeping exercise of power asserted here, and” the government’s “actions therefore amount to a constitutional violation of the major questions doctrine.”

The challengers also argued that DHS will not suffer any permanent harm if the construction is temporarily blocked – one of the factors that courts consider in deciding whether to award temporary relief. To the contrary, they noted, before Cardone issued her order halting construction, “in response to intense local opposition,” DHS “voluntarily paused construction for weeks in vast portions of the project area.”

Amy Howe is the co-founder of SCOTUSblog and its primary reporter.

#7392. Mass shootings over Halloween weekend leave at least 6 dead and dozens injured across US

One shooting happened after a football game in Alabama.

Mass shootings over the Halloween weekend â largely in nightlife districts across the U.S. â left at least six people dead and dozens injured, officials said.

The deadliest violence occurred in Dallas, where a handful of shootings in the city’s Deep Ellum neighborhood, a center of music and restaurants, killed four people and injured 15 others, police said.

Police in college towns like Fayetteville, Arkansas; Birmingham, Alabama; Newark, Delaware, and Bloomington, Illinois, also reported shootings in their nightlife districts.

Dallas Police Chief Daniel Comeaux said investigators were still trying to determine if three separate shootings Saturday night over the span of about an hour and 15 minutes were related, and it wasn’t immediately known why they started. Comeaux said some arrests were made but he didn’t specify how many or what charges were involved.

“This is a really big scene. It’s spread out,” Comeaux said.

The department had increased police presence in the district before the shootings. No police officers were injured.

In Birmingham, one person was killed and eight others were wounded in two separate shootings just outside Legion Field after the annual “Magic City Classic” football game on Saturday night, Mayor Randall Woodfin said at a news conference Sunday.

Two were listed in critical condition Sunday, fire officials said.

Alabama State and Alabama A&M are archrivals whose annual contest has been played for more than 100 years. Nearly 70,000 fans attended Saturday’s game, won by Alabama A&M 31-28. The event draws some of the largest crowds in the country for games played in their college football division.

Michael Pickett, chief of the Birmingham Police Department, said most spectators and families had left the stadium property after the game. The first shooting happened nearby, where vendors were set up along Graymont Avenue.

The circumstances of the shootings were unclear, and it was also unclear where the fatality occurred.

Police spokesperson De’Rell Freeman said one person had been detained and that “multiple weapons” were found.

In Newark, Delaware, six people were shot late Saturday near the University of Delaware campus, Newark police Lt. Greg D’Elia said.

Video shared on social media showed people running for safety from the scene. One stretch of the city’s Main Street was closed for several hours after the shooting, police said.

All six were transported to hospitals for treatment and their conditions were not available. A university spokesperson said they would provide updates on the investigation online as they become available.

A shooting early Sunday in Bloomington, Illinois, left a 19-year-old woman dead and another woman in critical condition. Six others had injuries of an unknown nature that were not life-threatening. The shooting happened near the campus of Illinois Wesleyan University. Bloomington is about 135 miles (217 kilometers) southwest of Chicago.

In Fayetteville, Arkansas, six people were taken to hospitals with gunshot wounds from a shooting early Sunday near the University of Arkansas. No arrests have been made, police said in a news release. A preliminary investigation indicates an altercation preceded the shooting.

Halloween stores were the scene of two attacks

On Friday, two people were killed in separate shootings at Spirit Halloween stores in California and Michigan.

Police said a shooting inside a store in Fairfield, California, was a targeted attack. Family members told police that the 31-year-old woman who died was pregnant. Six other people were wounded, police said. There were no immediate arrests.

In Madison Heights, Michigan, just north of Detroit, a 21-year-old man was fatally shot Friday afternoon. A man who was assaulted by bystanders as officers took him into custody was hospitalized with injuries that were not life-threatening, police said.By JOHN RABY Associated Press

#7390. Lawyer, business partner accused of defrauding cannabis investor of $750K

A Los Angeles attorney and his business partner are accused of paying for their personal expenses with investor money instead of funding business-to-consumer cannabis trade shows. (Image from Shutterstock)

A Los Angeles attorney and his business partner are accused of paying for their personal expenses with investor money instead of funding business-to-consumer cannabis trade shows, including the unsuccessful Green Street Festival in 2022.

A Los Angeles County court complaint filed by investor Jamie Chisick alleged that attorney Joshua Shelton of the Winston Wolfe Law Firm and his business partner, Rama Mayo, took $750,000 for a 15% ownership stake in the Green Street Symposium.

According to the Oct. 19 complaint, Shelton and Mayo, cannabis entrepreneurs, promised to organize large trade events that would attract thousands of attendees and generate “millions of dollars in revenue,” according to coverage on Law360.

Chisick obtained documents that he said shows that his money had been used for “personal payments, including but not limited to private jets, health insurance, bar dues (Shelton) and general overhead unrelated to GSS operations.”

The 2022 Green Street Festival brought in about $190,000 with about $178,000 refunded. A 2023 festival with projections of attracting over 10,000 attendees and up to $4.7 million in revenue drew a smaller crowd and did not produce a profit.

Chisick seeks to recover his investment and punitive damages, according to the complaint.

#7389. Sheila Chepkirui wins matchup of past champions in NYC Marathon, Andreas Almgren makes winning debut

Chepkirui pulled away from defending champion Hellen Obiri in the final 150 meters.

NEW YORK (AP) â Sheila Chepkirui of Kenya won the women’s race of the New York City Marathon for the second time in three years on Sunday, while Andreas Almgren of Sweden was victorious in his debut in the distance.

Chepkirui pulled away from defending champion Hellen Obiri in the final 150 meters to seal the victory in 2 hours, 24 minutes and 36.

“The last mile was really tricky,” said Chepkirui, who also won in 2024. “I had to be patient because I knew Hellen was really strong, so I had to really push up to the finish line.”

What Chepkirui didn’t know was that American Jessica McClain had been gaining on both of the Kenyans in the final 800 meters of the race. McClain finished 6 seconds behind Chepkirui after passing Obiri â a two-time winner who set the course record in 2025 â in the final few strides. It was the first time a U.S. woman finished in the top three since 2018.

“It was a really fun, magical day out there. New York, you never know what to expect and I honestly didn’t feel like amazing through (Mile) 18, and just kind of had to stick in it and adjust as I went,” McClain said. “Top five was top of mind, then podium. I was just like, stick with it. And then all of a sudden Hellen was coming back to me, so I don’t really know what happened, but I couldn’t be happier right now.”

Almgren was making his debut at 26.2 miles after a successful career running half-marathons. He pulled away from Yemaneberhan Crippa of Italy in the final mile to take the victory in 2:6.1.

“This is my first marathon. I didn’t know how I was supposed to feel,” said Almgren.

Crippa finished 13 seconds behind Almgren. Kamohelo Mofolo of Lesotho was third, edging out defending champion Benson Kipruto.

Almgren’s time was the third fastest in the course’s 50-year history, and six runners went under 2:07 to finish in the top 10 all-time times.

“I just tried to stay up at front and see what happened and see how the race developed,” Almgren said. “I didn’t think it was going to be that quick of a finish, but I didn’t really know anything about that. One of the reasons I choose to race New York is that you don’t care about the time but just get as good a position as possible.”

He became the first marathoner to win his debut in the event since Gebre Gebremariam of Ethiopia won the 2010 race. American Zouhair Talbi finished sixth on Sunday and ran the fastest time ever by a U.S. runner in the event.

It was the 50th time that the race has run through all five boroughs of the city. There were just over 2,000 competitors in 1976, the seventh running of the race, including only 88 women. About 60,000 runners stepped up to the starting line Sunday, with nearly half of them women.

There were runners from more than 140 countries competing, including defending men’s champion Kipruto. He won in thrilling fashion last year, edging Alexander Mutiso by three-hundredths of a second.

The New York City Marathon began in 1970, and the first six years it was run entirely inside Central Park, with runners doing loops. The race was moved out of Central Park in celebration of the U.S. bicentennial and to help uplift the city, which was struggling. It ended up turning into one of the marquee events in New York.

For the first time in 15 years, there was a minor change in the course. The runners took a slightly different route at Mile 20 when the race entered the Bronx. The move was made to reduce the number of turns in the borough from seven to five and ease some of the street closures in the area.

Marcel Hug won the men’s wheelchair race for the eighth time, edging Daniel Romanchuk by just over a second. Romanchuk made a move to take over the lead in the last mile as the pair entered Central Park for the final time. Hug passed him in the final 100 meters to win.

Hug’s Swiss countrymate Catherine Debrunner pulled away from the field early to win the women’s wheelchair race, finishing in 1:40:02. It was the second-fastest time in race history, trailing her own mark by about 30 seconds from 2023. Two-time defending champion Susannah Scaroni finished third, three months after giving birth to her first child, more than eight minutes behind Debrunner.By DOUG FEINBERG AP Sports Writer

#7387. The November argument session begins on Monday

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

It was a relatively quiet week at the court, as the justices – and the SCOTUSblog team – prepared for the November argument session to begin next week. On the interim docket, the court decided one immigration-related dispute and moved closer to being able to decide another.

On Thursday, an environmental group, a local landowner, and a group formed to preserve a church urged the Supreme Court to deny the Trump administration’s request to be allowed to resume construction of its border wall in the Big Bend region of southwestern Texas. For more on their filing, see the On Site section below.

On Tuesday, the Supreme Court denied a request from three cities and a group that provides legal services to immigrants to pause an agreement between Texas and the Department of Justice that prevents enforcement of a Biden-era rule allowing immigration judges to pause certain deportation proceedings. There were no noted dissents.

The court’s November argument session will begin next week. On Monday, the justices will hear argument in two cases: Maxwell v. Dinis, on a federal inmate’s ability to use a habeas statute, 28 U.S.C. § 2241, to contest the Federal Bureau of Prisons’ refusal to accelerate his transfer to a halfway house or home confinement; and Younge v. Fulton Judicial Circuit District Attorney’s Office, Georgia, on whether an affirmative defense may be asserted as a basis for summary judgment if not presented earlier in a pleading.

Congress may be “the battleground in the 2026 midterm elections,” but the Supreme Court is playing a role in many races, according to USA Today. Republican and Democratic candidates alike are highlighting “disputes about the high court’s membership, its size and its ethics” and calling on voters to keep these battles in mind when they head to the polls next week. In particular, candidates are raising the possibility of a Supreme Court vacancy during President Donald Trump’s final two years in office and emphasizing that the party that controls the Senate will be able to determine whether another Trump nominee is confirmed to the court.

U.S. District Judge Maame Ewusi-Mensah Frimpong has “barred immigration agents in Southern California from stopping people based on racial stereotypes,” citing what she described as “a mountain of evidence” showing that agents are “targeting people who appear Latino,” according to the Los Angeles Times. “The injunction … requires agents to establish individualized reasonable suspicion before detaining someone for immigration enforcement.” The Times noted that the evidence cited by Frimpong in her new order “had not yet been turned over by the government when the Supreme Court last year stayed the judge’s earlier order barring stops based solely on race or ethnicity, language, location or employment, either alone or in combination.” Frimpong acknowledged the Supreme Court's decision in her new order, but emphasized that the court “had not explained its reasons for granting the stay.” “This Court cannot be faulted for failing to follow guidance that was never given,” the judge wrote. The Trump administration has indicated that it will appeal Frimpong’s order to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit.

On Wednesday, Utah “filed criminal charges against prediction market operator Kalshi and two of its executives, months after a federal judge rejected Kalshi’s effort to prevent Utah from enforcing its strict anti-gambling laws against the activity,” according to the Associated Press. “The charges include 13 counts of violating the state’s prohibition on gambling and another charge involving profiting off illegal activity.” The AP noted that “[t]he felony charges could represent a new tactic in how states try to assert regulatory authority over the fast-expanding activity, a clash that appears headed to a showdown at the U.S. Supreme Court.”

Last week, the University of North Carolina School of Law “tested whether AI could replicate the reasoning of US Supreme Court justices” by staging “a simulated Supreme Court argument based on an actual case the high court heard in 2025,” according to Reuters. Participants found that although the three AI justices used in the test drew the same conclusions as the real-life justices, “deciding the case the same way the actual court did,” the bots did not excel at mimicking their behaviors during oral argument. “The AI justices asked questions and hypotheticals of the law students who argued the case, but their interactions felt robotic and they didn’t interrupt or interject the way the real justices do.” “There’s still this huge gap in it actually feeling human,” said Nicole Downing, the law school’s assistant dean for AI, to Reuters.

In his newsletter for The New York Times, Adam Liptak explored the Trump administration’s battle against what it describes as “rogue activist judges,” a category that has come to include judges who expressed frustration with government lawyers or criticized the administration’s actions in media interviews. Liptak noted that the Supreme Court held, in a 1994 opinion from Justice Antonin Scalia, that “[e]xpressions of impatience, dissatisfaction, annoyance and even anger” are “within the bounds of what imperfect men and women, even after having been confirmed as federal judges, sometimes display” and do not necessarily establish “bias or partiality.”

The plaintiffs challenging the Trump administration’s efforts to build a border wall in the Big Bend region of southwestern Texas urged the Supreme Court on Thursday to leave in place an order by a federal trial judge in El Paso temporarily halting the construction.

The court will hear oral argument on Tuesday in a challenge brought by Catholic preschools. The schools argue that their exclusion from Colorado’s universal preschool program is a form of religious discrimination in violation of the First Amendment, because the state will not provide them with an exemption from rules that would require them to admit everyone – including LGBTQ children and children with LGBTQ parents.

(SCOTUSblog Plus) Earlier this month, the concept of cruel and unusual punishment briefly captured the country’s attention after the state of Tennessee on Sept. 30 tried and failed to execute Christa Pike. The botched execution drew attention to a range of past rulings on the death penalty, while also highlighting a number of unresolved issues in this fraught area.

In his Controlling Opinions column on Wednesday, Richard Re reflected on Justice Samuel Alito’s effort in his new book to discourage judicial “insecurity” – that is, “a judge’s self-conscious worry that he might be advancing his own policy preferences under the guise of impartial adjudication.” According to Re, “what Alito labels insecurity is better understood as a form of humility and self-awareness,” impulses that are laudable, not problematic.

As it currently stands, the 2026-27 term is much less Trump-centric than its predecessor. But that could soon change, because by mid-January the justices are likely to consider a number of petitions for review from the Trump administration or Trump himself.

In his Justice, Democracy, and Law column on Tuesday, Edward Foley explored a growing battle over the division of authority between states and the federal government when it comes to “determining who can vote in congressional elections and regulating how the voting process occurs.” One such case involves the issue of alleged noncitizen voting in California, which may soon arrive at the Supreme Court.

In her In Dissent column on Monday, Anastasia Boden explored 1926’s Village of Euclid v. Ambler Realty, in which the Supreme Court, after rehearing the case and “a dramatic reversal in several justices’ positions,” paved the way for modern zoning. Boden noted that “[t]hree justices dissented, though they never said why.”

Sarah Isgur and David French zoom in on the cases prosecutors have brought against political enemies of the Trump administration. Then, they review the latest news from the battle over a Washington, D.C., golf course before tackling the administration’s sue-and-settle case in Texas.

The election is upon us, and worries about possible anti-democratic actions have many on alert. Akhil Amar and Andy Lipka peer ahead to see what to watch out for and review the relevant constitutional law and history.

Friday’s A Closer Look is typically a judicial biography. This week we cover Justice John McKinley, who served on the court from 1838 to 1852.

With the Eighth and Ninth Circuits Act of 1837, Congress added two more seats to the court. The first went to Justice John Catron, and the second went to Justice John McKinley, whose confirmation created a nine-justice court. While the seat itself was an honor, its duties were less so, as McKinley would discover.

McKinley was born in May 1780 in Culpeper County, Virginia. His family soon moved to Kentucky, where he taught himself law, passed the bar in 1800, and practiced in both Frankfort and Louisville. After moving to Alabama around 1818, McKinley grew wealthy from land speculation, partnered with Andrew Jackson in the Cypress Land Company, and helped found the city of Florence, Alabama. Jackson himself called McKinley “the most prominent man” in the state.

McKinley entered the Alabama Legislature in 1820, and, after backing Jackson for the presidency (he had previously supported Henry Clay), won a U.S. Senate seat in 1826. In the Senate, McKinley advocated for bankruptcy policies “favorable to small farmers.” However, his vote to override Jackson’s Maysville Road veto (the Maysville Road Bill essentially proposed federal stock purchases for internal improvements, like state roads) raised doubts about his loyalty, and he was not reelected in 1830. After one term in the U.S. House and another in the state legislature, he won a second Senate term in 1836, only to leave the seat within two months due to his Supreme Court appointment.

In 1837, the Eighth and Ninth Circuits Act expanded the court to nine justices, and Jackson’s advisers pushed McKinley for one of the new seats, but Jackson preferred his friend William Smith instead. When Smith declined, the pick then fell to the newly inaugurated President Martin Van Buren, who went with McKinley. Van Buren gave McKinley a recess appointment in April 1837, and the Senate confirmed him by voice vote that September.

After his nomination, McKinley wrote to then-House speaker James Polk that he had “accepted the appointment, although it is certainly the most onerous and laborious of any in the United States.” The new 9th Circuit included Alabama, Arkansas, Mississippi, and eastern Louisiana and required eight circuit terms a year. McKinley told Polk he would travel more than 5,000 miles annually, although McKinley later reported a figure closer to 10,000. The duties also likely ate into his finances (the justices were required to personally pay for their own circuit court duties) and took a toll on his health (he later had a paralyzing stroke on his way to Jackson, Mississippi).

Even before his first term started, McKinley asked Van Buren in person about changing the new 9th Circuit, but the president left the issue out of his next annual State of the Union, upsetting McKinley. Following McKinley’s first full term, the justices disbanded in March 1838 to “confront some 6,000 cases on their cumulative circuit dockets,” according to Steven Brown, who wrote McKinley’s first full-length biography. McKinley’s share from the 9th Circuit alone made up 4,700 of those.

Brown detailed one of the more interesting stories from McKinley’s extensive circuit duties in a 2011 Journal of Supreme Court History article. In April 1839 while holding circuit court in Jackson, a fight spilled into the courtroom and an officer of the court (who had been called “a stupid jackass” by McKinley for not bringing in the court marshal) pulled McKinley’s nose. Newspapers reported that the justice swore never to return to Jackson, and McKinley referenced the “gross personal indignity” in a letter to Van Buren.

In his 1839 State of the Union address, Van Buren told Congress that the circuit’s schedule and distances made it “impossible” for its judge to keep up. McKinley missed much of his circuit duties, along with the entire 1840 term, due to illness. Combined with his failure to hold court in Arkansas for almost five years, states in his circuit felt “neglected,” and the Mississippi Legislature called for McKinley’s impeachment. Congress eventually reorganized the circuits in August 1842, relieving McKinley of Mississippi and Arkansas; beginning in 1843 he rode the reconstituted 5th Circuit, which covered Alabama and Louisiana.

As for McKinley’s actual approach to cases, he was strongly for states’ rights, supporting them “over the authority of the federal government.” During his time on the court, McKinley wrote 19 majority opinions, four dissents, and two concurrences by one count, 22 opinions by another, and 23 by a third, the lowest per-term rate of his era. One of his opinions for the court was in 1845’s Pollard’s Lessee v. Hagan, where he held that new states enter the union on equal footing with the original 13, including ownership of the lands beneath navigable waters. Four years later in the 1849 Passenger Cases, McKinley argued in his concurrence that the federal government, not the states, controlled immigrants arriving from overseas until they became permanent residents of the states.

Increasingly ill after a stroke in 1842, McKinley died in Louisville in July 1852 at age 72, after 14 relatively difficult years on the court. He was replaced by Justice John Archibald Campbell, also from Alabama.

CHIEF JUSTICE ROBERTS: "I think we're... I think it's safe."

CHIEF JUSTICE ROBERTS: "It's a trick they play on new Chief Justices all the time."

#7386. Gabby Williams leads Valkyries to WNBA championship in second season, beating Dream 68-63 in Game 7

The Valkyries captured a championship in just their second season by beating the Atlanta Dream 68-63 in a sensational first WNBA Finals Game 7 on Saturday night.

SAN FRANCISCO (AP) â A fresh WNBA CHAMPIONS T-shirt over her uniform, Gabby Williams cradled the shiny MVP trophy in one arm and gave it a kiss. She held up a No. 1 with her left hand, then hugged and high-fived her supporters all the way to Golden State’s locker room, where she pulled on some goggles for the celebration.

Williams made her way back to the Bay Area where she cherishes so many youth basketball memories exactly for a chance to do something like this â to win it all and be part of building something special.

“I just walked into a group full of love,” Williams said. “And that just changed the entire trajectory of my career.”

Williams scored her team’s final 11 points of the third quarter and dazzled through the fourth on the way to 30 points, and the Valkyries captured a championship in just their second season by beating the Atlanta Dream 68-63 in a sensational first WNBA Finals Game 7 on Saturday night.

“Gabby is our closer; she stayed patient, she stayed with it,” coach Natalie Nakase said. “Closing with 30, that is incredible!”

Williams joined Penny Taylor in 2007 for Phoenix as the only players in WNBA history to score 30 or more points in a winner-take-all Finals game.

Jordin Canada scored 18 points, Allisha Gray 16 and Angel Reese had eight points and 12 rebounds for the Dream, denied another championship in the franchise’s fourth try.

Gray made two free throws with 11 seconds left then Atlanta forced a jump ball â Gray against Williams â and Veronica Burton corralled it and converted two free throws with 5.1 seconds to go.

“I’m just so blessed, this is insane!” said Burton, cut by Dallas two years ago.

Rhyne Howard’s layup tied it at 57 with 2:41 left only for Williams to answer once more with a clutch 3-pointer. She converted two free throws with 1:40 remaining, then Kiah Stokes scored a late basket. Stokes â now a four-time WNBA champion â pulled down 13 rebounds and blocked two more shots to cap her spectacular postseason.

Williams left Seattle with a great feeling about joining Golden State and its close-knit culture, returning to the Bay Area determined to prove herself as a WNBA star after all her international success â and now she’s a postseason icon. Fans chanted “Gabby! Gabby!” throughout the fourth quarter.

“All it took was good people,” she said. “All we heard last year was we don’t have no stars. We don’t have no talent. Yeah right! We got good people. We got good people. We got winners. We got people who are ready to put their bodies on the floor to win a game.”

When the final buzzer sounded, the violet-clad sellout crowd at Chase Center went into a frenzy as players sprinted to the middle of the floor to hug and celebrate as confetti fell from the rafters.

“Ballhalla” had become “Boohalla” for this far-but-haunted Halloween night in the raucous arena. Now, with a women’s championship to its name right alongside the one earned by the Golden State Warriors in 2022.

“We gotta build a bigger trophy case,” co-owner Peter Guber said.

The team that led at halftime in the first six matchups had won every game so far, and the Dream were ahead 30-24 at the break. Atlanta also had been 16-0 this season when Reese made at least one 3. The Dream’s DeWanna Bonner became the first player in WNBA history to reach 600 career postseason defensive rebounds.

Nakase insisted to Williams at halftime the game would open up for her.

“Nat told me to stay patient, I trust her with my life,” Williams said. “I stayed patient.”

Nakase changed her starting lineup for Game 4 in a move that paid huge dividends after Golden State fell behind 2-1, inserting Kaila Charles and Tiffany Hayes and bringing Kayla Thornton and Cecilia Zandalasini off the bench.

The 37-year-old Hayes, who came out of retirement two years ago and spent 10 seasons with the Dream, scored 11 points in the winner-take-all Game 7 and brought energy all series that made Nakase want to win for the veteran guard as much as anybody.

Valkyries owner Joe Lacob guaranteed a championship within the first five years for this franchise three years ago when the Bay Area was granted an expansion team, and in improbable, joyful fashion, his team accomplished it in Year 2. That after becoming the first expansion organization to reach the playoffs in its inaugural year in 2025.

During the victory ceremony, Lacob shouted out the team and its leaders, while Nakase, general manager Ohemaa Nyanin and President Jess Smith hugged. And Lacob thanked the fans who have sold out Chase Center for every game since Day 1.

“These ladies deserve all the credit in the world for the incredible resilience, every last one of them, and our coach,” he said later. “I can’t even say how proud I am. I don’t care men, women, whatever, it doesn’t matter, that is an incredible year, an incredible performance, not only tonight but the whole playoffs.“By JANIE McCAULEY AP Sports Writer

#7385. Five November criminal law arguments, and one last look at the 2025-26 term

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

While all eyes are on what seem like inevitable Supreme Court election law “emergency” petitions, it may be comforting to realize that the regular business of the Supreme Court still goes on. Argument calendars released months ago show five criminal law and related cases set for argument in November. Below are some quick summaries of them. But first, an announcement and one more quick look at last term.

My ABA “Annual Review of the Supreme Court’s Term: Criminal Cases”

For some 30 years I have written and the American Bar Association has published an “Annual Review of the Supreme Court’s Term: Criminal Cases” for the prior term. This is a booklet of manageable size for persons interested in a complete picture of the hundreds of pages the justices write every year on topics and cases related to criminal law. That’s also what this regular SCOTUSblog column aims to do – but the review provides a lot more detail. This effort – and believe me, it takes hours to compile – is a fun and (I hope) useful part of my pro bono work.

This year’s booklet will be published here on the ABA Criminal Justice Section‘s website next week. It is downloadable, and while I hold the copyright, anyone can use and distribute it. Summaries of 45 merits decisions and 26 separate writings by justices on the orders docket last term are included, as well as 14 criminal law and related cases granted for argument (so far) this term can be found in it as well. If you enjoy the booklet or have suggestions or criticisms, please let me know.

Before getting to the November sitting, here’s one interesting question from last term (more can be found in the booklet) that only recently occurred to me regarding two pairs of very different cases: Olivier v. City of Brandon versus Fernandez v. United States, and Hunter v. United States versus Clark v. Sweeney. At a high level of generality, is one case in each pair inconsistent with the other?

In brief, the court ruled in Fernandez that doubts about a prior conviction must be pursued in habeas, not the federal compassionate relief statute. Two months earlier in Olivier, however, the court ruled that a prospective challenge to a statute under which a person was previously convicted need not be pursued under habeas but instead can be filed under §1983 – even though that challenge might well “imply the invalidity of Olivier’s conviction.” Justice Elena Kagan wrote Olivier for a unanimous court, while Justice Amy Coney Barrett wrote Fernandez in an 8 to 1 result.

Similarly, in Clark v. Sweeney the court summarily reversed the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 4th Circuit for granting habeas relief on grounds not argued by the parties. But then, seven months later in the term in Hunter, the court ruled that a court of appeals can ignore a waiver of appeal if a “miscarriage of justice” is perceived – presumably even if that miscarriage has not been raised by the parties. The court emphasized that the independence, discretion, and “integrity” of the judiciary is at stake. Again, the votes were not close: Hunter (Kagan again) was 8-1, and Clark was an apparently unanimous summary reversal.

I wrote separately about both Clark and Hunter in columns last term, and now, the broad overview of all the decisions together occasioned by compiling my booklet led me to comparisons not apparent at the time. The pairings I have identified are not directly inconsistent, and cases can always be distinguished from each other on a granular level. But at some general level I think there are clear tensions between the animating philosophies in each pair. Those tensions reflect deep differences among the justices on fundamental liberty and fairness questions reflected in their approach to criminal law. More of which we turn to now.

As indicated in my September column about upcoming criminal cases, December will be a “big” month, with AR-15 rifle possession and “forfeiture for a six-pack of beer” set for argument on Dec. 1 and 2. One criminal case, Beaird v. United States, has already been argued, presenting a relatively abstract question about how much deference to give to federal Sentencing Guidelines commentary notes. But November will be action-packed with five cases related to criminal law.

To be fair, none of the five cases raises what I would call a “pure” criminal law issue. Instead, there’s a variety of topics related to criminal law: habeas corpus rules (two cases), immigration, private causes of action for constitutional violations, and a purely civil procedure case arising from the firing of a supervisory assistant district attorney. But all present interesting legal issues for Supreme Court nerds like me (us?). Here are brief thumbnail sketches, in order of my own level of interest, not their respective argument dates.

For pure fireworks among the justices, the oral argument a week from Monday may be quite a show. But the result seems pretty much preordained: the court will either overrule an old civil rights precedent or once again limit it to its exact facts.

In 1970, the liberal Warren court ruled in Bivens v. Six Unknown Federal Narcotics Agents that individuals may sue federal officials directly under the constitution for damages caused if they have violated the Constitution, despite there being no statute that provides for such a “cause of action.” The vote was 5+1 to 3 and the decision has been controversial ever since. Multiple justices have said or suggested that without a congressional statute approving such claims, Bivens violates the constitutional separation of powers. Over time, and with changing personnel and views on the court, Bivens has thus repeatedly been limited, with the court declining to extend it to other circumstances over a dozen times.

In the instant case, Kekai Watanabe was attacked in a federal prison gang riot, and he alleges that he was denied medical care (with prison paramedic Francis Nielsen allegedly saying “stop being a cry baby”) and instead placed in solitary confinement for months. Only then was a serious spinal column injury identified and addressed. In 1980, the Supreme Court had extended Bivens (which had been based on the Fourth Amendment) to Eighth Amendment deliberate indifference claims. But that was the last time the court has ever looked favorably on Bivens. Nielsen now asks that Bivens be overruled, while the solicitor general suggests more mildly that the court might wait for a Fourth Amendment case to do the same.

At oral argument, I have no doubt that the three liberal justices will speak vigorously for Bivens and about the injustice of not allowing remedies for wrongs that violate the Bill of Rights. Chief Justice John Marshall’s famous invocation of the maxim “every right ... must have a remedy,” in Marbury v, Madison, will almost certainly be brought up. But just as vigorously, other justices will invoke the constitutional separation of powers and say that it is Congress, and not an unelected judiciary, that must write legislative protections for legal wrongs. The rhetorical and emotional heroics in this argument may rival those heard in voting, abortion, and birthright citizenship cases. Yet an anti-Bivens result seems virtually pre-ordained.

When a federal prisoner is nearing the end of their term of imprisonment, they often can be transferred to a “halfway house,” which is just what it sounds like: the prisoner is confined to a group home setting at night, but free to leave during the day (with conditions) to look for employment, attend rehabilitation programs, and the like. The prisoner is still within the government’s control and supervision. But is a halfway house “custody” so that legal aspects of it – or in this case, alleged entitlement to it – can be challenged in a habeas corpus proceeding?

Richard Cooke has published on SCOTUSblog a nice account of the issues and briefed arguments. William Maxwell, a mafia-affiliated fraudster who was sentenced in 2015 to 20 years in federal prison, filed a habeas petition claiming that he is entitled to “accelerated release” to a halfway house. The U.S. Court of Appeals for the 5th Circuit affirmed dismissal, ruling that habeas does not encompass a mere transfer between prison settings. As Cooke writes, the issue is “tricky” because prior cases have used various words to describe the reach of the federal habeas statute, including one (back in 1973) that habeas corpus can extend to a claim for “good conduct” time credits. The federal habeas statute explicitly also addresses prisoners “in custody,” but then lists specifics that don’t quite capture the claim here. And yet, a halfway house is certainly a “level of custody,” even if less restrictive than prison. Moreover, if Maxwell can’t use habeas, he does not appear to have any other judicial remedy available, because 42 U.S.C. §1983 (which authorizes people to sue state officials for violating a constitutional right) can’t be applied to federal officials (as noted in my description of Watanabe).

Neither the solicitor general nor Maxwell liked the 5th Circuit’s description of the proper habeas analysis. So a former law clerk of Justice Samuel Alito has been appointed to argue for affirmance here. Folks who love the intricacies of habeas law – imagine tax law mavens but in criminal law – will find the Maxwell arguments fascinating. But I imagine that the overall numbers of listeners who tune in for Monday’s live argument – has anyone ever filed a FOIA request to get those numbers? – won’t be very high.

This is another case involving the intricacies of habeas law. And it is founded on a complicated procedural history, which is often the case in state criminal cases that finally make their way to the Supreme Court after multiple rounds of lower court litigation. Statutes that regulate habeas petitions filed by both federal and state prisoners permit successive habeas petitions to go forward, even if a prior habeas petition has been filed and denied, if the new petition raises a “new rule of constitutional law ... that was previously unavailable.” The question presented here seems relatively simple (after the procedural thicket is penetrated): is a rule “previously unavailable” when it was “practically unavailable” because the federal courts with jurisdiction over the prisoner would have automatically denied it?

Dexter Johnson is on death row in Texas and says he is intellectually disabled. In 2002, the Supreme Court ruled in Atkins v. Virginia that intellectually disabled persons are protected from execution under the Eighth Amendment’s cruel and unusual punishment ban. In 2015, the 5th Circuit denied a habeas petition Johnson had filed, but then in 2017 the Supreme Court issued a decision that Texas’ definition of intellectual disability was wrong. That is, a new psychiatric Diagnostic Manual allowed a person like Johnson to be declared intellectually disabled. Johnson then filed a successive habeas petition arguing that the change in Texas law created a “new rule” allowing an Atkins claim in his jurisdiction, which had been “previously unavailable” because circuit precedent had declared it meritless. In other words, Johnson says the 2002 Atkins rule was “unavailable” to him until 2017, because it would have been a waste of time, even frivolous, for him to file it prior to the change in the legal standard for Atkins protection. The 5th Circuit appears to have accepted that idea in the litigation leading to this case.

At oral argument next Wednesday, plain language textualists may have a field day. The Atkins ruling was clearly available prior to 2017, and Texas argues, quite simply, that its new constitutional rule was thus not “unavailable” when Johnson filed his first habeas petition. However, as Johnson contends, “available” is variously defined as “capable of being employed with advantage” or “usable.” He therefore argues that the Atkins rule was simply not usable – it was “previously unavailable” to him – until the legal standard for Atkins was made clear in 2017.

It thus turns out that the statutory phrase at issue here is not “plain,” but rather subject to different textual interpretations. Which means, I think, that the oral argument is likely to fall back (as is often the case in habeas cases) on the ideological orientations of various justices. It will be the kind of semantic battling and linguistic nitpicking that, although obviously important, can make the average American simply sick of lawyers.

Although this important immigration case will be argued on the first day of what insiders call “the December calendar,” it actually occurs on the last day of November, when some of us may still be eating Thanksgiving leftovers. Like Guerrero, the case involves the practical application of a simple phrase that literally might mean something else.

There are two noncitizen cases consolidated in one petition here, but discussing the lead respondent is enough for today. Tamer Wassily is a noncitizen who was granted asylum in the United States in 2000, and the applicable statute says that “any alien granted asylum” is eligible for adjustment to permanent resident status. The twist is that Wassily’s asylum status was terminated in 2004 following his conviction of a crime. The U.S. Court of Appeals for the 2nd Circuit ruled that “granted asylum” must mean “presently be granted asylum” and so it does not encompass applicants whose asylum status is later terminated. The solicitor general agrees, contending that a “common-sense understanding” of the statute must mean that a person who was once granted asylum status which was later terminated cannot take advantage of that prior status. In opposition, Wassily takes the textual position that the unqualified statutory phrase “any alien granted asylum” describes him, and the statute says nothing about a later revocation.

One might cynically guess how this case will come out, but that is not what interests me most. Instead, note how the textualist arguments flip between Guerrero and Wassily. The government seeks a simple plain meaning result for “previously unavailable” in Guerrero but wants a non-textual “common-sense” interpretation in Wassily. There’s nothing wrong with using different arguments in different cases – that’s what law and lawyers are for (smiling emoji). But I sure wish these two cases were being argued on the same day: the combined debate between textualist and commonsense-driven justices and their ideologies likely switching in mere hours might make our heads spin.

Younge v. Fulton Judicial Circuit District Attorney’s Office, Georgia (Nov. 2)

Finally, if you feel like Maxwell (described above) might be a bit of a snoozer, wait until the next argument the same day. I wouldn't include Jasmine Younge here at all if she weren't a fired supervisory prosecutor suing her former district attorney office. According to Younge, she was fired about two weeks after telling her boss that she was pregnant. She sued on the basis of pregnancy discrimination, and only months later did the DA’s office invoke a statutory exemption to pregnancy discrimination statutes, something the office had not asserted in its answer to Younge’s complaint or earlier discovery maneuvers. The U.S. Court of Appeals for the 11th Circuit affirmed judgment for the DA’s office on that exception, saying there had been no prejudice to Younge from the DA’s delay in bringing up this affirmative defense. Other circuits have ruled that an affirmative defense simply cannot be raised that late – so we are off to the races.

Rodger Citron writes for this blog that the case “will quicken the pulse of civil procedure afficionados.” I’ll be calmer, listening with only one ear to hear how the DA’s attorney explains how they missed the statutory exemption, as well as wondering whether the number of listeners has gone up or down from the Maxwell argument immediately prior.

Rory Little has been teaching Constitutional and Criminal Law topics at UC Law SF (formerly Hastings) for over 30 years, after 12 years of practice.

#7384. Platform Engineer, Managed Postgres at Supabase

Supabase is the Postgres development platform, built by developers for developers. We provide a complete backend solution including Database, Auth, Storage, Edge Functions, Realtime, and Vector Search. All services are deeply integrated and designed for growth.

We are seeking a Platform Software Engineer with deep experience in distributed systems to help design, build, and maintain core platform services. You will work primarily in TypeScript and Go to deliver reliable, scalable, and secure systems that power Supabase at massive scale.

Design and implement distributed services and APIs that power the Supabase Platform.

Lead projects that improve scalability, reliability, and cost efficiency across existing systems.

Build data-intensive workflows, background jobs, and event-driven pipelines.

Own service SLIs/SLOs and collaborate on incident response and post-incident reviews.

Improve system observability with metrics, logging, tracing, and profiling.

Contribute to our CI/CD and release processes to ship safely and quickly.

Partner with product teams to deliver features end-to-end, from design docs to production.

Write clear design documents, RFCs, and high-quality tests.

Experienced in designing and operating distributed systems, with strong foundations in consistency, fault tolerance, partitioning, consensus, and back pressure.

Proficient in TypeScript and/or Go, ideally with 5+ years building production services in one or both languages (other languages also considered).

Comfortable with cloud infrastructure (AWS preferred) and container orchestration.

Familiar with multi-tenant architectures, API design, and data modelling.

Knowledgeable about networking fundamentals and security best practices.

Experienced with Infrastructure as Code (Pulumi preferred; Terraform/CDK also fine).

Comfortable participating in on-call rotations for large-scale production systems.

Experience with Postgres internals, logical replication, or CDC pipelines.

Experience with service meshes, workload identity, or zero-trust networking.

Background in performance engineering and capacity planning.

Open source contributions in systems, databases, or runtime tooling.

We hire globally. We believe you can do your best work from anywhere. There are no Supabase offices, but we provide a WeWork membership or co-working allowance you can use anywhere in the world.

Every team member receives ESOP (equity ownership) in the company. We want everyone to share in the upside of what we’re building together.

Use this budget to set up your ideal work environment—laptop, monitor, headphones, or whatever helps you do your best work.

Supabase covers 100% of health insurance for employees and 80% for dependents, wherever you are. Your wellbeing and your family’s health are important to us.

Once a year, the entire company gathers in a new city for a week of connection, collaboration, and fun. It’s a highlight of our year.

We operate asynchronously and trust you to manage your own time. You know what needs to be done and when.

Every team member receives an annual education allowance to spend on learning—courses, books, conferences, or anything that supports your growth.

Supabase was born-remote and open-source-first. We believe our globally distributed team is our secret weapon in building tools developers love.

Over $1B raised (including our $500M Series F)

We move fast, build in public, and use what we ship. If it’s in your project, we probably use it in ours too. We believe deeply in the open-source ecosystem and strive to support—not replace—existing tools and communities.

New remote jobs delivered to your inbox, every week.

Location independence is the future of work. It serves companies with best talent from around the globe. And benefits employees with a greater work life balance and the ability to work in their pyjamas.- Nithur, founder.

#7383. Trump administration’s social media posts ahead of elections criticized for being inflammatory

Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins posted Saturday on the social platform X a photo of the Black man standing in front of stacks of what appear to be U.S. currency with the headline, SNAP FRAUDSTER.

The Trump administration’s online accounts are circulating images of a pumpkin carved with a sombrero design and a fake Halloween-themed background around a Black man apparently accused of food assistance fraud, in social media posts slammed by critics as inflammatory rhetoric.

Only days before the midterm elections, the posts coincide with the government’s sweeping campaign to show its aggressive immigration enforcement, and highlight efforts to crack down on fraud to save taxpayers money when rising healthcare costs and other economic stressors have made affordability a top voter concern.

Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins posted Saturday on the social platform X a photo of the Black man standing in front of stacks of what appear to be U.S. currency with the headline, SNAP FRAUDSTER, an apparent reference to the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, formerly known as food stamps.

He is holding aloft what appears to be a bill set aflame.

“Some costumes come with a price tag. This one comes with a prison sentence,” it says to the backdrop of fake Spirit Halloween costume packaging.

Another photo posted by the White House on X on Thursday showed a pumpkin with the shape of a sombrero carved across it and the words “Spooky szn is here.”

The post by Rollins, who was nominated by Trump to serve as the U.S. Secretary of Agriculture in November 2024, appears to be taken from an Instagram post from September 2025 by an account under the name Shawty Dred.

Earlier this month, Mercedes Reshard New, identified by the Justice Department as a social media personality also known as “Shawty Dred,” was arrested on federal charges for fraudulently obtaining more than $4 million in Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program benefits in Georgia.

It’s not the first time the White House has been accused of posting inflammatory images on official government social media accounts.

Just over a year ago during the government shutdown, the White House revived a deepfake video posted by Trump of House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries in a fake mustache and sombrero to accuse the Democrats of acting on behalf of illegal immigrants instead of U.S. citizens. Jeffries described the meme as bigoted. They played it on repeat in the White House briefing room, though Vice President JD Vance promised that the “sombrero memes will stop” when Democrats agreed to end the shutdown.

The NAACP did not respond to an email seeking comment, nor did the White House or Rollins.

The Trump administration in recent weeks has ratcheted up its anti-immigrant rhetoric and accusations of fraud, including against U.S. Rep. Ilhan Omar, whose Washington, D.C., home was searched by federal agents earlier this month. Federal authorities are investigating potential fraud in her family’s immigration paperwork. Omar, who was born in Somalia, is a naturalized U.S. citizen.

It also has taken a series of punitive steps linked to allegations of fraud in mostly Democratic-led states, including California and Minnesota whose governors accused the federal government of targeting their states for political reasons.

Federal prosecutors said in a news release Oct. 21 that the influencer, New, controlled more than 350 fraudulent SNAP accounts under stolen identities between January 2020 and July 2026. He allegedly applied for his company, Shawty Dred LLC, to become an authorized SNAP retailer and used EBT debit cards to extract about $4 million from the accounts.

New’s Instagram account, which has more than two million followers, has flaunted his extravagant lifestyle, federal prosecutors said. Posts depict him flying on private jets, posing with Rolls-Royce vehicles in front of his “super mansion,” and handling massive stacks of cash.

“Instead of this money feeding families in need, New, the social media personality known as ‘Shawty Dred,’ allegedly used the cash to bankroll a life of luxury,” Special Agent in Charge of FBI Atlanta Marlo Graham said in the release.

New was indicted by a federal grand jury Oct. 7 on dozens of counts of mail fraud and aggravated identity theft, and one count each of SNAP fraud and illegal transactions with access devices. He was arrested Oct. 13 and remains in federal custody.

According to Fulton County jail records, New has been arrested multiple times on suspicion of crimes including identity theft, insurance fraud, financial transaction card fraud, forgery and simple assault.

A federal defender listed in court records as representing New, Joseph Austin, did not return a phone message.

#7382. Rivals race to rescue Weil Gotshal lawyers as firm heads toward closure

Several leading law firms are looking to take on junior lawyers and trainees from Weil, Gotshal & Manges after its management committee recommended an orderly wind-down of the firm’s global operations. (Photo from Shutterstock)

Several leading law firms are looking to take on junior lawyers and trainees from Weil, Gotshal & Manges after its management committee recommended an orderly wind-down of the firm’s global operations.

Law.com reported Thursday that Sullivan & Cromwell and Paul, Weiss, Rifkind, Wharton & Garrison are speaking with Weil Gotshal’s associates and trainees, and that other firms—including DLA Piper, Simpson Thacher & Bartlett and Latham & Watkins—have varying degrees of interest and engagement. According to Law.com, Weil Gotshal is working to find employment for as many people as possible.

Law.com further reported that priorities differ among the suitors. One source said Sullivan & Cromwell is currently favoring associates over partners, while another said Paul Weiss has already brought on several Weil Gotshal partners and is still courting junior lawyers. Meanwhile, another source told Law.com that some firms are offering places to prospective trainees who were due to join Weil Gotshal in September.

The wind-down still needs formal approval, with a partnership vote expected this week. Weil Gotshal’s leaders said the recommendation followed a thorough review of alternatives, and sources said partners have begun telling clients that the firm cannot continue. According to Law.com, the firms named were approached for comment.

#7381. Rankings

Ranking schools is a tricky business. Not all rankings are helpful.

I donât usually pay a lot of attention to press releases, but my eye was caught the other day by one with this headline: âStanford Law School delivers top-five financial return for future lawyers, study reveals.â

Why do I care who placed fifth? Was this an announcement from Stanford, patting itself on the back?

Instead it turned out to be a release touting a âa new study carried out by legal research company Studicata.â

Legal research company? Well, not exactly. If you check out Studicataâs website, you find that itâs actually a law study aid site. Thereâs no mention of this new study, thereâs no link to a full study in the press release, and Iâm way too lazy to call someone for an explanation.

Anyway, what Iâm interested in is the concept of the value of a law school. Assuming you have the credentials to get in, how do you choose your school? Does a study like this help?

(Side note: I think the explanation for the Stanford headline is that the release was sent to me, a person in California. But I donât know.)

Iâve always thought there was an element of self-fulfilling prophecy to school rankings. Is a school highly ranked because its educational programs are the best or is it because it gets the best students?

The Studicata rankings take a different tack: return on investment. Hereâs the chart from the press release:

Youâre at the top of the rankings if, based on the median income of graduates and the median amount of student debt, it takes you the least amount of time to pay back the debt.

The release claims the study rankings are based âon the financial return it offers degree holders.â Letâs check this out.

Harvard and Northwestern are at the top of list. Not terribly surprising. But check out number three: Antonin Scalia Law School.

Scalia grads make less money than anyone else in the top 10 but they also have the least amount of debt. So they can repay the debt in .6 years.

Number 4 in the rankings is the University of Pennsylvania, where grads supposedly earn more than twice as much as Scalia grads and repay their debt in .62 years.

Can you see the problem? Those Penn grads will be making $302K (and probably more) while the Scalias are making $135K for years and years.

Iâm not sure this study is a good advertisement for a study aid company.

I should probably point out the other problem with rankings â those annoying kids who want to go into low-paying public service or charitable work. Theyâre screwing up the earnings numbers for their law schools!

Maybe we need a school ranking for churning out lawyers who do good things for society.

Announcement . âThis is the most exciting time in history to be a lawyer.â

Congratulations, lawyers! I assume all of you are dancing in the streets, or at least cracking a smile.

How do I know this? Itâs part of an online video announcement by a company called Legora reporting it just raised â$550 million Series E at $8.8 billion valuation to accelerate growth.â

If you havenât heard of it, Legora is a company that sells AI legal software to law firms. As far as I can tell, the software can do practically anything and, as depicted in the video, a lawyer can go hiking and just check in to see what the AI did.

Pre-election pledge. Despite what you may have heard, I will not be running for president in 2028. You may rest assured that my full attention will be on column writing.
