#7379. Justices to debate when an established rule is “previously unavailable” in habeas case

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

The Supreme Court will hear oral argument on Nov. 4 in Guerrero v. Johnson, a case about the limited circumstances in which a state prisoner can return to federal court for a second round of post-conviction review.

But let’s back up a bit: If inmates want to challenge the grounds for their detention, they must typically bring a habeas claim. The Antiterrorism and Effective Death Penalty Act of 1996, seeking to curb the number of such petitions, made it significantly more difficult to bring successive applications. Specifically, under 28 U.S.C. § 2244(b)(2) of AEDPA, a new claim in a second federal habeas petition is barred unless it falls under one of two exceptions. The first is when such a claim “relies on a new rule of constitutional law, made retroactive to cases on collateral review by the Supreme Court, that was previously unavailable.” The second exception covers claims based on “the facts underlying the [initial] claim,” but only if those facts would show “by clear and convincing evidence that, but for constitutional error, no reasonable factfinder would have found the applicant guilty of the underlying offense.”

Texas inmate Dexter Johnson brought his claim under the first exception, contending that he cannot be put to death based on the court’s 2002 ruling in Atkins v. Virginia, which held that executing people with intellectual disabilities violates the Eighth Amendment’s ban on cruel and unusual punishment. Johnson did not present the Atkins claim in his initial petitions but, after qualifying as intellectually disabled under revised diagnostic standards, raised this in a subsequent petition. The question before the justices is whether Johnson’s Atkins claim was “previously unavailable” to him.

In 2007, Johnson was convicted of capital murder and sentenced to death in Texas for his role in the double murder of 23-year-old Maria Aparece and 17-year-old Huy Ngo. At trial, a defense expert testified that Johnson’s IQ was between 74 and 88 and he “did not have obvious deficits” with regard to “personal independence and social responsibility when compared to other people of similar age and sociocultural background.” Under the diagnostic standards in place at that time, the expert concluded that Johnson was not intellectually disabled. (Johnson did not raise an Atkins claim in his initial habeas petitions but invoked Atkins in those petitions to argue – unsuccessfully – that its protections should extend to people with mental illness.)

In May 2013, while Johnson’s federal petition was pending, the American Psychiatric Association published the fifth edition of its diagnostic manual, known as the DSM-5, which Texas’ highest criminal court adopted in 2018. The new edition de-emphasized IQ cutoffs and recognized that someone whose score is above 70 may still be intellectually disabled. In April 2019, an expert gave Johnson an IQ test on which he scored 70, and a second expert agreed that Johnson met the DSM-5’s criteria for intellectual disability.

Johnson filed a successive habeas application in the district court, in which he claimed that he could not be executed under Atkins. After an evidentiary hearing, the trial court determined that Johnson’s Atkins claim was previously unavailable and consequently stayed his execution. The state appealed to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 5th Circuit, which in July 2025 affirmed the district court’s decision. The full 5th Circuit then declined to rehear the case by a vote of 9-7. In February, the state asked the Supreme Court to weigh in, which the Supreme Court agreed in June to do.

In its brief, the Office of the Texas Attorney General maintains that “Johnson’s Atkins claim does not rely on a change in the law.” Instead, it emphasizes, Atkins was decided well before Johnson filed his initial habeas application, and “before Johnson even committed the capital murder for which he was sentenced to death.” Nor, according to the Texas AG’s office, would permitting Johnson to bring such a claim serve the purpose of enabling successive petitions, which is to allow for new evidence as to whether a person is “guilty of the underlying offense.”

The state further presses the point that no “rule” was previously unavailable here. “An object—or a rule—can be available even when it is not needed or useful. A carpenter, for example, likely has a hammer ‘available,’ even when working on a task for which a hammer would not be necessary or useful,” the state writes. The publication of the DSM-5 may have allowed Johnson to discover a new factual predicate, according to the state, but it does not change the availability of any rule. Instead, the 5th Circuit’s approach “erases the line Congress drew between new law and new facts and effectively writes § 2244(b)(2)(B)’s limitations out of the statute.”

Johnson’s attorneys counter that something is “available” only if it is “capable of being used by a person, for a purpose”; prior to the publication of the DSM-5, no such usage was possible. “No one would say the hammer was available to the carpenter if it were locked in a toolbox he couldn’t open,” Johnson’s team writes. “Mr. Johnson did not change; his intellectual and adaptive characteristics are the same as always. What changed was the framework that made Atkins capable of protecting him. Atkins was not available to him before; now it is.” Nor, contrary to the AG’s claim otherwise, Johnson’s lawyers argue, would this open the “floodgates” to many other such challenges. Because very few rules are retroactive, such issues rarely arise.

Perhaps unsurprisingly given its stance on capital punishment, the Trump administration filed a “friend of the court” brief supporting Texas. Echoing several of the state’s arguments, U.S. Solicitor General D. John Sauer asserts that “[s]tandards promulgated by a board of psychiatrists cannot transform a decision of this Court that predates a prior habeas application into a ‘new’ and ‘previously unavailable’ rule of constitutional law.” Louisiana and 21 other states, also supporting Texas, call the 5th Circuit’s rule “a recipe for eternal Atkins claims and zero finality,” pointing out that a professional association also moved the age by which intellectual disability must appear from 18 to 22 in 2021 – raising the possibility that such age-based claims could also be brought and questioning the possibility that the habeas floodgates would remain closed were the court to agree with Johnson.

On Johnson’s side, the National Association of Criminal Defense Lawyers compares Johnson’s claim to second petitions based on new science about “microscopic hair comparison analysis, arson science, and shaken baby syndrome.” According to the NACDL, “claims of constitutional error grounded in faulty science in a second or successive petition” must be allowed to go forward because “flawed analytical methods may not be debunked until” it is too late.

One final thing worth mentioning: Last term, after hearing argument in Hamm v. Smith, a dispute over how courts should weigh multiple IQ scores in Atkins cases, the justices dismissed the case as improvidently granted (known as a “DIG”) – that is, they decided that it was a mistake to have agreed to hear the case in the first place and did not resolve it. At the end of his brief, Johnson asks the court to do the same in his case on the ground that the state has continually changed its arguments. Whatever the merits of Johnson’s position on that front, it seems unlikely the court will DIG two Atkins cases in successive terms.

The decision in Guerrero v. Johnson is expected by late June or early July.

Nora is an editorial assistant at SCOTUSblog, based in Washington, D.C.

Zach is the executive editor of SCOTUSblog.

#7376. A surge in cases on religion and schools

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

Welcome to a new month and a new argument session. The justices will hear argument in seven cases over the next nine days.

Today, the justices will hear argument in two cases: Maxwell v. Dinis, on a federal inmate’s ability to use a habeas statute, 28 U.S.C. § 2241, to contest the Federal Bureau of Prisons’ refusal to accelerate his transfer to a halfway house or home confinement; and Younge v. Fulton Judicial Circuit District Attorney’s Office, Georgia, on whether an affirmative defense may be asserted as a basis for summary judgment if not presented earlier in a pleading.

On Tuesday, the justices will hear argument in St. Mary Catholic Parish v. Roy, a religious discrimination challenge brought by Catholic preschools in Colorado over the state’s requirement that all schools participating in its universal preschool program must admit everyone – including LGBTQ children and children with LGBTQ parents.

On Oct. 21, the Trump administration asked the justices to allow it to resume construction of its border wall in the Big Bend region of southwestern Texas. The request is now fully briefed, and the court’s decision could come at any time.

#7372. Justice Kagan: firing point blank in Smith & Wesson v. Estados Unidos de Mexico

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

In the 1983 movie A Christmas Story, Ralphie’s teacher, Miss Shields, assigns her students the task of writing “a theme.” The fourth-grade class at Warren G. Harding Elementary school erupts in groans; after all, writing is hard work.

But Ralphie sees it as an opportunity to make his case for a Red Ryder BB gun, “the Holy Grail of Christmas gifts.” And as the words “pour[] forth from [his] penny pencil with feverish fluidity,” he gets right to the point: “What I want for Christmas is a Red Ryder BB gun with a compass in the stock and this thing that tells time.”

Doubtless, Miss Shields had admonished her students – like our teachers admonished us – that each paragraph of a theme must begin with a thesis (or topic) sentence. But is that always right? Pay attention to skilled writers, and you’ll discover that – like many things – it depends.

Skilled writers do locate a paragraph’s issue (topic) and its point (thesis) where readers expect to encounter them. But readers have different expectations about where that should be. Sometimes readers expect the issue and the point in the first sentence, but sometimes they expect them to be separated. Readers change their expectations depending on what type of paragraph they are reading. And sometimes a paragraph has no point at all.

Justice Elena Kagan shows how this works. She never makes a reader hunt for her point, even though she might locate that point in different places for different types of paragraphs.

Take Smith & Wesson v. Estados Unidos de Mexico as one of many potential examples. In Smith & Wesson, the court held that Mexico had failed to plead its way around a federal statute barring claims against gun manufacturers. Starting with meat-and-potatoes paragraphs, Kagan does exactly what Miss Shields might insist upon. She locates both the issue and the point of the paragraph right at the beginning, then uses the rest of the paragraph to prove her point.

In Section I.A. of the opinion, for example, Kagan sets out the requirements of the statute being interpreted, the Protection of Lawful Commerce in Arms Act. Taking only the first sentence of each paragraph, readers learn exactly how the statute works with zero effort. We read:

“[The PLCAA] bars cer­tain lawsuits against manufacturers and sellers of fire­arms.”

“But PLCAA’s general bar on those suits has an exception, usually called the predicate exception, relevant here.”

“Notably here, the predicate violation PLCAA demands may come from aiding and abetting someone else’s firearms offense.”

After each thesis, Kagan deploys the PLCAA’s language to prove that she’s right. For example, to prove that the PLCAA “bars certain lawsuits,” she quotes language providing that a “qualified civil liability action . . . may not be brought in any Federal or State court.” But again, before she shoves the reader’s nose into the language, she first tells us the point of it all.

In adopting this structure, Kagan is giving English readers what they expect. In his book “The Sense of Structure,” George Gopen calls these meat-and-potatoes paragraphs “medial paragraphs.” Here, in the middle of an exposition, “readers tend to appreciate being given the point up front.” Fail to put the point up front and one risks “having the reader disappear before the point actually arrives.” You run an especially grave risk if you are writing for busy legal readers – an audience that’s typically looking for a reason to stop reading.

But in other types of paragraphs, Kagan does not front-load a traditional thesis sentence, and she’s right there too. Consider the way Kagan writes introductions and narrative paragraphs.

In her Smith & Wesson introduction, Kagan reveals the issue or the topic in the first sentence, but she only gives the point or thesis in the last sentence. In the first sentence, we read that Mexico has sued American gun manufacturers – what the case is about. But before we can understand the court’s holding – the point – we need to learn some context. We need a sketch of what the law requires. So Kagan next sets out the statutory requirement: Mexico must plead that the gun manufacturers aided and abetted unlawful sales to the cartels. Only now, at the end of the paragraph, do we know enough to understand the point: Mexico did not plausibly plead aiding and abetting.

Again, according to Gopen, Kagan is satisfying her readers’ “remarkably fixed expectation that the point of an opening paragraph will arrive at the end.” We readers don’t want to be punched in the face with an answer before we know enough to understand it. Writers should make us “comfortable with the surroundings before we have to go to work.”

Narrative paragraphs involve yet another difference: readers don’t expect a traditional thesis in a passage that feels like “once upon a time.” Gopen notes, “Not all paragraphs were born to make a point.” Sometimes writers write “just to tell a story, to put some facts on the table.”

In her narrative paragraphs, Kagan sometimes just tells the story, and sometimes she fires a thesis point blank:

In the end, your old English teacher was mostly right. Ordinary, meat-and-potatoes paragraphs ought to have a sentence in which the issue and the point are together at the beginning of the paragraph. But specialized paragraphs might be different. So, before you start line-editing the sentences of a draft, employ a process to evaluate the strength of your paragraphs.

For your meat-and-potatoes paragraphs, prefer paragraphs that state the point and then prove it. Be on the lookout for paragraphs that write to a conclusion rather than stating it up front. To diagnose these paragraphs, try to create a reverse outline by copying the first sentence (sometimes two) into a different document. Ask yourself whether the argument makes sense with only those sentences. It will if the issue and point are stated up front.

In your statement of facts, mark which paragraphs have a thesis and which don’t. Know that you have a choice about when to include one, and make that choice.

Finally, give special attention to paragraphs that begin a text or a new section. Take the reader from the issue, through the necessary context, and then conclude with the point.

Why so much care? Because hitting the wrong target can be dangerous; you’ll shoot your eye out. A legal reader won’t just stand by trying to guess where the next round is being aimed.

Professor Gray teaches legal writing courses for first-year and advanced students at Duke Law.

Recommended Citation: Kendall Gray, Justice Kagan: firing point blank in Smith & Wesson v. Estados Unidos de Mexico, SCOTUSblog (Nov. 2, 2026, 10:00 AM), https://www.scotusblog.com/2026/11/justice-kagan-firing-point-blank-in-smith-wesson-v-estados-unidos-de-mexico/

#7370. Tatari Gives CTV Ad Matching The Max Treatment

The recent surge in AI tools means that it’s easier than ever for advertisers to generate multiple versions of an ad for different audiences, but increased versioning is moot if the right ads aren’t reaching the right people. The challenge, of course, is figuring out the best ad for a given person.

CTV ad platform Tatari believes that accurate targeting relies on a wide scope of data and inventory, as well as machine learning that’s constantly training on the latest data.

On Thursday, it announced the launch of Tatari Max, an optimization engine that sits at the ad server level to help brands and publishers decide which TV ads to serve to what audience.

Although Tatari Max uses AI optimization to determine the most relevant ad placements for a client, Tatari CEO and Co-Founder Philip Inghelbrecht is adamant that the product is a far cry from agentic AI.

While agentic AI relies on a series of “if, then” rules and automates existing processes, machine learning (which is what Tatari Max relies on) evolves over time as new data emerges, Inghelbrecht said.

By looking at signals, including device IDs, shopping behavior and demographic information, Tatari Max can determine which people – and types of people – respond best to specific ads.

It also calculates what it calls an “affinity score,” which measures “the extent to which an impression is best fit for a particular brand,” based on previous viewers’ engagement, said Inghelbrecht.

Activewear brand Rhoback, an early tester of Tatari Max, hopes the self-learning element of the tool will help it determine which creatives are most relevant to which viewers, said Caroline Nemceff, senior digital marketing analyst at Rhoback.

Rhoback was initially founded as a men’s clothing brand, but this year it’s been focused on expanding its women’s line as well as its collegiate sportswear. Since those sects of the brand are newer, Rhoback has less data on how potential customers will respond to the ads. TV mainly serves as an “awareness play” for the brand to find new customers, said Nemceff, and it’s optimistic that Tatari Max will help it “learn who the correct user is” for a given piece of creative.

It’s too soon to see demographic results on exactly what kinds of people are responding to which creatives, Nemceff said, but early results are promising.

Over a one-month period of testing an ad on Hulu marketing a new women’s activewear collection, Rhoback saw a 32% increase in purchases and a 10% increase in site visits.

Soon after implementing Tatari Max, Rhoback had to pull back on streaming spend and pause the tests (due to external factors) – but, thanks to strong performance results from that early testing, said Nemceff, it plans to return to using Tatari Max later this year. “We are planning to test Max again on ESPN using our collegiate creative, and expand into Hulu during [Black Friday and Cyber Monday] with our sale creative,” she added.

“It’s only going to get better,” she said, “because you’re feeding it more data and more data points.”

Tatari Max is built on Upstream, Tatari’s supply-side stack that integrates with publishers at the ad server level.

Some similar products, like Meta’s Advantage Plus and Google’s Performance Max, only connect to the company’s own inventory. Upstream, on the other hand, plugs into several premium TV publishers, including Paramount, Peacock and Disney, so clients can see all accessible inventory across the TV world.

Plus, Inghelbrecht said, Upstream isn’t just limited to programmatic inventory. Since it sits at the ad server level, it can see data on inventory that’s only available as direct buys as well. Since the AI is receiving so much data, it has more to learn from and can improve rapidly.

The wealth of data is a draw for captioning and live transcription app Rylo, which started working with Tatari about two months ago and began testing Tatari Max at the same time.

Tatari has been more effective for Rylo than other CTV ad platforms, said Annica Lin, the app’s VP of growth, adding that since adopting Tatari’s tech, she’s seen an increase in customers saying that they discovered the brand on TV.

Most of Rylo’s users are older individuals, since the app is specifically aimed at people who are deaf or hard of hearing.

The problem with targeting older folks directly, though, is that many of them “are not tech-savvy,” said Lin. Tatari Max, which was doing household targeting, found that the people who actually respond best to Rylo’s ads are often younger household members, like the older individuals’ adult children or caretakers.

“They are the people who actually [are] influenced and then help their parents to download the app,” said Lin.

Tatari Max was able to determine that the most effective ads among that younger demographic were testimonials, in which hard of hearing individuals describe their experience with Rylo. Personal testimony emphasizes the resources that are available to people who are hard of hearing, and often leads to these other household viewers helping older relatives download the app.

Now, said Lin, Rylo thinks more about “how to communicate with the caretaker or the kids,” rather than exclusively targeting potential app users themselves.

#7369. DoorDash Acquires Instacart As Consolidation Comes For Mobility Media

DoorDash on Thursday confirmed the rumors and announced its intention to acquire Instacart at a $17 billion valuation.

The deal is a logical one for a variety of reasons.

The two fit into the same category of mobile app-based, last-mile-fulfillment specialists that have shoehorned their way into the brick-and-mortar shopping habits.

These companies fall into a sort of “mobility” sub-category of retail media, too. While DoorDash doesn’t regularly break out ad revenue, it disclosed a year ago that it had surpassed $1 billion in such revenue in 2024. Instacart does discloses advertising revenue, and announced it earned it more than $300 million in Q3 this year. So these are billion-dollar ad businesses.

And Instacart and DoorDash are neatly incremental to each other. At least that’s the framing from the companies’ joint press release on the deal.

“Families turn to Instacart for the big weekly shop and to DoorDash for meals and nearly anything else they need from their neighborhood in under an hour,” per the release.

In other words, the two may seem to have competitive friction, since they work with many of the same convenience, pharmacy, grocery, clothing and apparel chains. But they exist as part of different types of shopping habits and convert different types of purchases, even if it’s the same product from the same store. Imagine an impulse-buy snack and soda order and the same items in a grocery cart.

And this somewhat anecdotal hypothesis is borne out by their respective data. DoorDash reported in its quarterly earnings today (busy day!) that it processed 993 million total orders in Q3. It earned $33.9 billion on those orders.

Instacart had only 91.4 million total sales, per its quarterly earnings report (also today, can you imagine?). And it earned $10.5 billion.

Instacart converts a tenth as many checkouts, but its gross marketplace sales are a third the size of DoorDash. Thus proving, at least, that its average order size is much larger.

When considering the timing of this proposed acquisition, one cannot ignore the politics of antitrust and acquisition, and of this moment.

DoorDash has expanded its lobbying presence in recent years and has ingratiated itself with the Trump administration. Perhaps you caught this DoorDash-White House photo op. The delivery firm was a Trump inauguration donor, too, but it has been opposed by some prominent Democrats with stances on labor policy and litigation.

The Biden administration would perhaps have taken a sharp look at this merger as a potential antitrust violation. Especially considering the spree of mobile marketplaces DoorDash has acquired, including Wolt (in Finland), Deliveroo (the UK) and SevenRooms (a marketing platform for restaurants, hotels and venues).

Compare what I predict will be the breezy way this DoorDash-Instacart deal goes through to the nightmarish undoing of the proposed merger between Kroger and Albertsons, which was opposed by the Biden-era DOJ. The two grocery chains are now embroiled in a massive lawsuit themselves over who caused the deal to crash and burn.

If Kroger and Albertsons had waited – and, frankly, paid some millions of dollars in lobbying funds to a President Trump-approved recipient – that deal might have skated by without a fuss.

Which is all to say, don’t expect the deal-making to stop. There are still valuable independent mobility-and-advertising businesses like Lyft, Gopuff (which white labels its own ad sales through DoorDash, by the way) or even GSTV (it sells ads on gas pump screens).

It’s fall, and M&A is in the air. Two acquisitions happened this week: Stagwell bought Freestar, and DoorDash bought Instacart.

#7365. Unrealized AI Investments Drag Amazon’s Income, But AWS And Ads Are Still Growing

Amazon’s third-quarter earnings missed the mark – but that isn’t how CEO Andy Jassy sees it.

“Our operating margins have long been strong on our core offering,” Jassy told investors during Amazon’s Q3 earnings call on Thursday, adding that they’re “rapidly improving on the AI side, too.”

Still, it’s hard to argue with the numbers: Amazon’s net income decreased to $20.7 billion from $21.2 billion last Q3.

Amazon’s Q3 2025 numbers look better because of $9.5 billion in pre-tax gains that the company accrued last year from its investments in AI startup Anthropic, according to Amazon’s earnings report. Without a similar windfall this year, the difference is stark.

But, apparently, that explanation wasn’t enough to sway investors. Amazon stock dropped 7% in after-hours trading on Thursday.

Unsurprisingly, investors expect a company’s payout from AI investments to keep growing over time, and aren’t loving what they’re seeing. Still, Amazon certainly hasn’t slowed down its activity in this department. It reported cash flow of negative $42.4 billion over the past 12 months, compared to a positive cash flow of $14.8 billion last year.

Even if the comparison to last year’s AI gains isn’t great, AI is still the driving force behind nearly all of Amazon’s revenue increases this year.

For instance, AWS – which provides AI and cloud computing infrastructure – grew 39.3% year over year, its fastest growth rate in nearly five years.

AWS could grow into “a trillion-dollar revenue business in the next five to 10 years,” Jassy said, due to the surge in businesses running their core workloads on it.

As it becomes more focused on developing AI infrastructure, Amazon hasn’t lost sight of its ads business – though, of course, that’s built on AI now, too.

Amazon Ads revenue was up 12% year-over-year, totaling $19.6 billion.

Double-digit ad revenue growth is nothing to sneeze at. But the Q3 numbers lagged behind the rest of the year, with Amazon Ads reporting 22% growth in Q1 and 26% in Q2.

Jassy chalked up Q3’s slower growth to Amazon rescheduling Prime Day from Q3 to Q2. He also pointed to the fact that Q3 didn’t include any NBA games on Amazon Prime Video.

To spur future growth, Amazon is fleshing out its ads business with new agentic AI features, including Amazon Ads Agent (a merging of the Amazon Ads console and Amazon DSP), which was launched in September. The new platform allows advertisers to launch full-funnel campaigns and continually optimizes them once they’re live.

But while agentic AI is all the rage on the advertiser side, it hasn’t been fully embraced by the consumer side just yet.

“The natural question is whether agentic shopping from external horizontal agents is meaningfully impacting Amazon ads,” Jassy said, “and the answer is no.”

Agentic shopping is “still not great,” he added, and isn’t meaningfully more convenient than humans completing one-click orders themselves.

Still, Jassy tacitly acknowledged that agentic shopping is likely to take root down the line. “Few customers are doing much shopping this way yet,” he said – “yet” being the key word.

#7361. Reddit Is Going Login Only. Blame Google

Reddit is getting ready to shift to a login-only experience, CEO and Co-Founder Steve Huffman told investors on the company’s Q3 earnings call on Thursday.

Starting in Q4, Reddit will test logged-in-only mode in “select markets outside the US,” Huffman said, calling it the first step toward bringing Reddit in line with how every other social media platform operates.

Logged-in users already account for more than 80% of Reddit’s monetization, Huffman said, so going logged-in only doubles down on that strength.

But making users sign in to read Reddit isn’t just about driving engagement, he said. It also strengthens ad targeting and first-party data collection, and it protects Reddit’s content from being scraped by AI crawlers.

Plus, it puts Reddit on firmer footing for complying with global regulation, Huffman said, alluding to the worldwide push for tighter age verification on social media.

The shift is also a response to the internet-wide drop in search traffic, which has largely been attributed to the rise of AI search. Google is one of the biggest culprits, increasingly pushing searchers to AI Overviews and its Gemini chatbot.

In October, Reddit’s search traffic dropped by 1 million referrals per week, Huffman said.

Google’s search algorithm changes this year also appear to have downranked machine-translated content, Huffman noted. Reddit has been touting AI translation as a way to reach more users internationally, where its brand is less well-known than in the US and growth potential is greatest. That strategy has quickly become a liability thanks to Google.

But in the US, at least, “Reddit” still ranks among the most-searched terms on Google, Huffman said. That shows user demand for Reddit content hasn’t changed; Google is just sending less of that traffic to Reddit.

Meanwhile, “Google is crawling us as hard as ever,” Huffman said, so Google AI’s demand for Reddit’s content hasn’t changed either.

However, he said, “The reality is, AI Mode does not drive traffic, not for us and not for anybody, as far as I know. And so that’s just a fundamental shift in how Google works. It used to be a traffic driver. Now it’s not.”

But search traffic isn’t Reddit’s main priority, Huffman said.

Going forward, Reddit is focused on building and retaining its logged-in user base, he said, the goal being to “make Reddit a direct daily habit for more people.”

Part of that strategy is pushing users to download the Reddit app, where there’s potential for deeper engagement. In fact, the percentage of new app users who return to Reddit in the first week after downloading its app increased by double digits in Q3 compared to Q2, and by 50% YOY.

Ironically, Google’s attempts to keep users locked into its search ecosystem actually help Reddit’s strategy of getting more users to come to its platform directly, Huffman said. Users are still searching for Reddit, but Google doesn’t want to send them there, which is training them to go straight to Reddit instead.

Despite its referral traffic woes, Reddit’s ad business continues to grow rapidly.

Q3 revenue was up 53% year over year, a growth rate few companies are achieving these days, Huffman noted.

Ad revenue, meanwhile, grew 54% YOY in Q3 to $847 million, thanks to growth in both impressions and pricing, said Jen Wong, Reddit’s chief operating officer.

Reddit joined the S&P 500 in Q3, which Huffman attributed to its strong growth since going public in 2024.

Reddit also passed $3 billion in revenue over the past 12 months, he said, and is now targeting $5 billion in annual revenue.

And ad performance is also up, Wong said. Click volume grew 50% YOY and conversion volume tripled, helping lower-funnel performance revenue (shopping and app-install campaigns) grow more than 95%.

Part of what’s driving performance is Reddit’s investment in AI ad optimization, Wong said. Its machine learning platform, Reddit Max, entered public beta in Q3, and a new Max feature lets advertisers manage multiple product lines or creative themes within a single campaign.

Reddit is also seeing strong adoption among mid-market advertisers, a segment that grew 50% YOY.

Video-based campaign revenue from upper-funnel advertisers doubled in Q3, and Reddit also introduced a new 15-second engaged video view objective in public beta to “help advertisers optimize for people more likely to engage with longer-form video,” Wong said.

For lower-funnel advertisers, Reddit improved its shopping campaign platform, which can now support up to 20 million products.

For B2B brands, Reddit introduced “in-market audience targeting tools,” Wong said, which have improved “average cost per action” by 7% compared to other first-party targeting options.

On the ad tech side, Wong said revenue from advertisers using Reddit’s ads API grew 45% compared to Q2. She also announced Reddit’s first third-party API integration for Max campaign management, with ad optimization platform Smartly.

Wong also pointed to measurement integrations with Innovid and Skai, which Reddit announced in August, and touted a beta integration with HubSpot.

On top of that, she highlighted Reddit’s Shopify integration for lower-funnel campaigns, which became generally available in May. Ethnotek, a backpack and accessories brand, saw a 4x improvement in ROAS and a 40% improvement in CPA from testing it, she said.

All of these ad stack improvements contributed to a 36% increase in average revenue per user (ARPU) to $6.87.

Next up: seeing how much higher ARPU can climb with a larger logged-in user base.

#7356. ‘E’ For ‘Exactly The Same As Always’; Google’s Very Bad Day On Wall Street

An academic study co-authored by researchers at Indiana University and New Jersey Institute of Technology, working with ad tech research firms Adalytics and DeepSee.io, raises serious concerns about the misuse of extended identifiers (EIDs) in programmatic advertising.

EIDs are persistent user identifiers, such as hashed email addresses, that are used to link and track users across different domains and devices.

The study found that ad tech companies were attaching real human tracking data to automated internet bots, falsely making it look like real people were visiting certain sites. In some instances, they even bundled multiple different human IDs into a single bot session or advertising bid.

Zeta Global’s LiveIntent was singled out for particularly brazen behavior, as per Jack Neff’s writeup on the study. Criteo, ID5 and Experian’s Audigent were also observed assigning different EIDs to separate supply paths in multi-SSP auctions.

Flashtalking, however, received a gold star, as it was the only one out of 18 ad tech vendors that was never documented serving human EIDs to bots. The Trade Desk, meanwhile, came close, keeping its hands almost entirely clean.

It’s worth noting that the practice doesn’t qualify as sophisticated invalid traffic under the Media Rating Council’s standards. And, as a spokesperson from the MRC tells Neff, the organization “does not currently audit or accredit any identity solutions/providers nor audience targeting.”

Google may consider itself an AI company these days, but as far as investors are concerned, it’s still mainly an advertising business.

The share price for Google’s parent company Alphabet dropped roughly 13% yesterday after its Q3 earnings call on Wednesday. It was the worst day for Alphabet’s stock since the company went public in 2004, according to The Wall Street Journal.

It was softness in Google’s search ads business that spooked investors, the FT reports.

During the earnings call, an investor pointed out that Google’s search revenue growth had gradually slowed this year. It went from 19% in Q1 to 17% in Q2 and 12% in Q3.

This observation prompted Google’s chief business officer, Philipp Schindler, to confirm that “the strong growth in AI Mode queries had an impact because of the lower monetization we were seeing in AI Mode.”

In other words, Google’s AI search business isn’t just making less money than traditional search; it’s actually dragging down Google’s search revenue. Cue the investor panic.

“In a market worried about AI chatbots cannibalizing [Google’s] key franchise, investors need to see [search] accelerating, not decelerating,” David Wagner at Aptus Capital Advisors tells the FT.

But Google is betting that by cannibalizing one of its strongest revenue lines in the short term, it’ll achieve even greater growth later on – after it loads up AI search with ads, that is.

These days, sports coverage can make or break a media company’s earnings report card.

TelevisaUnivision reported a 14% drop in US revenue during the third quarter, and US advertising revenue in particular tanked 24%. Ruh-roh.

The Spanish-language media giant faced tough competition for viewers and advertisers last quarter, given that its rival Telemundo had snagged Spanish-language US rights to cover the 2026 FIFA World Cup. But it’s not all doom and gloom for TelevisaUnivision, which luckily had airing rights to the tournament in Latin America via its TV network and streaming service, ViX.

TelevisaUnivision credits its LATAM World Cup coverage for a 30% increase in overall subscription and licensing revenue, with Mexico proving to be an especially valuable tailwind. The company’s quarterly revenue rose 51% in the region, and ad revenue spiked 19%.

Those gains somewhat offset steeper losses in the US, with TelevisaUnivision’s overall ad revenue declining by an average of 5% last quarter (a far more palatable number than 24%).

Going forward, company executives told investors that the plan is to continue growing audience reach across linear and streaming platforms – which, predictably, includes expanding its sports portfolio.

WPP’s revenue was down 2.1% in Q3, but WPP Media saw positive growth for the first time in six quarters, at 0.3%. WPP CEO Cindy Rose details how the holdco’s priorities have changed since she took the helm last year. [Adweek]

Health, food and news publishers have suffered the steepest declines in organic search traffic over the past two years – but AI isn’t the only culprit. You can blame search ads, too. [Search Engine Land]

The Trump administration is increasingly using subpoenas to obtain information from Big Tech companies about users who criticize its immigration policies. [WSJ]

#7352. Ghost Audiences Are Haunting CTV Measurement

Streaming is officially an advertising business. According to Antenna, nearly half (48%) of all premium subscription video-on-demand (SVOD) accounts in the US were ad-supported in Q1 2026, and 59% of new subscriptions in the quarter were for ad tiers. US ad-supported Premium SVOD subscriptions, meanwhile, hit 110 million by the same quarter, up from 53 million two years prior.

In digital advertising, there is a growing risk of conflating audience size with audience availability. There are now improved ways to think about metrics:

The closer buying moves to the impression, the more costly it becomes to confuse these audiences. Just because a platform’s audience is large doesn’t mean it’s available. And even if it’s available, it isn’t always addressable. The delta between the audience a platform reports on and the audience an advertiser can actually reach is the key gap to close. Consider new viewers who download an app to stream NFL games during the regular season. Samsung Ads recently found that two of every three of these new viewers had “ghosted” the streaming service after the NFL season ended – nearly twice the churn rate of existing users. These ghost audiences remain part of a platform’s reported audience, yet contribute little to campaign-ready inventory. The result is a widening disconnect between reported audience size and the transactable supply advertisers are actually bidding on.

The industry’s next evolution isn’t happening on the demand side – it’s happening closer to the supply. As selling moves closer to the glass, OEMs and SSPs are evolving from distribution partners into intelligence partners, enriching inventory with real-time viewing signals that help determine the value of every impression before it reaches the auction. In that environment, competitive advantage will no longer come from reporting the largest audience. It will come from identifying the best available audience at the exact moment an impression becomes available. The next currency in streaming will be the strongest combination of reach and availability.

#7349. Your Media Plan Might Be Missing Its Best Customers

If you plan media, you’re being asked to find new customers across more screens with fewer partners and to prove that what you’re doing worked. The IAB’s September outlook shows 63% of buyers say acquiring new customers is a top-three goal this year.

But the best media plan is only as good as the data behind it. The limiting factor is often not the sophistication of the targeting tools but what the underlying data can actually reveal. When advertisers rely on the same familiar signals, they risk overlooking valuable audiences that don’t fit their existing definitions.

That’s where carrier data can add a different perspective. By combining insights into mobile app activity with broader patterns of real-world movement, it can uncover connections between consumer behaviors that traditional audience strategies might miss.

Consider a pizza chain trying to acquire new customers. Its media plan might start with people who order from competing pizza restaurants, use pizza delivery apps or exhibit other signals of interest in pizza.

That’s a logical approach to winning market share. But it also assumes that the most valuable prospects are already interested in pizza.

In reality, consumers aren’t always choosing between pizza chains. They’re deciding what type of food they want in the first place. Reaching the right people and understanding what they’re deciding are two different problems.

What happens when you build an audience around that broader decision? Instead of limiting the search to pizza-related signals, marketers can incorporate observed behaviors across restaurant categories, mobile apps and real-world locations. That broader perspective can help identify consumers whose habits and interests make them promising prospects, even if they weren’t included in the original audience definition.

It’s a different way to approach the same marketing objective. Rather than simply refining a model to find more people who fit the presumed target audience, advertisers can use additional evidence to reconsider who belongs in that audience at all.

Advertisers are using T-Mobile carrier data to surface exactly these kinds of audience opportunities.

Take the users of one food delivery app. T-Mobile carrier data shows that this audience is 57% more likely than the national average to also use Gopuff. The audience overindexes on Grubhub and Uber Eats, too. That validates the competitive assumptions most plans start from.

But that same audience is also 45% more likely to be heavy streamers, and overindexes with fantasy sports fans, expectant parents and college students.

Together, these signals suggest an opportunity that a category-focused audience strategy might overlook, such as reaching people during a night in with a show queued up, a game on and dinner handed off to a food delivery app.

That doesn’t mean the data proves these activities are happening together. But it gives advertisers a new hypothesis to explore and potentially new audiences, messages and media placements to test.

A data set that only looks at one category can help find the next pizza order. But looking at data across apps and mobility patterns can reveal a broader range of behaviors and potential new occasions to reach consumers.

The effectiveness of audience modeling depends on the quality and breadth of the signals behind it. Carrier data provides a particularly useful foundation, combining observed app ownership and engagement with patterns of real-world movement and available demographic attributes.

Because consumers carry their phones throughout the day, these signals offer a perspective on behaviors that might otherwise be scattered across different apps, platforms and physical environments. Combining them at the audience level helps advertisers build a more complete understanding of consumer interests and activities without relying on individual-level tracking.

It’s also important to distinguish what’s observed from what’s modeled. Carrier data is observed and deterministic. The scale is modeled.

Platforms such as Blis and Vistar Media use carrier data as a starting point to model and activate audiences across connected TV, audio, mobile and digital out-of-home, including environments where traditional device identifiers aren’t available.

The modeling is only as good as what it starts from, which is why the breadth and quality of observed behavioral signals matter. And while identity still matters, strategies that don’t rely exclusively on any one identifier or platform provide additional resilience as advertising identifiers face continuing restrictions.

For media planners, four questions are worth exploring:

These questions expose a hard truth: A media plan can only be as comprehensive as the view of the consumer it’s built on.

Carrier data is a stronger starting point. Because it draws on observed behavior across apps and location patterns, it can inform more dynamic approaches to reaching customers. With Blis, carrier-informed audiences can be activated across omnichannel media. With Vistar Media, those same audiences can help identify relevant digital out-of-home screens by location, frequency and daypart. This approach can help brands strengthen existing connections and reach new audiences in relevant moments.

Tonight, people across the country will decide what to eat, with plenty of restaurants competing for their attention. Reaching them with a relevant message at the right moment requires more than knowing which restaurants they’ve visited or which apps they use. It requires understanding how their behaviors fit into a broader picture of their interests and habits.

The clearer that picture, the better equipped advertisers are to recognize valuable prospects, including the ones their original audience definitions overlooked.

#7344. Smart Acquisition Or Frankenstack? Stagwell-Freestar And DoorDash-Instacart

It’s fall, and M&A is in the air. Two acquisitions happened this week: Stagwell bought Freestar, and DoorDash agreed to buy Instacart.

Here at AdExchanger, we’re always intrigued by the rationale for acquisitions – from the ones that feel like yin meeting yang to the ones that feel more like stitching together a Frankenstack. (Had to get a spooky reference in!)

In the first half of the podcast, we discuss Stagwell buying Freestar. Why would an indie agency want to build a company that helps open web publishers better set up their ad stacks? Our managing editor, Anthony Vargas, who covered the acquisition, talks about the hints the companies dropped, including how Freestar’s 1,000 publisher site connections could support Stagwell’s principal media business. Are we seeing a rehash of GroupM buying ad network 24/7 Real Media – 19 years later?

Then, when retailers merge, could the extremely fragmented retail media space defragment just a bit? At the time of the recording, DoorDash was in advanced talks to buy Instacart – and on Thursday, news dropped that the acquisition was official.

Pending approval, DoorDash Ads and Instacart’s Carrot Ads will likely come together. Carrot Ads also offers a white-labeled retail media business, which recently added Gopuff as a customer. So imagine Russian nesting dolls, or that image of a whale eating a shark eating a fish – because this type of M&A is going to change how marketers work with retail media companies, which our senior editor, James Hercher, discusses to close out this week.

#7338. Down To The Wire To Acquire; Meta Wants To Be TV, Too

Are we in for a year-ending blockbuster M&A spree?

The Information jokes that CEOs ought to “get your deals in while ya still can, folks.”

A convergence of factors could make for a splashy Q4. As AdExchanger discussed in our Big Story Podcast last week, The Trump administration hasn’t been opposing acquisitions that would have drawn tough scrutiny under the Biden admin. Well, DoorDash CEO Tony Xu confirmed to The Information that he backed out of the company’s previous attempt to buy Instacart in 2021 because he worried Biden-era regulators would squash it.

Another factor in M&A’s favor: Many valuable businesses are struggling with risk-averse investors who don’t know how the AI revolution will shake out. The Information cites Duolingo, Coursera and Zoom as companies that have lost investor support but that would be attractive to buyers. They could join Bumble or Roku in limping to an exit.

Interestingly, what Duolingo, Coursera and Zoom have in common is that they’ve put little effort into earning ad revenue. In 2021, Zoom briefly tested a pilot ad program to monetize free users. That went away a year later.

These companies have the scaled user bases and first-party data assets marketers covet, but not much appetite for the ads biz. Could M&A flip the switch?

If YouTube’s TV, And Meta’s TV, Then Who’s Flying The Plane?

Everyone’s sick of the “Is YouTube TV?” debate. Great news: Now we can argue about whether Meta is TV, instead!

Last week, Meta announced that it’s testing long-form content on Instagram, allowing creators to share content up to 90 minutes long. The announcement comes alongside an influx of CTV spending among direct-to-consumer brands as platforms court midsize advertisers.

Cody Plofker, former CEO and CMO of makeup brand Jones Road, had been against TV advertising until he realized spending 80% of the company budget on Meta was limiting brand exposure, he said at Tatari’s Forward event in New York on Thursday.

Like Jones Road, many DTC brands have “[maxed] out social platforms” and are now putting more focus on TV advertising “as a performance vehicle,” Mike Shields writes in Next in Media.

And CTV ad platforms like Tatari are taking inspiration from Meta and Google by launching their own optimization engines.

Never one to back down from a fight, Meta is searching for its own spot in the TV landscape.

But YouTube is already known for engaged, loyal followings, Shields points out. And YouTube’s content is delivered on demand, which is a fit for TV, whereas Instagram’s algorithmic feed isn’t the traditional TV experience.

As one insider in the creator market tells Shields, why take away what’s working on YouTube TV and redirect resources to Instagram TV?

AI search is the new boogeyman robbing publishers of ad revenue. But another long-feared boogeyman – brand safety – can still spook the sell side.

Last week, former writers for the feminist news site Jezebel raised the alarm that hundreds of articles had been removed from the site. They pointed the finger at Jezebel’s new owner, Paste Magazine, which acquired the publication from G/O Media in 2023.

Anna Merlan, a former Jezebel writer now reporting for Mother Jones, says she heard from sources familiar with Paste that its publisher, William Sagan, decided to remove the articles after an “advertising and analytics company” flagged more than 4,000 articles as “not brand safe.”

But Sagan denied that Paste deleted the articles over brand safety concerns in statements provided to Mother Jones and The Washington Post. He says Paste often flags articles for any number of reasons, including grammatical errors, and temporarily reverts these stories to “draft” status. Indeed, many of the Jezebel articles taken down last week were republished soon after their authors started raising questions.

Paste’s exact motivation for taking the articles down remains unclear. But you can’t blame former Jezebel writers for being sensitive about brand safety.

Jezebel has long suffered monetization troubles tied to advertiser concerns over its coverage. Former Paste editor-in-chief Josh Jackson even claimed he never knew the extent to which brand safety solutions can demonetize publisher content until Paste acquired Jezebel.

Challenger social platforms saw their stock prices drop significantly after reporting Q3 earnings on Thursday. Reddit shares fell 29% and Roblox dropped 17% on Friday due to user growth concerns, while Pinterest dipped 3% after missing ad revenue expectations. [Yahoo Finance]

People Inc. lays off 195 employees, largely in its “print and legacy web businesses,” due to “rapid changes in media,” according to memo from CEO Neil Vogel. [The Hollywood Reporter]

A network of 37 fake local news websites is boosting mainly Democratic candidates in swing states ahead of the midterm elections – and their content is being picked up by ChatGPT. #7335. AI Labels Don’t Tell Consumers Whether An Ad’s Claims Are Real

Disclosure: Sourin Chakrabarti works on AI labeling for advertising at Meta. The views expressed are his own and do not represent Meta.

In October 2025, three clips appearing to show police detaining and pepper-spraying protesters racked up millions of views across X, Instagram and TikTok. Created with OpenAI’s Sora, the videos carried visible watermarks, yet NewsGuard found that users still cited them as evidence that the events occurred. The footage crossed an unsettling threshold: It didn’t just look realistic; it functioned as visual proof.

Most concern about deepfakes has focused on politics. But the same tactic is now appearing in advertising, where synthetic content can make a product claim look proven.

In a recent campaign investigated by Full Fact, a supposed doctor claiming to be affiliated with Guy’s and St Thomas’ NHS Foundation Trust tested a weight-loss patch and appeared to grow thinner on camera. The trust called the posts “completely fraudulent,” while Google’s Gemini detected SynthID watermarks confirming AI involvement. Yet that watermark only revealed that AI was involved, not where the fiction ended. Was only the doctor’s face synthetic? Or were the medical authority, hospital connection, personal experience and physical transformation invented, too?

This exposes the fundamental blind spot of AI disclosures: they flag the production tool, not the illusion. A generic label tells consumers that AI was used to build an ad, but leaves them to guess where reality ends and fiction begins.

The fraudulent NHS weight-loss ad was not an isolated incident. In 2025, the Australian Medical Association warned that deepfakes impersonating prominent doctors were promoting unproven products, with clinicians discovering the fraud only when patients asked whether to swap prescribed treatments for advertised miracle cures. In 2026, Chinese regulators launched an enforcement campaign targeting businesses that mass-produced fabricated consumer-experience posts.

The legal principle predates generative AI. In FTC v. Colgate-Palmolive Co., a shaving cream commercial used a plexiglass prop in place of real sandpaper. Viewers were misled because the simulation was presented as a genuine product test. The case offers a useful test for AI advertising today: Does an ad merely illustrate a claim or does it ask viewers to treat a synthetic scene as real-world proof?

Platforms and regulators are building substantial disclosure systems to track synthetic content. Google displays “How this ad was made” panels, Meta attaches “AI info” labels and TikTok offers “AIGC” self-disclosure controls. Governments are pushing in the same direction: The European Union’s Article 50 rules require transparency for synthetic media, China mandates explicit AI markers and New York requires advertisements to identify synthetic performers.

Yet current AI-labeling systems mostly tell consumers that AI was used, not what it changed or why it matters. The same label can appear on an ad with a decorative AI background and one with an entirely fabricated testimonial. Those uses are not equally misleading, but a generic label may not distinguish between them.

Some policies address the clearest cases. The Advertising Standards Council of India’s 2026 draft guidance identifies fabricated experts, endorsements and exaggerated results as high-risk uses that labeling alone cannot fix. TikTok Shop prohibits AI-generated professional identities used to sell health products and alterations that misrepresent product performance. But a harder question remains: What about AI simulations that are lawful but could still be mistaken for real-world evidence?

The disclosure gap is becoming urgent as AI ad generation reaches industrial scale. In 2025, advertisers created three times as many Gemini-generated assets on Google as in 2024, including nearly 70 million in the final quarter alone. Meta has reportedly aimed to automate ad creation and targeting with AI by the end of 2026. Because these tools are embedded directly into ad-creation systems, safeguards cannot rely on post hoc consumer complaints. They must operate systematically across millions of ads.

The answer is not to label every synthetic pixel. Building on the IAB’s January 2026 disclosure framework, regulators should adopt a risk-based approach requiring specific disclosures whenever AI material appears to provide evidence for a product claim. This approach would produce three outcomes:

Platforms could implement this approach by requiring advertisers to disclose three things: the role played by any AI-created person or scene, whether the generated material depicts product performance or results and what real-world evidence supports the claim. Meta, Google and TikTok already accept advertiser declarations, so these questions could fit into existing workflows. Platforms should also retain a record of the advertiser’s answers and the notice shown to consumers, creating an auditable trail of how each ad was reviewed and presented. An emerging industry proposal calls this a served disclosure receipt.

Consider the weight-loss patch video. Under this system, an “AI was used” label would be only the starting point. The advertiser would have to identify the doctor as a synthetic expert, classify the apparent transformation as a product-performance claim and clarify whether the testimonial represented a real customer. It would also have to provide evidence supporting the weight-loss claim. If the doctor was falsely presented as real, the testimonial was fabricated or the result lacked substantiation, the ad would not be approved.

The goal is labels that answer the question consumers actually face: not just whether AI made the ad but whether AI made up the reason to buy.

But other parts of Alphabet‘s business aren’t faring so well.

The company’s stock sank 10% after Q3 earnings missed both revenue and profit expectations, and revealed that for the second quarter in a row, hefty AI spending has kept cash flow in the negative.

Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

Alphabet posted revenue of $127.6 billion, compared to analysts’ expected $128.2 billion, and reported negative cash flow of $9.07 billion.

You may remember that Alphabet’s Q2 earnings cast a pall: It posted negative cash flow for the very first time since Google went public in 2004. Analysts expected it would come nearer to breaking even in Q3, but instead, cash burn worsened. At -$9.07 billion, it’s wrapping up Q3 with capex $5.9 billion further into the red than they were in Q2.

And things are only going to get worse. Anat Ashkenazi, Alphabet’s Chief Financial Officer, told investors Alphabet “continue[s] to expect our CapEx to increase significantly in 2027” as it pays for everything associated with AI, including R&D and building out more cloud computing capacity.

He pointed to deeper brand partnerships between Google and advertisers as the “largest contribution” to ad growth, and gave a nod to YouTube Shopping’s partnership with Amazon–the latest component of YouTube’s many-years-in-the-making attempt to turn itself into an ecom hub.

“Our YouTube Creator Partnerships program connects brands with over 3 million creators to drive highly effective campaigns. Brands like Lexus continue to partner with creators like Colin and Samir, driving an 11% lift in brand consideration,” Schindler said.

He also brought up YouTube Premium subscriptions, which contribute to the platform’s overall income but are not separated out into their own figure during earnings. Schindler hinted that the lower-cost Lite version has played a role in pushing subscriptions up to their current high.

“With Premium and Premium Lite, viewers have choice,” he said. “As more people opt into premium experiences, it’s a win for viewers, creators, and our business. Subscriptions help fund the creator ecosystem and drive the platform forward.”

No word on cash from more direct creator support mechanics like Channel Memberships, Super Thanks, and Super Chats (YouTube takes a 30% cut from all of those). Alphabet’s call firmly focused on how it wants more advertising and AI money. Judging by Ashkenazi’s comments, the latter will be a long time coming.

“Our commercial priorities are clear. Expanding advertiser ROI, systematically advancing our AI monetization efficiency, and scaling our ecosystem partnerships to support the next era of discovery,” Schindler said in his wrap-up.

“At Made on YouTube last month, we announced more than 30 products and features for creators and viewers. For horror creators on YouTube, a lot has changed between last October and the present. Kane Parsons‘ Backrooms and Curry Barker‘s Obsession were two of the biggest sleeper hits of Hollywood’s summer season, and Markiplier brought his project Iron Lung to theaters as well.

If the momentum those creators generated is going to be sustained into 2027, then spooky season is a crucial time of year. Horror movies can be big draws during the fall, but at least one of the horror maestros who broke out this year is returning to his roots. Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

#7324. Pornhub is calling on its community to upload safe-for-work content (and get paid for it)

It’s time to dust off one of the age-old debates of the internet era: Can a platform known for pornographic videos become a viable home for safe-for-work creator content?

Pornhub is trying to do exactly that. The popular site owned by Aylo (formerly known as MindGeek) has launched a campaign that invites creators to share videos of any type with Pornhub viewers.

In the campaign video, a broken-down car looks like the end of the road for a mother and her son. Luckily, mom explains that she learned how to change a flat by watching how-to content uploaded by pornographic actress Natassia Dreams. The car starts moving again, and viewers are left to consider whether Pornhub can really be an alternative to the likes of YouTube, TikTok, and Instagram.

Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

We’ve asked that question before. Nearly a decade ago, friction between creators and platforms led some musicians and firearms enthusiasts to set up shop on Pornhub. As part of its current campaign, Pornhub is once again positioning itself as a solution for creators who are banned or restricted on other platforms.

There are plenty of reasons why Pornhub’s offer is worth considering. Creators typically go to the platforms that can offer access to new audiences, and porn sites have never been lacking in the scale department. Pornhub claims to reach more than 130 million users each day. Some advertisers have taken advantage of the relaxed guidelines on racy platforms like OnlyFans, and Pornhub has a built-in premium subscription creators can link to their safe-for-work uploads. The recent arrival of Shorties — TikTok-style videos on Pornhub — provide yet another distribution option.

“Pornhub is a cultural access point where creators can build an audience around the full range of who they are,” said Pornhub VP of Brand and Community Alex Kekesi in a statement. “Creators invest time, creativity, and resources into their content. Safe-for-work uploads give them another way to earn from the broader range of what they create, including content they may have published elsewhere, giving content a second life and earn more.”

Clearly, some creators have already taken Pornhub up on its offer. On the platform, the popularity of searches like “gaming,” “fitness,” “cooking,” and “travel” have trended up over the past year.

Can those searches form the foundation of a safe-for-work hub that can rival the one OnlyFans has built? Pornhub clearly thinks so, and it is hoping that its new campaign will convince creators to try a, shall we say, unusual distribution strategy.

#7323. Instagram is offering YouTubers up to $500,000 to post with its new horizontal format

Instagram isn’t just chasing YouTube‘s TV watch time and ad revenue–it’s chasing its talent, too. The Meta-owned platform has offered to pay some YouTubers up to $500,000 to post videos with its newly announced long-form horizontal format “Features.”

According to Business Insider, Instagram has approached “select” YouTubers with a floor price of $50,000; others have gotten six-figure offers, and things top out at a half-million dollars.

“We’ve been public about the fact that we are funding Features content directly with some creators right now to support them,” a Meta spokesperson told BI. “The details of those deals are confidential, but we’re excited to see the content going live.”

Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

It’s not clear how Instagram is paying out these amounts–per video, per month, or as one-time flat compensation. We’d bet the latter, and perhaps the pot’s sweetened with a promise to pay creators performance bonuses or an ad rev share if their Features content does well (especially on TVs, where pricier ads slots can pull in serious cash for platforms).

Meta already said, though, that it’s “too early to share a long-term monetization model [for Features], but we’re exploring ways for creators to earn from brands, fans, and Instagram, including performance-based incentives.”

Introducing Features earlier this week, Instagram hyped its established TV viewership, with VP of Product Tessa Lyons saying “people love to watch Reels together in their living rooms with their friends, so we’ve been working on a TV version of Reels.”

“[W]e know to do that well, we need more than just short-form video,” she added.

Insta chief Adam Mosseri chimed in Oct. 28 after concern from creators, tweeting that “[w]e understand the economics matter a ton, and are exploring multiple options to help long-form creators get paid.”

This YouTuber-bait program is perhaps one of those options.

People familiar with the deals told BI Instagram’s terms just ask creators to post their long-form videos as Features on the same day they upload to YouTube.

Reza Izad, who reps Kareem Rahma, Noah Beck, and more as co-founder and co-CEO of Underscore Talent, told BI these deals are an “exciting opportunity” for YouTubers. The money is part of that excitement, sure, but Izad said this is also an opportunity for creators’ content to get a boost.

“Every time there’s a new feature in these apps that the company’s promoting, people will have more opportunity to be seen because there’s going to be algorithmic preference to this kind of content,” he said. “And unlike short-form, there’s not a lot of abundance.”

What he’s saying is true: We already know Instagram plans to pump posts made with Clips as Reels (a tool that takes snippets of Features videos and posts them to Reels with a link back to the full long-form upload) on its Explore page, and in other areas around the platform.

Something to think about in all of this is that a major part of YouTube’s living room success is the relative attractiveness and easy UX of its TV app. Google has put stock into making the TV app a banger, and Instagram isn’t there yet.

As Mosseri put it, “We’re going to try to support these different types of formats, both in the mobile app, but also on the TV app, which […] is going to take some time to get it right. But I’m actually very excited about it, and we’re very committed to it long-term.”

Creators looking for equal viewership across YouTube and Features will likely be disappointed–at least for now. But for the folks Instagram wants to pay, this is indeed a rare chance to get get cash for cross-posting.
