#7313. “Uber agents,” undercover AI personas, and other ways newsrooms are using AI in investigations

All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

Hacks/Hackers and The New York Times hosted more than 100 journalists at the AI x Investigative Journalism Forum.

Late last month, about 150 journalists, researchers, and technologists gathered on the 15th floor of The New York Times Building for a forum on how AI is changing investigative journalism.

Just outside the event space was a hallway commemorating the paper’s more than 140 Pulitzer Prize winners, dating back to 1918. One photograph had yet to be hung: a portrait of this year’s winners of the Pulitzer Prize for Investigative Reporting. For one of their winning stories, a team of Times reporters conducted an audit of the SEC’s crypto lawsuits to show weakening enforcement under the second Trump administration. The reporting was assisted by large language models (LLMs).

The Times isn’t the only major newsroom using AI tools in major investigations. A record-breaking eight Pulitzer awardees this year disclosed AI use to the judges. They used LLMs to organize, summarize, analyze, and translate large document dumps.

“At the Times we’re not doing ‘robots tell the news,’ but a number of different [kinds of AI adoption] that can make the work we do more efficient, more effective, and able to do things that otherwise would be very, very hard to do,” said Juliana Castro Varón, the Times’ senior design editor of AI initiatives, in a keynote. Often, “the most useful part [of AI] is the fact that it understands images and understands text, more than creating [them].”

RELATED ARTICLEA record-breaking eight Pulitzer awardees disclosed AI use this yearAndrew DeckAugust 3, 2026The Times’ AI Initiatives team, a group of nine journalists and technologists leading AI strategy and deployment in the newsroom, co-hosted the event with Hacks/Hackers, a nonprofit that brings journalists and technologists together to discuss media innovation. (Hacks/Hackers hosted a summit on AI and journalism in Baltimore for the past two years.)

The day was packed with workshops, panels, and presentations about the promise of AI for investigative journalism, led by the technology’s most vocal advocates in newsrooms. But the limitations of these tools — including persistent hallucination problems in LLMs, concerns about vibe-coding errors, and budget constraints as AI token costs pile up — were also a common theme.

“AI is very good at generating leads, but much less capable of establishing publishable evidence,” said Afrooz Mosallaei, a research associate at the Center for News, Technology & Innovation, during a talk about the nonprofit’s recent report on the topic. “A lot of tasks in an investigation — including verification, source development, textual understanding, and editorial judgment — remain fundamentally human responsibilities.”

The release of the Epstein Files was a huge moment for AI in investigative journalism. Journalists across the U.S. woke up on January 30, 2026 to a Department of Justice drop of over 3.5 million pages of documents and tens of thousands of images and videos.

Duy Nguyen, who leads AI science research at the Times, noted that the PDFs in the Epstein Files would stack as high as the Empire State Building if they were printed out, and would take 11 years for one reporter to read. (Epstein sent an average of 65 emails every day for a decade.) It would take a reporter a month to listen to and watch all the audio and video clips.

RELATED ARTICLEAI-powered search is fueling a wave of Epstein Files transparency projectsAndrew DeckMarch 4, 2026Many newsrooms decided that the early organization and research into these documents was a task primed for AI technologies. Engineers from the Associated Press, NPR, and the Times led a session on how they built tools to help reporters sift through the documents.

NPR built an internal search tool that let reporters across the newsroom find the documents relevant to their beats, said Kriti Singh, a design technologist at NPR’s AI Labs. Her team classified documents by type (email, legal filing, flight log, witness list), grouped them by location (city, county, hotel, university), and extracted entities (making sure, for instance, that a search for “Prince Andrew” also surfaced files that mentioned “the Duke of York”).

The Times AI Initiatives team built the Epstein Files Engine, an internal chatbot to help reporters comb through the files. “There are so many sorts of threads that you can pull from such a big corpus, and the chat interface really allows [reporters] to dive deep,” said Nguyen. The engine’s interface was built with LibreChat, a free, open-source, self-hosted AI chat platform.

“Look at our Epstein coverage over the past three months and cross-reference with names of people most mentioned in the documents. Give me a subset of names we haven’t covered as often.”

“Find me Kathryn Ruemmler’s email where she said she is missing her ring in Epstein’s apartment.”

“Construct a timeline of Epstein’s death, give me a table that I can copy into a spreadsheet. Be very detailed. Surface witnesses, links and quotes where available.”

Ultimately, more than 100 Times journalists posed more than 5,000 questions to the engine, and it contributed to at least 20 published stories. “This was a signifier of just how powerful an agentic chat interface could be in a newsroom,” said Nguyen. (His team recently published an academic article detailing the tool’s development.)

Since then, the team has created other agentic search tools. Ahead of the Times’ 175th anniversary series, they built “Morgue Bot,” which made it easier for reporters to dive into the Times’ archive.

Now, the team is taking chatbots to the newsroom at large. In July, they launched News Agent, which they’re calling the “front door to AI at The New York Times.” The general-purpose internal chatbot plugs into not just the Times’ archives and the Epstein Files, but other databases, internal documents like the Times’ style guide, and the web. News Agent also allows any Times reporter to build their own custom agentic search tool, tailored to a specific project.

“It’s an omnibus agent or an uber agent that basically acts as a drop-in replacement for chatbots like Gemini or ChatGPT,” said Nguyen, “but specifically geared to help reporters and editors within the Times newsroom.”

The team’s copy for the tool reads, “Ask anything.”

Any beat reporter will tell you they have a love-hate relationship with their source spreadsheet — that Google Sheet or Excel file that lists the name, title, email address, and phone number of every source they’ve spoken to over the years. Such documents are perfect for remembering the name of a researcher you spoke to five years ago without having to dig through your inbox. But they’re tedious to update.

“It can become a dead document that never gets checked,” said J.D. Capelouto, a technology reporter and the newly named AI lead at Semafor.

RELATED ARTICLEHow The New York Times uses a custom AI tool to track the “manosphere”Andrew DeckFebruary 11, 2026To try to keep his own source spreadsheet alive and up-to-date, Capelouto made a tool in Google Apps Script, a platform that lets users build small “assistants” within Google Workspace. When he emails someone for the first time, he adds an inbox tag called “New Source.” At the end of each day, the script scans his inbox for any tagged emails, then populates a Google Sheet with all the relevant information about them, including adding a category tag and generating a logline summarizing what they discussed. (There are obvious risks in handling anonymous or sensitive sourcing, but Capelouto said the tool creates minimal new security vulnerabilities since it stays within Google’s ecosystem.)

From there, Capelouto started building on top of the spreadsheet. A pop-up sidebar lets him ask who might be a good person to speak with for a story; the tool combs through the spreadsheet and suggests names.

Every morning, a script also scans the web for the news of the day on Capelouto’s beat, cross-references those headlines with the source spreadsheet, and sends him an email suggesting a topic to cover and a source to contact. Some of the suggestions aren’t useful, Capelouto admitted, but others have actually prompted him to reach out to someone he’d forgotten about.

“A lot of times in journalism, some of the source management work is just saying, ‘Hey, how’s it going?” he said. “This can begin a conversation, then you get a scoop from that.”

Philip Bump of Hearst Connecticut Media Group presents at the AI x Investigative Journalism Forum in The New York Times Building on September 25, 2026. (Photo courtesy of Hacks/Hackers)

Most conversations about AI-generated imagery in investigative journalism revolve around verification. As AI-altered images and deepfakes flood the internet, how do reporters verify the images they come across online, or those sent to them by whistleblowers?

The forum didn’t tackle these questions head on, but one presentation highlighted the ways that AI image generators can be harnessed to protect the identity of journalists.

Last year, The Markup co-published an investigation into Match Group, the dating app giant that owns Tinder, Hinge, and OkCupid. The nonprofit tech publication owned by CalMatters found that despite an official policy of banning users who are reported for assault, the company failed to keep them off their platforms and hid the scale of the problem from the public.

In one case, a Denver cardiologist who was repeatedly accused of drugging and sexually assaulting women he met on Hinge remained active on the platform for three years, even after two different women reported his abuse. (In 2024, he was convicted of crimes against 11 women and sentenced to 158 years to life in prison.)

RELATED ARTICLECan we gamify that? The innovators turning investigations on spying scandals and vote rigging into video gamesBhavya DoreAugust 17, 2026The Markup’s reporters decided to go undercover. They posed as users on Match-owned apps, then reported themselves from other accounts to see how easy it was to stay on the platform.

There was only one problem. “We came across this ethical dilemma: Am I gonna ask my staff or myself to take a photo and put it on the Tinder account?” recalled Sisi Wei, the chief impact officer at The Markup and CalMatters.

Even stock photos would subject real people, who had not consented to their likeness being used in the investigation, to reputational harm. Instead, The Markup turned to AI image generators. They found a company that generates visual test imagery and had developed a way to train models without relying too heavily on images of real people.

“They look like real human beings, but if you turn on a light switch, you can tell that AI is here,” said Wei. But they were still “real” enough to bypass the dating apps’ content moderation filters. With these new AI headshots and personas in hand, the reporters went back on the apps and created 50 different accounts.

Ultimately, their investigation found that even after one of these personas was reported and kicked off a Match-owned dating app, they could get back onto the platforms without changing identifying information. Earlier this year, the 18-month long investigation won a SABEW Award for best technology business reporting.

“AI became a way for us to protect our own staff from needing to be a part of the experiment,” said Wei.

#7312. Meta’s new app lets AI plan your outfit of the day

Generative AI can be an automated agent, a creative strategist, and a research assistant. Now, Meta has figured out another occupation for its arsenal of LLMs: Personal stylist.

That’s the basic idea behind Style Sketch, a new app that Meta has quietly launched. Though the tech giant provided no official announcement pertaining to its new platform, Style Sketch is already helping its users pick out their outfits and match the items in their wardrobes.

The news of Style Sketch’s launch came from a familiar herald: Matt Navarra. The notable tech leaker posted about Meta’s fashion app on X. He noted several of the app’s features, including integrations with weather apps and a travel planner that chooses an itinerary of outfits for a chosen destination.

Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

Style Sketch is arriving at a time when creators are gaining more influence and credibility in the world of haute couture. Kai Cenat recently took New York Fashion Week by storm with an event that promoted his apparel line Vivet. Meanwhile, Theorist Media’s Creators in Fashion shows have given YouTube stars the chance to strut their stuff in a runway setting.

Many creators express their fashion sense with “outfit of the day” posts, which are typically tagged with #OOTD on social media. Some tech companies, like ShopMy, have developed products that support #OOTD posts.

Style Sketch’s links to the #OOTD phenomenon make it an intriguing addition to the glut of fashion apps. Users can link their profiles to their accounts on Facebook and Instagram accounts — where #OOTD is a popular hashtag — allowing the app’s AI engine to detect the apparel they have already featured in posts.

The potential is there, but users in the West will have to wait before they can try out Style Sketch themselves. For now, the app’s rollout is limited to three Southeast Asian nations: Singapore, Indonesia, and Thailand.

November 3 is Election Day in the United States, and Jubilee Media is keeping its eye on the night’s returns. The Gen Z-focused media company will host its first-ever election special as it tracks the results in several key races across the country.

Jubilee has made a name for itself with political coverage that walks down the center of the aisle on platforms like YouTube and Instagram. Earlier this year, it doubled down on that approach by launching The Split, a semi-regular news program designed as an antidote to siloed feeds on social media. With both liberal and conservative viewpoints, The Split is a Gen Z answer to the bygone CNN program Crossfire.

Now, the bipartisan hosts of The Split will anchor Jubilee’s election coverage. David Mauricio and Austin Julio Broughton will go live on YouTube, with “surprise guests” waiting in the wings, according to a Jubilee press release.

For Jubilee, the November 3 stream will be the culmination of a busy election season. Three weeks before Election Day, the media company teamed up with CNN and Texas Senate candidate James Talarico for an innovative town hall event.

Talarico has made digital outreach a key part of his campaign. In Texas, creators Destiny, Mr. Mouton, and I’mReallyImportant have teamed up with Digital Ground Game to mobilize Gen Z volunteers and get out the vote. That level of engagement has given Talarico a great chance to defeat Republican opponent Ken Paxton, and Jubilee has put itself at the heart of that political action.

That sort of energy has been everywhere in 2026. The 2024 cycle may go down in history as the “influencer election,” but this year has been the time when creators took their organizational efforts to the next level. #7310. Sinclair’s new Substack repackages its local TV reporting into a video podcast

All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

“How young is too young for a life in prison?”

“SpaceX debris is washing ashore. Who’s responsible?”

“Why schools get paid even when students fail.”

Those are the top headlines so far on Sinclair Broadcasting Group’s new Substack publication, The National Press, launched this week.

The National Press repackages some of the top stories from Sinclair’s 178 local news stations — which employ around 1,200 journalists — into a daily, 30-minute broadcast-style show. The program is hosted by former Newsmax and Christian Cable Network anchor Lyndsay Keith, who summarizes the stories and interviews the local journalists who first reported them. In the videos, Keith sits at a desk with a microphone; the dimly lit background is illuminated just enough to make out two American flags in a mug. (It gives off a true-crime YouTube podcast vibe.)

As Axios’s Sara Fischer noted on Tuesday, Sinclair has long been accused of conservative bias in its local news operation. The National Press is launching in partnership with New Media, the company behind Bari Weiss’s The Free Press, and the two publications look somewhat alike (in part because they both run on Substack). New Media staffers will help create the content and maintain the site and the company will take a portion of Sinclair’s revenue from Substack, Fischer reported.

The National Press is currently free to access, but has paid tiers that include ad-free viewing, community chat access, and merch. Subscriptions start at $5 per month or $50 per year. The five posts on the site so far have between seven and 14 likes each.

Wednesday’s episode focuses on a story about how Michigan is reconsidering lifetime sentences for people sentenced between the ages of 18 and 20. It also tackles AI regulation debates in Congress, drawing on reporting by Capitol Hill reporter Ahtra Elnashar. The show doesn’t appear to be filmed in one take like a true TV news broadcast (Keith is first seen in a black blazer, then a brown one, before switching back to black by the end of the video).

Another video, “Worth Noticing: School Bus Incidents,” is just two minutes long and compiles stories of school bus crashes from around the country. From the text accompanying the video:

We trust school buses to get our kids from the safety of our homes to school every day. So why are we seeing so many serious injuries and incidents? Is this simply a string of unrelated tragedies? Are staffing shortages the problem here? Training gaps? Weak safety protocols?

We’re going to be following these stories. Have you seen incidents like this in your community? Is this something that is keeping you awake at night?

Because these stories are horrific; we’re talking about every parent’s nightmare.

The National Press isn’t Sinclair’s first effort to reach a younger, video-first audience. In 2015, it launched millennial-focused news site Circa, which shuttered four years later.

“Disparaging journalism is a far more central part of Fox News programming than it is of either MSNBC or CNN programming.”

In 2025, trust in journalism reached a record low. According to Gallup, only 8% of Republicans expressed trust in the news media, compared with 51% of Democrats. New data show an uptick among Republicans, but overall trust remains near this record low, and the gap between Republicans and Democrats remains substantial.

One of the key drivers of this lopsided decline in trust in journalism may be the extent to which news outlets spend time bashing other news outlets, or bashing the news media in general — a phenomenon we call inter-journalism disparagement. Our research team at Duke University’s DeWitt Wallace Center for Media & Democracy recently completed a study of the prominence of this phenomenon on each of the “big three” cable news networks (CNN, Fox News, MSNBC/MS NOW); whether it has increased or decreased over time; and whether there are significant differences in the rate of disparagement across networks.

The results were stark. Fox News far exceeds the other networks, with inter-journalism disparagement taking place once every 14.5 minutes. In contrast, CNN engages in inter-journalism disparagement roughly every 140 minutes, and MSNBC every 61 minutes.

To conduct this analysis, we gathered 15 years of cable news transcripts (2011-2025) for each network. We gathered a random sample of one week’s worth of programming for each year.1 With this approach, we ended up with 3,543 transcripts and almost 19 million words across the three networks, which equates to roughly 62,000 pages of text.

Given the volume of text to be analyzed, we trained OpenAI’s GPT-5.5 to identify attacks against the news media. We developed a 20-page instruction document to help the model code instances of disparagement. GPT-5.5 consistently achieved 99.5% accuracy at identifying inter-journalism disparagement and 100% accuracy for avoiding false negatives, compared to human-coded samples. (You can read more details about the entire training and analytical process here.)

We defined inter-journalism disparagement as negative statements about the conduct or content of an explicitly identified journalism target (such as a specific news organization, or the news media in general). Our definition, which is described in greater depth in the full paper, needed to be quite detailed in order for ChatGPT to produce accurate results. Examples of inter-journalism disparagement include:

What we found when comparing the three networks tells us a lot about the dynamics of contemporary cable news and partisan journalism.

First, Figure 1 shows the rate of journalism disparagement across each of the big three networks. Because the volume of text that we analyzed varies across each network, our primary metric was the rate of disparagement per 1,000 words of transcript text. In this figure, we show not only the rate per 1,000 words, but we also convert that rate into a time-based frequency, using the industry standard of 1,000 words equaling approximately six minutes of air time.

In Figure 2, we graph the frequency of inter-journalism disparagement over time. Here, we see that the massive difference between Fox News and CNN/MSNBC persists over the 15-year time period. Still, we do see some dips in the volume of disparagement on Fox News in the two-year periods leading up to the 2016 and 2024 elections, with journalism disparagement levels on Fox News rebounding to near-peak levels in 2025. We haven’t figured out yet what to make of this pattern.

CNN and MSNBC seem to converge in their disparagement activity starting around 2017, with MSNBC’s disparagement rate decreasing somewhat, and CNN’s disparagement rate increasing somewhat. This pattern aligns with recent research that has shown, in other contexts, that CNN and MSNBC programming are converging in ways that suggest diminished differences between the more “centrist” CNN and the more left-leaning MSNBC.

A key takeaway here is that we should not think about Fox News and MSNBC as flip sides of the same partisan journalism coin. At least in relation to inter-journalism disparagement, these left- and right-leaning cable networks behave very differently. Disparaging journalism is a far more central part of Fox News programming than it is of either MSNBC or CNN programming.

In order to get a deeper understanding of these differences, we also identified the targets of the disparagement. These results are presented in Figures 3 through 5.

Figure 3 presents a breakdown of the most common targets of disparagement on Fox News. By far the most frequent target of disparagement on Fox News is “the media.” Following in a distant second is CNN, with the “mainstream media” rounding out the top three targets. Other relatively frequent targets include The New York Times, MSNBC, and The Washington Post.

As should be clear, Fox News devotes far more attention to disparaging journalism as an institution than it does to attacking individual news sources. This stands in stark contrast to what we see when we look at the results for CNN and MSNBC. Looking first at CNN, Figure 4 shows that the network’s most frequent target is Fox News (though with a frequency that wouldn’t crack the top three of the Fox News list).

Similarly, as Figure 5 shows, Fox News is also the number one target on MSNBC. Both CNN and MSNBC have the same top three, with Fox News followed by “the media” and the “right-wing media.” These instances of institutional disparagement happen far less frequently on CNN or MSNBC than they do on Fox News.

Finally, we were also able to identify which hosts or anchors were the most frequent disparagers of their fellow journalists. Those results can be seen in Figure 6. Given the lopsided amount of inter-journalism disparagement on Fox News, it is not surprising that this graph is dominated by Fox News personalities, with Sean Hannity taking the top spot, followed by Greg Gutfeld and Tucker Carlson (note: our graph for Howard Kurtz reflects his move from CNN to Fox in 2013).

This study didn’t distinguish further in terms of the nature of the disparagement across the three networks (for example, in terms of severity or legitimacy). This is something we are exploring in the next stage of this work. Nor did we examine whether viewer exposure to inter-journalism disparagement reduces trust in specific outlets or the institution of journalism. That certainly seems like a reasonable assumption, given the dramatically lower levels of trust in journalism among Republicans that we noted at the outset. We plan to investigate this relationship directly in future research.

But what we do see in this research is that disparagement of the institution of journalism, and of particular news outlets, is a much more prominent component of Fox News programming than it is of either CNN or MSNBC. Some researchers have proposed that this kind of high-volume disparagement of news sources that don’t tow the same partisan line takes us beyond traditional notions of partisan journalism and into the realm of “anti-media media.” The goal of anti-media media is to “weaponize the facade of journalism against the roles assigned to journalism” in a democracy. Based on our findings, Fox News fits this characterization.

Philip M. Napoli is the James R. Shepley Professor of Public Policy, director of the DeWitt Wallace Center for Media & Democracy, and director of undergraduate studies for the journalism and media minor in the Sanford School of Public Policy at Duke University. Adam Meskouri is a politics researcher at Harvard and Duke. Anjini Mani is an undergraduate at Duke. Grant Socol is a graduate research assistant at Duke. Harrison Walley is an undergraduate at Duke. Rather than analyze the entirety of the networks’ output over this time, we created a “constructed week” for each year, which is a common practice in this kind of content analysis. This involves selecting a random Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, etc. within each year, so that the sample of programming was reasonably representative of the year as a whole. We included all programming across all dayparts in our constructed weeks. Note: MSNBC was only available through 2023; the network became MS NOW in late 2025. [↩]

#7307. Have you heard? ‘Chicken Shop Date’ in theaters, Hasan Piker in court, and CaylusBlox on shelves.

Each week, we handpick a selection of stories to give you a snapshot of trends, updates, business moves, and more from around the creator industry.

This week, it’s time for a deep-fried movie theater experience, a progressive firebrand is hitting back at his critics, and a top Roblox creative is capitalizing on his success.

The finale of Chicken Shop Date will be screened in movie theaters. Amelia Dimoldenberg is ending her iconic interview series, but Chicken Shop Date is going out with a bang. Across ten theaters in London and Paris, Dimoldenberg will deliver content intended for the big screen before sharing the finale of her long-running YouTube treasure. Forget the popcorn — grab some thighs and drumsticks.

Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

Radio Flyer brings back its animated series on YouTube. That’s right — the company known for its red wagons is in the content business now. Max & Maple are going on adventures and singing songs as they begin season two of their Radio Flyer series. It’s an interesting bet for a toy company — and we’ll surely see more of this strategy as the holiday season approaches.

CSI creator Anthony E. Zuiker is using AI to turn true crime cases into interactive stories. Zuiker has been engaged in our space for an extremely long time, and he’s continuing to embrace emerging technologies. At the MIPCOM conference in France, he demoed Cinemalistics, an app that brings true crime tales to life. Zuiker said it himself: The CSI guy is dead, and this is his “autopsy.”

Hasan Piker hits Scott Jennings with a $72 million lawsuit. Piker is looking for big damages by claiming that Jennings, a conservative commentator, doctored one of his Twitch clips. Piker has become a convenient target for the MAGA sect, but this case shows that the left-winger is willing to hit back when his content is taken out of context and used to defame him.

Tini Younger is bringing her social media following into the kitchen. After becoming one of the top chefs on TikTok, Younger is getting into the cookbook game with a culinary tome titled Today We Are Cooking… Younger may be just 24 years old, but she’s looking to spark a movement that gets Gen Z feeling more comfortable in front of the stove.

Minecraft creator Markus Persson lists his Beverly Hills mansion. The man known as “Notch” is looking for a buyer with enough wealth to buy his massive California abode. For that price, I would expect the mansion to come with some built-in creeper protection and a crafting table in every room.

Caylus is entering the consumer goods market by popping his own popcorn. After becoming one of the biggest stars in the Roblox community, Caylus bought a popcorn factory and turned it into the home base for Good Kernel, his new company. It’s the perfect snack to munch on while you watch all those creator-led movies that are screening in multiplexes across the country.

A new product suite will bring monetization to beehiiv podcasts. The platform that made its name by publishing newsletters launched podcasting tools earlier this year. Now, it is imbuing those audio programs with flexible revenue streams. Newsletter distributors are in the midst of an arms race, and the ones that help creators make the most money are likely to end up on the top of the heap.

Bluesky is letting creators link to the platforms they use to generate revenue. Monetization is still limited on the decentralized social hub, but its creator profiles now has a Links section that can be connected to Patreon accounts. Bluesky is taking the creator economy seriously without forcing its users to employ its own products. That’s a W!

K-pop idols are promoting Korean language learning on YouTube. Ever wondered what the singers are actually saying in those K-pop bops? A Korean language institute wants to encourage learners who are trying to understand Hangul characters, so it brought K-pop idols to its YouTube channel as part of a cultural project.

A Ramadan cooking show headlines YouTube’s MENA slate. At a Brandcast event in Dubai, YouTube revealed original programs led by Middle Eastern and North African creators. Highlights include AbuRob‘s competitive cooking series centered around Ramadan, Azza Zarour‘s parenting competition, and Sh5baar‘s eclectic travel vlog.

U.K. high court to Big Tech: Ofcom’s demands are valid. Meta, TikTok, and X took a public U.K. watchdog to court to challenge demands for safety data, but that case went in Ofcom’s favor. The high court ruled that regulators have the right to enforce the Online Safety Act, which requires platforms to provide a safe experience for younger users.

A hijacked QR code turned Lacy’s on-stream dinner into a nightmare. The Twitch star says that he ran up an unintended bill of approximately $12,000 after his viewers manipulated a QR code they noticed at the Japanese restaurant where he was eating. Note to streamers: Maybe blur out QR codes when you go out to eat, or, if it’s easier, just get nicer fans.

The iPhone Duo folds in two, but does it fold in two 10,000 times? Creator Tim Pan put Apple’s new product to the test by repeatedly folding it on its hinge to see how long it can stay operational. Apple might want to use this one in its ads, because after 10,000 folds, the Duo seemed to continue working.

Would you use hypnosis to forget your favorite film? A theater chain in the Netherlands is running a promotion for cinephiles who want to forget (and then remember) film classics. It would suck if you did the whole hypnosis thing only to read a spoiler on your phone while you’re walking in to the theater.

#7306. “We’re in their shit. They’re not in ours”: USA Today Co. execs defend Palantir deal

All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

USA Today Co. executives are revealing new details about a controversial deal with Palantir. In a joint interview with Fast Company’s Alex Pasternack, three executives from the country’s largest newspaper chain explained why they moved ahead with the Palantir deal despite major opposition from their own employees.

RELATED ARTICLE“An inherent conflict of interest”: More than 800 USA Today Co. employees want the company to end its new Palantir partnershipHanaa' TameezAugust 10, 2026Mike Reed, the chairman and CEO of USA Today Co., previously said that the deal — first reported by Nieman Lab’s Hanaa’ Tameez — is part of a larger shift the company is making to become “an intelligence organization.” At a Palantir conference last month, Reed said that the company’s services were a way for USA Today Co. capitalize on “the shift to online and the data we have on consumers,” Pasternack reported.

In this new interview, USA Today Media president Kristin Roberts detailed some of those services for the first time:

In all of our entertainment stories and our sports stories, we do affiliate links to our partners. So if you’re reading a sports story, you want to buy the jersey for that team, our reporters and editors used to have to go to a file, find a relevant link, copy that link, put it in. All of that is now automated, and that’s a Palantir project.

Lark-Marie Anton, then a communications executive at USA Today Co., chimed in, saying that Palantir’s current scope of work is focused on audience and advertising, but in the future that could extend to social media strategy and reporting tools.

What stood out about Palantir was its ability to create what it calls an ‘ontology’ layer — essentially a unified model that allows different datasets and systems to work together and be acted upon in real time….The challenge isn’t collecting more data, but making better use of the data we already have.

In August, more than 800 USA Today Co. employees from 31 unionized newsrooms called on the company to dissolve its partnership with Palantir. In a statement, staffers named ethical issues and uncertainty over how the software would be used. Throughout the Fast Company interview, Reed and Roberts heavily criticized the NewsGuild and internal efforts to oppose the deal.

Roberts leveled the strongest criticisms of USA Today Co.’s unions across the country, going as far as to say the NewsGuild was lying to its members:

Guild leadership is saying things that are factually untrue. They prey on fear. No matter that I will appear in front of any newsroom for a standup in which they ask me anything for an hour and a half at a time, and I explain to them all of the things.

I’ll give you an example that’s incredibly real for us. Palantir doesn’t work inside of any USA Today Company system. They don’t have access to any of the notes our reporters take. They’re not in the Microsoft suite of tools. They don’t have information directly about our consumers or our staff….They don’t work in our systems. We feed them highly controlled data. We’re in their shit. They’re not in ours.

Reed doubled down on these accusations, extending them to the work the NewsGuild has done organizing around AI in the company, including its push for clauses that would protect journalists from layoffs due to AI adoption.

“I think we’re having more success in newsrooms that are not unionized, with this new world, than those that are unionized,” Reed said.

Last month, USA Today Co. made significant layoffs across the company, including at its local newspapers, and reorganized its audience team. Reed, in a memo to staff, referenced AI-related traffic declines as a reason for the layoffs.

“USA Today Co. executives’ animosity toward their workers and unions is nothing new,” said NewsGuild president Jon Schleuss in a statement to Fast Company. “[We] fully stand behind the statement workers released when this deal with Palantir was first announced.”

You can read the full interview on Fast Company.

#7305. A new California law lets children of family vloggers make their parents take down all footage of them

A new California law will protect the children of family vloggers once they turn 18.

Senate Bill No. 1247 gives adults whose parents, legal guardians, or family members used them in social media content while they were minors the right to demand removal of said content.

Once served a notice of removal, parents/guardians/etc have 10 days to take down violative content or edit it to remove the requester’s appearances. If those 10 days pass and the content is still up, vloggers will face penalties of $3,000 per day moving forward, plus further potential damages, injunctive relief, and attorney’s fees.

Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

Now, to be clear, this law won’t let someone take their mom to court for posting Facebook pictures of them in an embarrassing Halloween costume (though we do think parents should more carefully consider what they post about their kid online, especially in the age of AI).

S.B. 1247 has a couple requirements that tune it to specifically target professional family vloggers.

We’re guessing it could potentially apply if a parent signed a financial agreement with a family vlogger to have their kid appear in the family’s content on a regular basis, but that circumstance isn’t accounted for in S.B. 1247’s current form.

The law will also lay a mandate on social media platforms: Once it kicks in, YouTube, TikTok, Instagram, and all other sites “shall provide a clear and conspicuous mechanism by which a child influencer can request a vlogger” remove content featuring them, according to the bill’s text. If a platform doesn’t have a built-in mechanism, it has to be responsible for receiving removal requests, and is required to forward those requests to vloggers within three days of receipt.

Vloggers who receive removal requests and comply with them will not face any consequences. It’s only if they refuse removal or if removal takes longer than 10 days that they open themselves up to further legal action.

This law kicks in in January 2027–and while it’s only a California law, we do expect other states might enact similar protections. YouTube just turned 20 years old, so the vlogging industry has now been around long enough that thousands of kids whose parents once featured them in videos are turning 18 and gaining control over their own lives. S.B. 1247 makes sure that control is retroactive, too.

#7302. From bad to worse: 2026 is shaping up to be “a super El Niño year for local news”

All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

RELATED ARTICLEIn Medill’s latest State of Local News report, a “festering, 20-year-old problem” looms larger than everSophie CulpepperOctober 22, 2025If you thought last year was bleak, Medill’s annual State of Local News Report is here to ring the alarm bell louder.

What was a “creeping erosion” has now “mushroomed into a full-blown super El Niño-like event for local news, leaving widespread and long-lasting displacement in its wake,” writes Tim Franklin, founding director of the Medill Local News Initiative, in his introduction to this year’s report, released Tuesday. The Northwestern University team’s research “paints a portrait of a local news ecosystem in a state of precarity.”

In the past year, Medill tracked 26 new news deserts, “the largest single-year rise by far since Medill began keeping records five years ago,” Franklin writes. The previous year, only six new news deserts emerged.

Medill’s team says to understand that acceleration, you have to look at where newspapers are disappearing fastest now. While about 70% of the papers that disappeared over the past 20 years were based in urban or suburban communities, in recent years a greater share of newspaper closures have happened in smaller, rural and poorer communities, according to the report.

“When the news disappears in these counties, it stays gone,” the report states.

RELATED ARTICLELast year, Illinois started giving local news outlets tax credits to support journalism jobs. A new report looks at how it’s goingSophie CulpepperFebruary 9, 2026Many of the new news deserts emerged because of small rural papers shuttering in the Midwest. In fact, the report notes that Illinois lost more newspapers than any other state: 30 newspapers shuttered in the state between July 2025 and August 2026, “all small to medium-size outlets.” That means nearly one in five of the 170 newspapers that shuttered in that year was based in Illinois. The state’s losses are especially notable because it enacted one of the first public policies to preserve and grow local journalism jobs in 2024.

“Independent owners of small to midsize newspapers especially were already operating on a knife’s edge,” Brier Dudley writes in his examination of newspaper losses in Illinois. “This past year, their slim margins were squeezed by shrinking revenues and steeply escalating prices for newsprint, fuel and other materials.”

The price of newsprint rose nearly 18% over the past year, Dudley reported, as U.S. mills closed or stopped production of newsprint. That’s about five times the national rate of inflation, he noted. As of April, the United States has just one newsprint producer left.

A few other highlights from this year’s report:

The extreme urban-rural divide: “Virtually all the new news sources are in urban areas, while rural America is increasingly arid news and information territory,” Franklin writes. “And virtually all the philanthropic support for local news is in metro regions.” The report notes that there are fewer than 50 counties in the U.S. “that lack a newspaper but feature an alternative digital or broadcast outlet.” Of the 287 news outlets to start up in the last five years, nearly 80% are in urban areas.

Traffic declines: Digital readership is in “precipitous decline” for many outlets. According to Comscore data from more than 700 local news sites, monthly traffic has dropped by an average of nearly 2 million pageviews, or almost 30%. Meanwhile, traffic to 100 of the largest local newspapers has declined by almost 50% since 2022.

Local TV news: This year, for the first time, Medill’s report included local TV newsrooms. The team identified 678 local commercial TV newsrooms across the country. The overwhelming majority are located in metro areas with existing local news outlets. (“Adding commercial television to the LNI database made little impact on which counties we identify as news deserts,” the team notes.) TV news is already highly consolidated — the five largest owners control more than half of newsrooms, and the 10 largest control 75% — and further consolidation is underway, if Nexstar’s $6.2 billion acquisition of Tegna survives an antitrust lawsuit. The deal would merge the second- and fourth-largest owners of local commercial TV newsrooms.

#7301. 7-Eleven made a micro-K-drama to promote its new noms

7-Eleven is going full microdrama to promote its latest munchies lineup.

Starting Nov. 2, 60-second episodes of A Convenient Love will pop up on 7-Eleven’s TikTok and Instagram channels to promote its new “Flavors of Korea” menu.

The mini K-drama follows two classmates whose destinies intertwine during late-night runs to (of course) the local 7-Eleven. A short trailer captures a 7-Eleven employee/classic Korean uncle telling the two not-so-star-crossed lovers that they should notice: opposites attract.

Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

He delivers this line holding what is arguably the centerpiece of 7-Eleven’s new collection: a KBBQ pizza that’s an official partnership with Korean frozen food brand bibigo.

“K-dramas run on heightened moments. And some of the most memorable ones happen over something as simple as a late-night meal at a convenience store,” Danny Lee, A Convenient Love‘s director, said in a statement. “That’s what made 7-Eleven’s new Korean-inspired menu a natural fit. We built 7 vertical episodes around it and shot all of them in a real 7-Eleven with the food at every turning point. In this genre the style is core to the storytelling, so we leaned into those familiar devices with some American cinematic flair, from the characters and humor to the visual details and, of course, the food from 7-Eleven.”

Pizza aside, the Flavors of Korea collection includes a gochujang remix on 7-Eleven’s iconic egg salad sando, gochujang boneless wings, bibigo spicy chicken dumplings, a KBBQ taquito, a KBBQ hot dog, and somyeon with kimchi.

7-Eleven will drop Convenient Love episodes throughout November, and each installment will “feature a limited-time discount on a spotlighted menu item,” according to a press release.

We have of course seen other brands capitalizing on the microseries trend, but 7-Eleven might be hitting the sweet spot. Microdramas got off the ground in Asia, and K-dramas specifically (long- or short-form) are an international sensation. Combining the two could push A Convenient Love to a level other branded series have yet to reach. We’re curious to see how it pays off.

Yo, 7-Eleven: Hit us up with performance data when the series wraps. (We also wouldn’t mind a sando or two.)

#7300. When Slate went back to its 1996 homepage, it learned some web design lessons for 2026

All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

“I am a direct traffic girly and I know I’m not alone.”

RELATED ARTICLESlate, now 20 years old, reflects on the value of taking the long view and not chasing digital media trendsShan WangSeptember 23, 2016The fonts are Times New Roman and Arial Narrow, the colors are maroon and mustard, and the cursor is the 8-bit pixel hand. When Slate revived its original 1996 homepage to celebrate its 30th birthday this fall1, the team found a lot to like besides nostalgia.

“I’ve read Slate since 1997, when I finally had access to my own computer at my first job,” Hillary Frey, Slate’s editor-in-chief, told me recently. At the age of 51, she said, “I’m speaking as an old. But I am a direct traffic girly and I know I’m not alone.”

Slate’s homepage has long functioned as a “fossil of what the internet was during that time,” said Ivylise Simones, Slate’s creative director. In 1996, Slate was trying to figure out what a magazine on the internet should even look like; in 2026, it’s among the last general-interest digital-native news sites, and print magazines are dying out. “Salon is one of our only lasting contemporaries,” Frey noted. “There are other sort of fellows from that era, like Feed and Nerve. They’ve been gone for awhile.”

RELATED ARTICLESlate launches a metered paywall to draw more membership revenue from readers, not just listenersSarah ScireMarch 26, 2020In its 30th anniversary campaign, Slate has found its fossil-like nature to be something of a selling point. (It can also be a challenge.) Over the years, the site has published a number of posts about its history and editorial and design choices. A decade ago, then–news editor Chad Lorenz wrote “A history of Slate in nine home pages.” (At launch, Slate articles included page numbers and printing instructions.) A 1998 paywall, Lorenz wrote, was “fortunately” abandoned by 1999. But the paywall returned in 2020. (It was metered at the start, but today it’s dynamic, changing based on user behavior.) For its 30th birthday, the site is running a promotion: a year of access for $19.96.

RELATED ARTICLECan’t read just one: Slate’s daily advice columns are strange, funny, deep, and increasingly a major traffic driver for the siteLaura Hazard OwenJuly 22, 2019“Going back to our roots, there are certain elements we are starting to really love,” Simones said, and she’s thinking about how to include them in the site’s ongoing redesign. She likes the spareness and simplicity of earlier versions of the site, she said, pointing to Reddit and Discord as places that are “more reminiscent of old homepages than the current, very stylized, very gridded layout” found across the internet. A less dense homepage on desktop, she said, is “refreshing.”

“Our editorial guiding light is the mix,” Frey added. Slate has verticals, but they’re not emphasized in the story selection at the top of the homepage; instead, life, politics, and advice stories are mixed together and weighted similarly. “Having an image for every story you share on the homepage is just not necessary,” Simones noted.

Some 1990s-era headline styles still work, too, Frey has found. One of her favorites is a 2002 piece by Slate founding editor Michael Kinsley: “The secret vice of power women.”

“He was writing it about his wife, who found tremendous satisfaction and relaxation in watching police procedurals,” Frey said. “That’s something I still identify with, though most of them now are from Finland and Norway. 100%, this headline would play on the Slate homepage right this second.”

Art courtesy of Slate A wrinkle for 2026: The 1996-inspired homepage had to work on mobile, even though nobody was reading Slate on a phone 30 years ago. [↩]

#7298. Two creators went to NYU’s business school, then decided to make a show about the news

All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

“Our videos are what we wish we could consume more of.”

The data is in: News creators and influencers are a major source of news for Americans, especially people under 30. This is the latest edition of Creators of Record, an occasional series of interviews with popular creators about how they do their jobs.

On a September afternoon in Manhattan’s Union Square neighborhood, Shreyas Sinha is sitting on a toilet, wearing a blue suit. Looking into the camera, he asks, “Why is it that everything I’ve been eating this year is giving me diarrhea?”

Sinha is about to link the 2026 cyclospora outbreaks to decades of problems at the Food and Drug Administration. “I’m only allowed to make three diarrhea jokes in this video,” Sinha says. “I live in tyranny.”

The toilet video is one of the tamer stunts that Sinha and his co-creator, Gaurav Srivatchan, have pulled for their YouTube channel, A Show About The News, a weekly deep dive into major business and politics stories (tagline: “Critics are calling it the worst alternative to mainstream media, and those are just the critics I’m related to.”)

In a video about why young people can’t afford to buy homes, Sinha pops out of a cardboard box on the street and takes former New York City mayor Eric Adams to a studio apartment filled with men. Other recent videos include a 45-minute interview on the street with former White House communications director Anthony Scaramucci, an explainer on prediction market ads, and a rap music video on why retirement investments are safer than get-rich-quick schemes.

Sinha, 25, and Srivatchan, 22, met in 2023 when they were students at New York University’s Stern School of Business. They teamed up to make short vertical explainer videos, but those didn’t take off as much as they’d hoped. In 2024, Sinha quit his finance job to pursue A Show About The News full-time, and they transitioned to creating long-form deep dives with a dash of their own humor.

I chatted with Sinha and Srivatchan about how they launched their media careers, how they use humor to explain the news, and what they think business opportunities are for creators today. Our conversation has been edited for length and clarity.

Tameez: Why did you start creating news videos? Sinha: Gaurav and I started making videos together during the spring 2023 semester, when I was a senior at NYU and he was a freshman. I had been doing a newsletter for a while, I had been doing stand-up comedy for a few years, and I was interning at CNN. It seemed like everything was [pointing to], “Hey, you should start making short-form videos.” And then Gaurav was like, “Hey, I’m actually really good at editing videos.” We were not really thinking of it as a YouTube channel, but as making short-form stories. At the time, we were called Fifty50 Media. We were all about trying to distill the world into bipartisan perspectives. We eventually started focusing more on deeper-dive stories. We renamed ourselves to A Show About the News. It’s very easy to put out a political opinion that goes viral, but we really wanted to focus on good stories. Eventually, we started making videos for Morning Brew, and we joined Morning Brew full-time as a franchise in August 2025.

I had been doing a newsletter for a while, I had been doing stand-up comedy for a few years, and I was interning at CNN. Srivatchan: We realized that building a loyal audience off shorts wasn’t feasible in the long-term. And we constantly [faced] the challenge of bringing in nuance. That’s one of the reasons we started working on long-form videos. We try to bring in the political economy lens from our college education and highlight the underlying principles [of] today’s headlines. Sinha: To be honest, we weren’t successful in short-form. We had made 50 or 60 shorts… Srivatchan: Some of them would pop off, get a million views. But the way people consume on the internet is very different from the way people consume when they go to a theater, [where] they’re paying for an experience and they’re going to watch a specific thing. YouTube and social media are like a theater where you can leave and go watch another movie at any time. That’s the challenge of making videos on the internet.

Sinha: After our first video that got a million views, we were like, “Oh shit, this is it.” And it wasn’t. We added followers, but it wasn’t like we were going to get 100,000 people to come back in the next short. We were competing against the new Frozen movie and The Office and Mr. Beast exploding dynamite in his backyard. Tameez: Tell me more about how the Morning Brew deal happened. Srivatchan: I was in London, studying abroad. I slapped a bunch of logos as watermarks on our old videos [and sent them as] demo reels to news outlets. Sinha: We literally got zero responses…then an opportunity came to make a video for [Morning Brew] and it was a great experience. We made another and another, and then they were like, “You guys should just do this for us.” Srivatchan: Morning Brew provided us access to this office. It’s great to not meet under a lofted bed in Shreyas’ apartment. Sinha: They’re an excellent partner [because] they believe in allowing editorial control to be with the person who makes the video. We’re not going into meetings asking, can we do this topic next week? It’s a very high-trust environment, which, from talking to other people who work at other media companies, is extremely rare. Tameez: You guys both left careers in finance to do this full-time. Sinha: It was an economically stupid decision, but I knew that if I failed now, I would be young enough to start again. It’s easy to have the golden handcuffs of waiting until the right time, but there is never a right time. It was taking a bet on myself and someone who I really trusted. Still, our videos were getting 12 views at that time; it wasn’t as if something took off and it was like, “Okay, this can pay our bills.”

Srivatchan: I had the advantage of being younger. [Shreyas left] a full-time job. I did my summer internship in consulting and got my return offer, but it was a lot less of a risk for me, personally. It obviously helped that we had some backing from Morning Brew. Tameez: Why is making A Show About the News important now? How does it fit into the larger information ecosystem? Sinha: What we do, in the context of where we went to school, is the equivalent of becoming ballerinas. All of my friends are investment bankers in private equity or in consulting. That is the tried and true method [for NYU Stern graduates]. If you tell people, “Hey, I’m not recruiting for banking, I’m thinking of doing consulting,” they look at you like you just said you want to be an art major. When we said we were going to build a media company, it was truly mind-boggling for people. I loved what Fareed Zakaria did, what Ezra Klein did, but my favorite people when I was a kid were Jon Stewart and John Oliver, Hasan Minhaj and Seth Meyers and Conan O’Brien and Nathan Fielder. I knew I wasn’t going to be a great stand-up comedian, I wasn’t going to be a great writer, but maybe I could combine those to make a job out of it. It’s easy to pat ourselves on the back and say there’s a lot of garbage out there. But also, it has never been a better time to be an independent creator. If we both wanted to go into media today, we would be grabbing water for hosts who get paid $60 million a year. Instead, we actually get to put our own ideas out there.

Tameez: Tell me about your workflow, from video ideation to posting. Sinha: We don’t do short-form clips [from longer videos]. We script our shorts. That takes a ton of time. [But] long-form is the priority. It takes much more time, but you really get to have a relationship with the audience. Srivatchan: When it comes to shorts, either Shreyas or I will have something that really interests us for the week. We start scripting it, then we switch the scripts and each of us does a pass on the other’s. Then we revise them and film them. That takes roughly two out of five workdays. We spend the rest of the time on long-form. We’re also doing a weekly livestream to discuss the headlines with the audience and build that audience connection. So our output is two native short-form, one long-form, and one live stream per week.

Sinha: Do we actually have something new to say about it? There’s no point in making a video that someone else has already made.

A lot of people have made videos about how people aren’t having kids anymore. That doesn’t mean we wouldn’t [cover that topic], but we need to have something new to say. In our video, we talked about how governments have spent tens of billions of dollars but it hasn’t resulted in any more babies. We talked about demographic trends and got into studies. We brought in a bunch of 19- and 20-year-olds and asked them why they’re not having more sex. Then we went to a bunch of older people and were like, “So, you guys were doing it hella in the 90s. What’s the secret? Let’s give it to these kids.”

Sinha: We try to be funny, maybe to a deficit. In one of our worst-performing videos, we had a guy come in on an inflatable horse. Gaurav was wearing a Will Smith mask and slapped me. But sometimes it really works. We filmed this thing where we were having a shootout with Abraham Lincoln as he smoked a vape. That did great for us.

I listen to a lot of podcasts of serious, smart people. The way they talk, I’m like, how are you not ripping your hair off right now? How are you not just slamming your head against your desk?

Srivatchan: We have all these sources that we regularly read. For a lot of politics and inside scoops on Capitol Hill, Politico is great. For more niche stories, ProPublica is great. Each source has its own strength. We send stuff to each other all the time.

Once we’re in the research phase of a video, we do everything possible to learn about what the scope of the video is and what sources and articles can fall into that.

Sinha: We do a lot of our own fact-checking. Corrections often occur in the way of Gaurav coming to me and being like, “Shreyas, you moron, you said this and it’s actually this.” Then we record a voiceover, or we change it in the captions, or we just put it up as text.

Sinha: If you go on YouTube right now, high production quality is the expectation. It’s not like when I was young and my favorite YouTubers were clearly filming in their bedrooms. There’s so much money that is being invested into it, which is awesome, but if you want to have authentic relationships with your audiences, you need to do more.

Srivatchan: Earlier this year, TBPN [Technology Business Programming Network] was sold to OpenAI for $100 million. Their whole thing was live-streaming. They didn’t get that many viewers concurrently on their livestreams — everything was clips, targeting a very specific niche — but we saw how they grew through clips.

Sinha: When we started making these videos, I was writing articles on the side and freelancing so that I could pay rent. Eventually, this was able to pay rent.

By no means are we rich. But we really believe in the business model of digital media. It’s important to incentivize people to invest in media that is fact-checked, that is telling stories that are new and not just polarizing or viral for virality’s sake. You can’t ask people to only think of [media] as a charity expenditure or as a nonprofit, because those are the first things that go away when the market goes down, and the first thing people are going to stop cutting checks to if they don’t see the ROI.

We spend most of our time thinking about content, but it’s important to be creative about our business models. We always tell ourselves not to think about ourselves as employees or YouTubers, but to keep reminding ourselves that we’re founders of a startup that is trying to do something for the world.

The prevailing narrative that news media is doing poorly is because news media for generations was run by journalists, and that was fine because they could get cable carrier fees. But the reason they were able to do that was because they had a monopoly. You could only watch CNN, CBS, and ABC News because that’s all you had.

[I asked Sinha and Srivatchan to answer a few final questions via email. Their answers are below.]

Sinha: It’s hard to say what’s legacy and what’s new these days. Morning Brew has never had a TV broadcast or print media arm, but it’s owned by a media conglomerate, Axel Springer. Other news companies, from CNN to The Wall Street Journal, have pretty successful social media presences and journalists who’ve made a name for themselves.

The crisis for news companies that dominated in the 20th century is that they relied on fixed distribution: cable, broadband, local stations, and papers. A random Joe couldn’t get their ideas placed in those, so the competition for viewership was highly limited.

Today, competition is high. Legacy journalists who struggle often blame the changing tides of information consumption, when in reality they’re just struggling to compete for attention. Many have been successful in making the transition, so we don’t think it’s fair to paint all of legacy journalism as having something to learn from news creators. But our message overall would be that traditional news shouldn’t blame consumers for not maintaining their expensive newspaper and cable subscriptions, but instead [should] figure out how to compete and win in this new age.

Srivatchan: For journalists who have been successful in their careers but want to transition to social media, we think they severely underestimate how well-prepared they are to make the jump. They’ve already been writing strong articles and hooks to get people to click. We think journalists underestimate how that skill can translate on a platform like YouTube, where everything is dependent on the packaging that gets someone to click on your video.

Often, when someone from traditional media starts a new Instagram or YouTube page, they make very lo-fi content, talking to their phone with their headphones mic. I think they see influencers doing that and think viewers want authenticity. That works for some people, but our view is that investing in strong production is the baseline expectation on social media.

Instead of seizing the social media opportunity, often, legacy journalism is falling into the trap of liquidating its reputation for more attention and to better monetize its declining assets. It’s partnering with gambling apps — CNN’s partnership with Kalshi, or [Dow Jones’] with Polymarket — and inviting inflammatory internet voices rather than the trusted ones that educate.

#7295. Google’s News AI pilot expands to over 400 publications, including U.S. local news outlets

All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

In December, Google launched its News AI pilot program, which licenses content from select publishers and uses it to test new AI features in Google News. On Thursday, the company announced that the program has added new partnerships, bringing the total number of publications in the pilot to more than 400 worldwide.

At launch, the program partnered with international publishers like The Guardian, El País, The Times of India, and The Washington Post. More publications are now coming on board, including CNN, The Financial Times, Axios, and Forbes.

RELATED ARTICLEDiscover isn’t the only place Google is experimenting with AI-generated snippetsAndrew DeckJanuary 26, 2026As part of the expansion, the program has also added local news publishers across the U.S., including The Post and Courier in Charleston, South Carolina; Oil City News in Casper, Wyoming; the Illinois- and Iowa-based newspaper chain Shaw Media; and the nonprofit newsroom The Texas Tribune.

“People’s information consumption habits are changing, and we want to make sure publishers of all sizes, local newsrooms included, can navigate these shifts,” Brianna Puccini Duff, a spokesperson for Google, said in a statement to Nieman Lab.

Google declined to comment on the exact terms of the deals. However, Duff clarified that the News AI pilot does not operate on a “pay-per-value” model, meaning publishers are not compensated based on how much their content contributes to an AI-generated output. (The pay-per-value model is part of a parallel program that pays publishers for content surfaced in AI Overviews, AI Mode, and Gemini, according to a recent report by Digiday.)

With the News AI pilot, publishers are instead paid to provide content that appears in experimental AI-powered features. That includes “story previews” — in-depth, AI-generated article summaries of recent stories that may show up on a publisher’s Google News page. Here’s a Washington Post example, with a disclaimer noting the copy is AI-generated and “may include mistakes.”

An AI-generated “story preview” on the Google News page for The Washington Post

Another test feature is “audio briefing,” a customizable, AI-generated podcast in the Google News app that stitches together daily headlines. Users can select the topics they’re most interested in hearing about, including “World,” “Gaming,” or “Sports” news. The feature includes citations that link to articles mentioned in the briefing.

About the RoleWe're looking for a FinOps Data Engineer to help drive cost optimization and cloud financial governance across our AWS infrastructure and GCP footprint. You'll work cross-functionally with Engineering, Finance, and Product to find and ship savings, build the tooling necessary to maximize efficiency of every dollar spent in the cloud, and cultivate a culture of cost awareness across engineering teams. This role owns the data side of that mission: the models, pipelines, and analysis that make cost, usage, and margin numbers trustworthy across the company.This is a hands-on engineering role, not an analyst seat. You'll do the schlep work other teams don't have time for, digging into a bucket's access pattern, writing the dbt model or Python pipeline that ships the fix, building the cost-vs-revenue mart that answers a margin question once instead of every time, and chasing a number until it reconciles. Strong communication matters as much as technical depth, you'll regularly explain a savings case or a data model's implications to an engineering team, a finance stakeholder, and a leadership audience in the same week.What You'll Be Responsible ForIn this role, you'll:

Find and ship savings across AWS and GCP: Analyze billing, usage, and cost trends to identify opportunities, rightsizing, storage lifecycle policies, data transfer, and spot/auto-scaling. Take ideas from identification through to a realized dollar figure, not just a recommendation.

Build and maintain the FinOps data pipeline: Design and run the BigQuery/dbt models that turn raw billing and usage data (CUR, Storage Lens) into reconciled, trustworthy mart tables, the foundation everything else in FinOps is built on.

Build cost-vs-revenue and customer segmentation models: Model unit economics and margin by product line and customer segment, and extend coverage as new products and segments come online.

Apply data science to cost and usage data: Build forecasting models, detect anomalies statistically rather than by threshold alone, and quantify savings opportunities (e.g. storage lifecycle, request-cost patterns) with rigor a spreadsheet can't match.

Build and maintain cost attribution: Tagging policies, cost allocation, and chargeback/showback so engineering teams can see and own their own spend. This is foundational work other savings work depends on.

Automate cost governance: Build automated cost reporting, anomaly detection, and alerting. Write the scripts and infrastructure-as-code (Python, Terraform, Lambda) that enforce cost policy rather than relying on manual review.

Partner with engineering on architecture decisions: Bring cost into the room early, cost-efficiencies are cheaper to get right at design than to retrofit.

Work with Finance on forecasting and reporting: Support budget tracking and financial KPIs; build dashboards and self-serve analytics engineering and finance can both read.

Have strong AWS expertise and working GCP knowledge, including pricing models, billing structures, and cost optimization mechanics.

Have data engineering depth: dbt, BigQuery (or an equivalent modern warehouse), SQL at scale, and data modeling for analytics (dimensional modeling, incremental models, testing).

Have data science fundamentals: statistical forecasting, anomaly detection, and experimentation, and know when a rigorous model beats a rule of thumb.

Have automation and scripting skills: Python, Terraform/ pulumi, Lambda, or Bash.

Are comfortable with cost/billing tooling: AWS Cost Explorer, Cost & Usage Reports, GCP Billing Reports, and BI/dashboarding (we use Hex).

Have experience with, or are comfortable picking up, Linear and Notion as the system of record for tracking and documenting FinOps work.

Experience with a dedicated cloud cost management platform (e.g. CloudZero, Vantage, or similar) is a plus, not required.

Can analyze cost data and present it clearly to both technical and non-technical audiences.

Have prior experience spanning data analytics, data engineering, or data science in a FinOps, cloud cost management, or cloud governance context.

Are energized by doing the unglamorous, high-leverage work (the schlep) that unblocks other teams, and by working cross-functionally without positional authority.

We hire globally. We believe you can do your best work from anywhere. There are no Supabase offices, but we provide a WeWork membership or co-working allowance you can use anywhere in the world.

Use this budget to set up your ideal work environment—laptop, monitor, headphones, or whatever helps you do your best work.

Supabase covers 100% of health insurance for employees and 80% for dependents, wherever you are. Your wellbeing and your family’s health are important to us.

Once a year, the entire company gathers in a new city for a week of connection, collaboration, and fun. It’s a highlight of our year.

We operate asynchronously and trust you to manage your own time. You know what needs to be done and when.

Every team member receives an annual education allowance to spend on learning—courses, books, conferences, or anything that supports your growth.

Supabase was born-remote and open-source-first. We believe our globally distributed team is our secret weapon in building tools developers love.

Over $1B raised (including our $500M Series F)

#7293. A new report argues newsrooms need to do more experiments — like, the kind with randomization and results

All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

Mississippi Today had a question. Did the stories around its Pulitzer Prize-winning investigative reporting affect the way those investigations were received?

It’s the kind of question local newsrooms can’t easily test on their own. But researchers from Local NExT Lab at Syracuse University could.

In a national survey, 1,768 adults were shown the same investigation surrounded by a different mix of stories. In one, the investigation was shown alongside positive community stories. (Think: “How a local fossil park changed science history.”) In another, the investigation was featured alongside other investigative stories.

The investigation was rated more accurate, important, and relevant when it was surrounded by community-focused stories, not other investigative stories. (Audience reaction to a third story mix, where the investigation was surrounded by stories about legislation, was not consistent.)

The result was described in the first report from the Local NExT Lab. Joshua Darr, director of the lab and associate professor at Syracuse University, believes that although dashboards and engagement analytics are “very important tools” for newsrooms, they aren’t enough.

“Engagement data can’t tell you what caused audiences to engage, settle a hunch, or isolate your contribution,” the report reads. “Randomization can.”

“The key word there is ’caused,'” Darr added in an email. “Without randomization, you can tell when engagement is up or down or if a particular story is doing well, but it’s hard to know exactly why that is happening.”

RELATED ARTICLESearching for gold: Making sense of academic research about journalismAngie Drobnic HolanApril 27, 2023At Nieman Lab, we often hear from both sides of academic-practitioner partnerships. Researchers wonder why newsrooms don’t pay attention to their findings or fail to respond to their overtures about experiments. Publishers, editors, and journalists, meanwhile, tell me they don’t have time to read dense and jargon-filled academic papers. They can be annoyed by requests to spend time or resources they don’t have. And it’s not always fun to be someone else’s test subject.

When partnering with Local NExT Lab, Darr emphasized, the local newsrooms don’t have to commit money or manpower. They agree to two or three conversations. The researchers listen and then design, field, and analyze the experiments. In return, the newsrooms get their ideas tested and causal evidence.

In another experiment, the Local NExt Lab found that Instagram Reels including reporters’ faces drove the most interest and engagement, but when it came to clicking “follow,” profiles that looked like traditional news brands won out. Respondents chose to follow newsrooms (in this case New Orleans Public Radio) more often than reporter-named accounts.

The first batch of tests was funded by the W.K. Kellogg Foundation. Additional support from the American Journalism Project will allow for further tests on a larger cohort next year. The full report is here.
