Google’s Tal Akabas says changing tCPA, tROAS, or budgets on steady-state campaigns won’t trigger Learning - read why to skip seasonality adjustments.

Google’s Ads Product Liaison, Ginny Marvin, recently interviewed Product Manager Tal Akabas for her Ads Decoded podcast. I always love when product managers share behind-the-scenes details; you inevitably learn more than what is shared in official blog posts or launch communications. While much of the episode focused on new channel prioritization, it revealed several tactical nuggets that are immediately useful for advertisers heading into the holiday season and Black Friday Cyber Monday.

In this post, I’ll share the most interesting tidbits from their conversation. I tend to focus on technical details because that is where the real impact lies. Let’s look at what one of the leaders building Google Ads just revealed and what it means for your campaigns.

If you haven’t watched the episode, here is the context. Marvin and Akabas spend roughly 40 minutes on a wave of bidding and budgeting updates, with Channel Prioritization and Budget Allocation as the headline. Brooke Osmundson already covered that launch here at Search Engine Journal, so I keep my take on it short and spend more time on the details that got less attention.

One of the most stubborn myths in PPC is that changing a tCPA or tROAS target, or moving a daily budget by more than 20%, wipes out what Smart Bidding has learned. Google’s learning guidance distinguishes the “Learning” status in the interface from the continuous adjustments happening in the background.

Akabas addressed this directly (25:14). On an existing, steady-state campaign, changing a target or budget does not erase historical data or trigger “Learning” status. He explained that the backend already has bid landscape data and can scale bids in proportion to target changes.

New campaigns can still need time to ramp up for their particular mix of assets, targeting, and goals (26:03). New or reactivated bid strategies, composition changes, and significant conversion-goal changes can also trigger “Learning” status. For new conversion-oriented campaigns, Google’s advice in the episode is to start with Maximize Conversions or Maximize Conversion Value rather than use Maximize Clicks as a mandatory first step.

This removes a psychological barrier to changing targets when business conditions warrant it. It does not mean performance cannot fluctuate as bids and traffic mix change. Allow for conversion delay and avoid repeated target changes within a single conversion cycle unless there is a clear business need.

See also: Ask A PPC: What Are Learning Periods In Digital Marketing?

Seasonality Adjustments let you tell Smart Bidding to expect a short-term change in conversion rates, such as during a sale. It is tempting to switch one on for Black Friday, but Akabas said you don’t necessarily need them just because it’s BFCM (29:12). Google’s year-over-year models already anticipate standard holiday spikes.

Our own study of BFCM accounts from 2022 to 2024 found that accounts using seasonality adjustments saw CPCs rise about twice as much as those that didn’t. The adjustment cohort’s ROAS fell in each year studied, while its revenue grew faster than the no-adjustment cohort’s. These observational comparisons show an association; they do not isolate the effect of the adjustment from differences between advertisers and promotions.

Accounts that used seasonality adjustments during BFCM saw CPCs rise about twice as much as those that didn’t, and lower ROAS. Source: Optmyzr BFCM seasonality adjustments study, 2022–2024. (Image from author, November 2026)

Save adjustments for anomalies the AI can’t know about, such as an off-cycle flash sale or a sitewide discount much deeper than last year’s.

In the episode, Akabas says Promotion Mode is rolling out to Search and PMax. It lets you schedule a promotional window with dedicated budget and bid changes (19:20). He explains that it combines faster ramp-up with Smart Bidding Exploration during the window to capture additional traffic.

It pairs well with Campaign Total Budgets, which remain limited to net-new campaigns. You can also schedule Promotion Mode on existing steady-state campaigns.

Smart Bidding Exploration, now rolling out to Retail PMax and coming to Shopping (17:13), gives the algorithm a small ROAS tolerance to bid into new queries and incremental auctions. That’s typically around 10% effective ROAS flexibility, per Google’s FAQs.

Here is the catch: Smart Bidding Exploration requires an eligible tROAS campaign with an unconstrained budget. That means a budget set high enough that it does not limit spend, so the ROAS target guides spending. If the budget becomes constrained, the exploration mechanism is disabled.

This is the headline feature of Ginny’s podcast episode. For the rollout scope, defaults, and setup, see Brooke’s report. Here is the short version, plus the mechanics that matter for governance.

The problem these controls solve is familiar. Cross-channel campaigns like Performance Max combine inventory in a single campaign, while Search campaigns have offered an on/off choice for Search Partners and the Google Display Network (GDN). The new controls add a middle ground for advertisers who want to retain access while steering allocation.

The episode introduces new controls for Search, Shopping, Performance Max, and Demand Gen (01:08). Channel Prioritization sorts supported channels into High Priority and Low Priority tiers. Budget Allocation adds an optional, best-effort daily spend limit for Low Priority channels in Search, Shopping, and Performance Max.

All channels start as High Priority. In Performance Max and Demand Gen, Google’s own properties are grouped as “Google channels.” Availability varies by campaign type and rollout timing.

One discrepancy to flag: Google’s help doc says Budget Allocation is not supported for Demand Gen, yet Akabas suggested that Demand Gen advertisers who opted out of Display could test back in by adding it at lower priority or with a budget allocation (04:52). Check what your account actually offers before you plan around it.

How the tiers behave depends on whether your campaign is limited by budget, as Marvin clarified in a follow-up note on LinkedIn. With a budget limit, spend flows to High Priority channels first. Once additional High Priority spend would miss your target, budget shifts to Low Priority channels, but only when they’re predicted to deliver conversions at or better than your target, and Budget Allocation caps are still respected.

Without a budget limit, which is Google’s recommended setup, Channel Prioritization alone changes nothing, because Smart Bidding already goes after every eligible conversion at your target across all the networks you’re opted into.

For Max Conversions, Max Conversion Value, and Max Clicks, Google’s help documentation describes a simple spill-over: High Priority channels get the budget first, and Low Priority channels see spend only when High Priority can’t use the full daily budget.

That creates a catch-22. Google recommends uncapped, demand-led budgets with tCPA and tROAS (32:26), but a budget that never limits spend leaves Channel Prioritization nothing to do.

Akabas notes it still works on any day your budget limits spend, even if the campaign is generally unconstrained (03:37).

To restrict Low Priority channels on an uncapped campaign, you need Budget Allocation, which sets a daily percentage spend ceiling on any Low Priority channel.

Per Google’s help documentation, a Low Priority channel set to 0% gets no spend. In Performance Max, where you can’t opt out of channels individually, that is effectively your opt-out.

How Channel Prioritization and Budget Allocation behave depending on your bidding strategy and budget state. (Image created by Optmyzr, November 2026)

Before you roll these settings out across accounts, check the limitations in Google’s current technical documentation.

The “ghost budget” trap: a 10% Display cap on a $5,000 budget still allows up to $500 a day on Display, as much as this campaign normally spends in total. (Image created by Optmyzr, November 2026).

Two more compatibility details to check, both from Google’s help documentation: Channel Prioritization works with Campaign Total Budgets only in Demand Gen, and both controls can be used in Custom Experiments, with restrictions. Multi-campaign shared budgets are unsupported in those experiments, and all channels in them are treated on the same priority tier.

Brooke’s report flags the February 2027 Display change as well. The podcast adds the detail on how today’s behavior works.

Right now, when a Search campaign is opted into Display through Display Expansion, the existing allocation behavior treats Display as a low-priority outlet for unused Search budget (07:17). This behavior is also described in Google’s Display Expansion documentation.

Google’s current documentation says Search campaigns with Display Expansion enabled will begin migrating to the new controls in February 2027. The episode describes the transition as a February-March timeframe (09:09).

The existing allocation behavior will be replaced, so advertisers may see a shift in spending between Search, Search Partners, and Display. Setting channel priorities before the migration replaces the old behavior right away.

Marvin has said Google will share clearer guidance as the date gets closer.

Action item: Audit your Google Ads Manager Account (formerly known as My Client Center of MCC) now and flag every legacy Search campaign opted into Display Expansion, so the February 2027 change doesn’t catch your team off guard. Also check which of those campaigns use Target Impression Share, because Google’s doc says the Display Network will no longer serve on Search campaigns that use that bid strategy.

Feeding better business data into Google Ads remains the highest-leverage activity for PPC managers. Customer Lifecycle Goals let you tell Google which kind of customer you are after, whether new, lapsed, or loyal. Three updates make that easier to execute and audit:

Make sure your product feed segmentation matches your financial goals, too. Keep custom labels for margin, inventory depth, and price competitiveness up to date, then use those labels to inform product selection and campaign structure. Labels alone do not change bids or prevent acquisition premiums on low-margin or low-stock SKUs.

A major theme of the episode was demand-led budgeting (30:10). That means pairing uncapped or highly flexible budgets with strict tCPA or tROAS targets, so campaigns expand automatically when consumer demand spikes.

In auction theory, this makes sense, as Google’s research on auto-bidding auction design explores. If you’re willing to pay $50 per acquisition, you should buy every $50 conversion available instead of shutting off at 2:00 p.m. because a daily budget ran out. Akabas makes the related point that missing efficient conversions early can mean paying more for them later in the day, week, or month (31:45).

In practice, PPC teams answer to CFOs and clients who run on fixed monthly budgets allocated by business unit. As good as the math is, the business rules become the limiting factor. Three steps can help bridge the gap between Google’s auction AI and your finance department.

Ground conversion values and efficiency targets in your economics (21:15), whether through profit-based values or revenue targets calibrated to margins and customer lifetime value. If values or targets overstate what an acquisition is worth, increasing budget headroom can scale unprofitable spend.

Google highlighted updates to Performance Planner (35:25), the Missed Opportunities Report (37:23), and V2 of the Recommended Investment Strategy tool (36:25). V2 now lets you filter budget reallocation suggestions by specific conversion goals or specific campaigns. To keep recommendations within Brand A’s P&L, explicitly restrict the selected campaigns to Brand A. The tool does not infer business-unit budget boundaries for you. Marvin also plugged the cross-channel budgeting tools in Google Analytics (38:42). They can pull in campaign data, including direct connections with platforms such as Meta, Pinterest, Reddit, and Snap, so you can run planning scenarios across channels.

If you can’t uncap a client’s monthly budget, give campaigns enough daily headroom that features like Smart Bidding Exploration aren’t throttled on peak days. Keep daily budgets realistic enough that percentage-based Budget Allocation caps still do what you want them to.

Then layer external pacing monitors, scripts, or automated rule engines over your account groups to track cumulative monthly spend. If a demand surge pushes spend ahead of your monthly trajectory, rules can:

That lets you capture demand-led upside while limiting the risk of an end-of-month overspend.

Product managers rarely go into this much detail in a launch post, which is why episodes like this one are worth the 40 minutes. Three details change what I would do this season. Leave your targets and budgets alone unless the business changes, because steady-state campaigns do not reset. Skip Seasonality Adjustments unless something truly unusual is happening that Google could not have seen coming. And check that your budget settings let Channel Prioritization and Smart Bidding Exploration do anything at all, since both depend on whether your budget is capped.

Then put the February 2027 Display Expansion change on your calendar, and feed Google the customer and margin data that make your targets worth trusting.

#7265. Meta delays rollout of terms that would allow broad scraping of news sites. Legal experts are still skeptical.

All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

Meta’s new commercial terms will go into effect three weeks later than initially planned.

RELATED ARTICLELegal experts warn Meta’s new terms still grant broad scraping permissions, despite language changesAndrew DeckOctober 17, 2026Meta has delayed the effective date of its new terms of service for business accounts to November 20 in the face of mounting pressure from the global news industry.

Nieman Lab first reported on the terms on October 15. They would allow for the mass scraping of websites “associated with” business accounts on Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp, and Threads. Virtually every news organization has at least one business account. On October 16, Meta removed the word “train” from its terms and limited the use of future scraped content to “advertising and business products.”

The terms were previously set to take effect on October 30, with no way to opt out, setting off an outcry from news publishers, politicians, and press associations on both sides of the Atlantic.

“We are extending the effective date of our updated Commercial Terms and Self-Serve Ad Terms to November 20 to allow more time for us to explain to our partners and stakeholders what’s changing and what’s not — including how Meta uses web crawlers and the fact that content owners will still be able to use robots.txt to signal preferences,” a Meta spokesperson told Nieman Lab in a statement Friday.

A Meta spokesperson said on October 17 that the company revised the language because it “wasn’t clear in the initial consolidation of terms that robots.txt preferences are respected. News sites, like all other content owners, still have the ability to disable the crawler via robots.txt flags. That has been the case, and it has not changed.”

As of October 23, Meta has made no other changes to the terms aside from the implementation date. No versions of the terms include language about respecting robots.txt preferences.

“Publishers should always be concerned about tech companies attempting to take content for free, and should assume that Meta is taking this additional time to either find a new way to try to mislead publishers into granting Meta free access to valuable copyrighted content or finally give up in the face of pressure,” said Matt Topic, a media and intellectual property attorney at Loevy & Loevy. “Publishers don’t need more PR statements or explanations. They need Meta to keep its hands off their copyrighted material and respect publishers’ terms of service.”

“I don’t think that repeating the same non-explanations for another three weeks will make much difference,” James Grimmelmann, a professor of digital and information law at Cornell Law School, added. “But maybe they’ll use the time to come up with better explanations.”

Thomas Höppner, a professor and attorney specializing in competition law in Germany, told Nieman Lab that “Meta’s conduct constitutes a prima facie infringement of European Union competition law, and a textbook case for imposing interim measures.”

The postponement could be a legal strategy that the company is exploring, he said.

“My fear is that this is merely a measure by Meta to reduce the risk of court actions for interim measures,” Höppner said. “If affected parties wait too long from the day of knowledge of the changes [until] the filing of an action, a court will assume that the matter cannot be urgent — and deny interim relief on this ground…Under some jurisdictions, a platform needs to give business users appropriate warning before implementing measures. It may well be that Meta just tries to reduce the risk of losing on the ground not having sufficiently informed business users about its new terms.”

News publishers and press associations have called on regulators to intervene before the terms take effect, and on Meta to include specific language about respecting publishers’ crawling preferences.

On Thursday, the News/Media Alliance in the United States sent a letter to Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg, demanding that the company suspend the terms before October 30. The World Association of News Publishers (WAN-IFRA) sent a similar letter to Meta’s chief global affairs officer Joel Kaplan on the same day.

Multiple European press associations signed a joint letter to the European Commission, citing potential violations of the Digital Markets Act and calling for intervention. Earlier this week, two German publisher associations called on the European Commission to prohibit the new terms from going into effect until a complete review has been conducted.

In the United Kingdom, the Competition and Market Authority sent a formal letter to Meta to discuss the terms. In a parliamentary committee session on Tuesday, executive director Will Hayter said he had a meeting scheduled with the company on Wednesday to learn more about the terms.

“The CMA has been in urgent discussions with Meta this week on this important issue,” a CMA spokesperson said on Friday. “Meta has now paused implementation until 20 November. We will continue to scrutinize these terms and engage with Meta and others as we consider our next steps.”

Theo Bamber, chief executive of the U.K’s News Media Association, wrote on LinkedIn on Friday that “this delay is welcome, but it is a pause not a solution.”

RELATED ARTICLEMeta’s new commercial terms will allow the scraping of news sites, legal experts sayAndrew DeckOctober 15, 2026“What needs to happen next is for the Competition and Markets Authority, and other regulators around the world, to secure clear, public commitments from Meta to abandon the offending elements of the new Terms before they take effect,” Bamber said.

Invalid traffic on AI Max search doubled to 5.28%. Get the channel-by-channel retail benchmarks before Black Friday.

Ask the SEJ experts you already read what AI, agents, and algorithm changes mean for your traffic. Private, human to human. $97/mo.

AI Search Tracking Checklist: How to Attribute Calls From ChatGPT, Claude, and Perplexity

Google's Q3 earnings call describes a future that could leave classic Search on the margins.

Google’s third-quarter earnings call reports its strongest year-over-year query growth in five years, explaining that AI Mode is creating additional searches. Google also laid out its plan to further transition away from classic Search toward a more agentic, task-driven experience.

The Q3 earnings call highlighted strong search query growth and the significant role AI Mode played in driving it. The company described its year-over-year query growth as its strongest in five years, including more searches with commercial intent, tying it to double-digit growth in Search advertising revenue.

Yet the earnings call made it clear that there’s a gap between the query growth and Search advertising revenue: AI Mode is driving additional queries, but those interactions generate less advertising revenue.

Google is reporting the strongest search query growth in five years but the web ecosystem is seeing the lowest levels of referrals from Google. The earnings call confirms what search marketers and site owners already know and the fact that query growth is at all time highs will no doubt sting.

“Search has strong momentum. Our AI investments are driving increased usage and overall query growth, including commercial queries. In fact, our year‑over‑year query growth rate is the highest it’s been in the last five years.

…Let’s turn to Search, which is bringing the benefits of AI to more people than any other product in the world. Just like our shift to mobile over a decade ago, we are focused on building the best Search user experience, followed by monetization.”

Philipp Schindler, SVP and CBO, at Google boasted of growth, including with AI Mode, but also explained that currency exchange rates (foreign exchange aka FX) was the reason for a slowdown in advertising growth. He also conceded AI Mode was monetizing at a lower rate.

“In Q3, Search grew 12% year‑over‑year to $63 billion, and when you look at the change in growth rate from Q2 to Q3, there were a few drivers here.”

First, there was FX. It was the single largest driver of Search deceleration relative to Q2.

…it’s worth noting that the strong growth in AI Mode queries had an impact because of the lower monetization we were seeing in AI Mode. To be clear, we feel very good about our trajectory here. Our ad experiments have shown promising results and we’re now scaling ads within both AI Overviews and AI Mode to more users and more queries; including, as I mentioned, international markets and multiturn ads in the U.S.”

Anat Ashkenazi, SVP and CFO, Alphabet and Google also boasted about high query growth:

“We’re in a unique position to be able to monetize our AI investments across many products that reach billions of users and enterprises. Our AI investments in Search are driving our highest query growth in half a decade.”

Another search trend that was called out was the transformation of Search into a task-based experience. CEO Sundar Pichai described AI agents as a new stage in Search’s evolution, enabling Google to satisfy needs that were previously not possible with classic Search.

The agentic transformation of Search is something that will be connected across Search, Gemini, Chrome, Android, and Workspace. Pichai viewed this transition as an opportunity to expand what Search can do but unfortunately he said nothing about what effect this transformation may have on the web ecosystem.

Pichai explained how Search is transforming:

“One area I’m excited about is helping people get things done, be it booking reservations, filling in forms, scheduling appointments, or making purchases. …People already put their trust in Google to get things done in their daily lives; and our leadership here remains an important differentiator.

…As a next step, we’re bringing these features to Search. And also, of course, to our billion users on the Gemini app. People are already using the Gemini app to do more than ask questions; they’re using it to do things, including complex, multi‑step agentic queries. Our Gemini 4 series has been a really big step forward here and has already been handling these complex tasks really well.”

See also: Google Reveals How AI Search Is Reshaping What Users Query

Pichai also returned to the theme of AI agents as a “unifying layer” across all of their products.

“Agents will operate as a unifying layer across our products, so you’ll see us extend these agentic experiences beyond Search and the Gemini app to Chrome, Android and our Workspace products as well.

…just like a few years ago, being able to incorporate AI chat use cases in Search allowed people to ask more and do more in Search, which is what is playing out in our usage.

I think agents would, again, be an opportunity to expand the types of problems we solve for our users.

I think people always underestimate all the components you need to deliver these complex experiences for users. And Search on the surface looks simple, but there’s extraordinary deep levels of investment and things we have built over time, like Knowledge Graph being an example.

And so our understanding of the world, et cetera.

So, I think I’m excited about agents, and I would view it as a new frontier, which brings in a new set of use cases to Search, and so we are excited to work through that.”

Google’s Q3 earnings call makes it clear that classic Search is increasingly going away in favor of of a more task-based orientation. SEOs talk about Answer Engine Optimization but Google’s not interested in providing answers. The future of Search is about helping users complete tasks, with Search being the starting point and another Google product at the other end.

Google intends to use AI agents across its products to give people more reasons to stay within Google’s ecosystem. That’s pretty bad news for SEOs and site owners because there is nothing in that scenario that speaks toward sending more referrals to the open web.

#7263. I went looking for the source of one little statistic. That was easier said than done.

All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

The claim: 75% of your emotions are generated by smell. It had to come from somewhere, right?

Apparently, 75% of your emotions are generated by smell.

Or that’s what the internet says, anyway. The statistic appears everywhere from marketing books and articles to academic papers about the power of scent. As a perfumer (someone who creates fragrances) and journalist who writes about these things, I came across it several times, and when I finally wanted to cite it for an article about the impact of scent on mood and memory, I went looking for the original research.

This wasn’t a totally new experience for me. One time, while working on a workplace story as the editor of a hospitality trade magazine, I couldn’t find the source of an employee retention statistic, so I wrote the people who included it in a study. They wrote back to say they had no idea what I was talking about.

In this case, there was no such dead end. I followed link after link, figuring surely I would get to the bottom of it, but every source pointed to another source, which pointed to another, and somehow none of them led to the original research I was looking for.

I asked ChatGPT, Google Gemini and Claude for help. They gave me links to wellness blogs, aromatherapy companies, and authoritative-looking PDF reports. But as I ruled each one out as the original source, the answers became more circular, and the trail ate itself.

Me: Where did the statistic that 75% of emotions are generated by smell come from?

Google Gemini The Sense of Smell Institute.

Gemini: There isn’t a specific study. The statistic was popularized through scent marketing research.

Gemini: Martin Lindstrom’s 2005 book Brand Sense.

Me: Does the book contain the original research?

Gemini: Lindstrom commissioned extensive research into sensory branding through the research firm Millward Brown.

Me: Does that research establish that 75 percent of emotions are generated by smell?

Gemini: Would you like to know how lavender and citrus can influence your mood?

Lindstrom did look like a real lead. Several writers and businesses traced the number to the Danish author’s 2005 book Brand Sense: Sensory Secrets Behind the Stuff We Buy. Simon & Schuster’s page for the book says it outright: “Research shows that a full 75% of our emotions are in fact generated by what we smell.” Aha!

I bought the book and read it. While there is talk of emotions and the senses, the number isn’t in there.

Next, I wrote to Lindstrom’s company asking them to point me toward the original research. They sent me a link to a copy of Brand Sense and told me I would find the research in the book.

I tried another route. Brand Sense was based in large part on an international study by market research company Millward Brown. The 75% figure has been attributed directly to that research. So I went looking for the Millward Brown study. But I couldn’t find it anywhere.

There were other questions: Does the stat even make scientific sense? How would you measure the percentage of emotions generated by smell? Do people with no sense of smell experience 75% fewer emotions? And what about emotions that seem to have nothing to do with the senses at all, like grief over someone’s death, a breakup, or anxiety over losing your job?

I asked Kristen Lindquist, a social and affective neuroscientist and psychology professor at Ohio State University who studies emotion. She had never heard of the statistic.

“I imagine if somebody had done that study I would be aware of it,” she told me.

There is a relationship between smell and emotion, and it may be possible to measure something like this, she said. Researchers could, for example, ask people throughout the day how they’re feeling and whether what they’re feeling is related to something they’re seeing, hearing, touching or smelling. But that still wouldn’t make emotion the product of one sense. “Emotions really arise from all of our sensations,” Lindquist said, including signals from within our bodies. Our brains process all of that information together to figure out what is happening and what it means for us.

RELATED ARTICLERepetition makes climate misinformation feel more true — even for those who back climate scienceYangxueqing Mary JiangAugust 12, 2024There’s a name for the particular way an unsupported claim can acquire the appearance of fact through citation: citogenesis. Coined by Randall Munroe in an XKCD comic, the term describes the process by which an unsupported claim gets repeatedly cited until the citations themselves make it look like truth.

I called Jodi Schneider, an associate professor at the University of Wisconsin-Madison Information School whose research includes scientific evidence and citation integrity, to talk about it. I sent her the 75% statistic, and she went looking for the source herself.

“It was not a casual ‘Let me look for 20 minutes, and there it is,'” she told me. “I would find a thing, [it] would go to something else, and that would be a dead end.”

The problem, Schneider said, is that repeating a claim is much easier than investigating it. “Somebody says something, it sounds like a thing you’d like to know or repeat, and you don’t trace it back to where it came from. You just pass it on.” Then repetition becomes the “evidence,” and “if you hear the same thing from multiple places, it’s harder to question.”

This psychological phenomenon is known as the illusory truth effect: We’re more likely to believe information we’ve encountered before. The effect was first demonstrated in the 1970s and has since been replicated many times. More unsettlingly, research has found that repetition can make a false claim seem more believable even when it contradicts something we know to be true.

In other words, seeing the same statistic everywhere doesn’t just make it look well sourced; it makes it feel true.

It’s hard to fully check every claim. Writers build arguments from dozens of pieces of information, and tracing each one all the way back to its origin can take an absurd amount of time.

Newsrooms have spent years cutting staff and budgets, including the fact-checkers and copy editors whose job was to catch this kind of thing. At the same time, the volume of information journalists have to sort through has exploded. Finding a source for a claim can take seconds. Establishing where it actually came from can take hours (or an eternity).

Meanwhile, the consequences of not checking facts compound. Once a bad claim gets published, it becomes another source for the next journalist, another search result for the next reader and another apparent confirmation that the claim must be true.

AI is making that problem worse. It repeats the same unsupported claims while stripping away some of the clues that might otherwise make us suspicious of the source.

“The polish that generative AI can put on just about anything is already a challenge,” Schneider said. More importantly, “Generative AI is really, really good at being persuasive, even if the claims inside the persuasion have no basis in reality.”

Most people are not going to track a statistic through six articles, buy the book everyone cites, email the author, and start calling academics. They don’t have the time or energy for that, and they shouldn’t have to do it anyway. One of journalism’s roles is to provide information that’s more reliable than TikTok or whatever nonsense Google Gemini spits out.

When we get it wrong, we don’t just add another bad source to the pile. We give the claim credibility and put it in front of more people. And once they’ve seen it, the illusory truth effect suggests they’re more likely to believe it the next time. (Research has also found that repeated misinformation is more likely to be repeated than new misinformation, and can continue to influence people even after it has been corrected.)

Nobody is going to die because they believe smell generates 75 percent of their emotions. But replace that claim with one about a vaccine, a war, an election or a medical treatment and the same failure becomes considerably less benign.

That’s why the difference between finding a source and finding the source matters. I found hundreds of sources for the 75% statistic. I still haven’t found the source. That doesn’t mean it’s not out there.

Can you find the source of the 75% stat? Email [email protected].

Uscreen is the video monetization platform for businesses building recurring revenue from video content. Our customers replace a patchwork stack of separate hosting, community, courses, email, and app vendors with one branded experience across web, mobile, and TV.

The platform is only half of it. We believe growth requires behavior, not just software. Customers don't stall because a feature is missing. They stall because they priced wrong, never built an email list, or launched an offer nobody wanted. Coaching is how we fix that, and it's part of the product rather than an add-on.

Maybe you ran marketing for a small business, coached founders, built your own audience, or worked inside a membership or subscription business. Search Console's Page indexing report has fallen behind before. Here's what Google has said and what each remaining check can show while the data lags.

A Reddit post this month reported the Search Console Page indexing report had not been updated since Oct. 16. The person later stated that other properties, including established sites, were experiencing issues as well.

John Mueller responded from Google stating it didn’t make sense for Google to comment on the refresh date of every single report all the time. In addition, Mueller suggested that “this is why we put dates in there.” Mueller then explained that indexing changes will appear in the Performance report first. He further went on to say Google prioritizes faster updates in areas they believe will be most beneficial. Roger Montti wrote up the exchange on Oct. 27.

An old date on that report tells you how current the report is. On its own, it doesn’t tell you whether Google indexed or dropped any pages. URL Inspection shows Google’s reported index status for specific URLs, and the Performance report shows recorded search activity for the dates it covers.

Google has provided information on how these checks work through their help pages and public comments about delays in late 2025 and also this summer. As of Oct. 29, the Page indexing report is listed with “No recent issues” in Google’s Data anomalies in Search Console page (which keeps a record of known data issues).

Page indexing data fell weeks behind in late 2025, and Google acknowledged the delay publicly. On Nov. 28, a user asked Mueller on Bluesky whether Google was “only updating page indexing reports” once a month, adding, “I’ve been trying to validate some fixes, and I haven’t seen a page indexing update in 11 days.”

Mueller replied within the hour, “I’ll check with the team.” The next day, he posted:

“Sorry! Looking at our data, the index coverage data is older than what we’d consider normal :-/ (this is usually just reporting, and not related to actual indexing). I don’t have any information on when it’ll catch back up for now, but I’ll update here as I hear more.”

Google Search Central then posted on LinkedIn:

“We’re currently experiencing longer than usual delays in the Search Console Index Coverage report. This only affects reporting, not crawling, indexing, or ranking of websites.”

The notice said Google would update the post once the issue was resolved. On Dec. 1, Mueller posted in the Bluesky thread that “We did an official confirmation” and included a LinkedIn link. I covered that notice the same day, when Google’s screenshot showed data last updated Nov. 18.

On Dec. 12, the same user said the last update they saw for the indexation reports was Nov. 21. Mueller answered, “I don’t have an update, sorry. Both the page indexing and the performance reports are currently delayed past what we’d consider normal.”

Six days later, the user posted, “Looks like the indexation reports have finally caught up.” Mueller responded, “I just got a bunch of error emails for my sites too :). Sorry it took so long!”

The report fell behind in June. On June 30, a user asked Mueller why the Page indexing report’s data still only went up to June 11 and when it would catch up. He replied on July 1:

“Sorry for the delay. We’re working on getting this back up to speed, but I don’t have an ETA just yet.”

The same day, another user stated they had been having the same issue with the links report not updating lately and the last time the report did update was the last date of Page indexing data, and wanted to know if this was possibly connected. Mueller answered, “I don’t think they’re related (at least we track them separately). I think the links report generally just doesn’t update as often, but it might be that the same bottleneck is involved.”

In mid-July other users replied saying the issue continued to happen for them. On July 23 the user from the June 30 post came back to say the report was still only current to July 9. In the late 2025 and summer threads Mueller also did not provide a date for when the data would catch up.

On Sept. 11, a user posted on Bluesky that they were seeing an issue across all their Search Console properties and asked, “The data was there yesterday?” Mueller replied that it was likely related to the data delay in June, explaining that “there just isn’t any data for that period” and that the Page indexing report hadn’t been updated. He also added:

“We don’t back-fill indexing data. I’ll check w/the team when they’re back from holidays to be sure.”

As of Oct. 29, that thread shows no follow-up from him. The exchange doesn’t settle whether June’s data was never collected or was collected and isn’t shown, since the user’s post suggested the data had been visible the day before.

His statement was about Page indexing data. Search Console has restored missing data in another report this year.

Google’s help page, About Search Console data, says, “You can see last updated dates on most reports.” It also notes that there may be a delay between when numbers are calculated and when site owners can see them, adding, “Normally, however, collected data should be available in 2-3 days.”

That guidance doesn’t specify a refresh schedule for the Page indexing report, and, as of Oct. 29, the report’s own help page doesn’t provide one either. It does say, “Validation typically takes up to about two weeks, but in some cases can take much longer, so please be patient.”

The validation estimate describes Google rechecking the URLs you fixed. It doesn’t tell you when the report will update.

The data anomalies page explains that it “records known issues in the last 3-16 months that might affect your data.” Its 2026 entries cover logging errors in the Performance, Discover, and Generative AI reports, as well as the end of FAQ rich results in May. One entry notes, “A logging error prevented Search Console from accurately reporting impressions from May 13, 2025 until April 27, 2026.”

An Aug. 21 update to the entry on missing Generative AI report data for Aug. 13 to 17 reads, “Missing data for this period has been restored.” Another entry says Feb. 28 and March 1 are missing from bulk data exports for some properties, adding, “This data won’t be recovered.”

In a report to leadership, a Page indexing chart can’t establish what happened after the latest date it covers. Fresh dates with the same totals show that the totals didn’t change. They don’t show whether individual URLs kept their status.

The report’s example list won’t settle that either. Its help page says the list “does not necessarily show all URLs with that issue, and is limited to 1,000 rows.” For the URLs that matter, Google says URL Inspection “provides information about Google’s indexed version of a specific page” and lets you test whether a URL might be indexable.

The tool’s help page says that indexed result “is not a live test” and reflects the most recently indexed version of the page. The live test checks whether Google can access the page now. Asked whether a valid live result means the page will be indexed, the same help page answers “No” and says, “There is no definitive test that can guarantee whether your page will be included in the Google index.”

The Performance report will display clicks and impressions of your search results within the time frame displayed by the report, and Mueller says that’s where indexing changes show up first. The URL Inspection tool’s help page states that a “URL is on Google” result “is not guaranteed to be there” in search results; therefore, getting no impressions in the Performance report does not mean the page is not indexed. Mueller’s response to the question asked on Dec. 12 also indicated that the Performance report was delayed at that point too; thus, its date needs the same caution.

When comparing data within trend reports, make sure to export with dates. Compare both the date range and the quantity of entries. Also, verify whether the chart ended at an old date; whether the graph is displaying previous quantities on newly reported dates; or whether some intervals were missed. Mueller stated in September that Google doesn’t back-fill indexing data, and Mueller further mentioned that he would ask his team about back-fill, therefore exporting these trends should continue.

Google’s Page indexing help page says, “Values shown as either ~ or – in the report (not available/not a number) will be zeros in the downloaded data.” As read on Oct. 29, the page doesn’t say how a reporting delay appears in an export. A screenshot saved with each export shows which values the report displayed as ~ or -.

The anomalies page says that “if we change our data aggregation methods or there is a logging error, you might see a dip or bump in your chart.” It doesn’t explain what qualifies a reporting delay for an entry. Whether the team check Mueller mentioned in September changed his back-fill answer is also open.

The Reddit thread reflects what its posters saw. It doesn’t establish whether the delay reported this month has ended or how many properties it reached.

Next time you send a report, look at the last-updated date of the Page indexing report and add that to the chart. This will show how current the data in the chart is. A newer update date indicates new data was added so we should compare those new numbers with the previous dated reports.

What do we mean when we talk about news deserts?

The term has become a shorthand for areas devoid of local news coverage. But a new essay from the Independent Journalism Atlas recalls that when Penny Abernathy popularized the term through her research, she used it to describe a more nuanced picture:

Things grow in a desert, she told Medill’s Tim Franklin in 2024, just not as abundantly. Asked why she didn’t say “news vacuum,” she answered, “There’s news; it’s just not necessarily the quality and the quantity of what you would find elsewhere.” RELATED ARTICLEFrom bad to worse: 2026 is shaping up to be “a super El Niño year for local news”Sophie CulpepperOctober 13, 2026To show what information can look like in news deserts, the Independent Journalism Atlas — an initiative that aims to “[document] independent creators who inform, educate, and advance public knowledge outside traditional media structures,” cofounded by Liz Kelly Nelson, Justin Bank, and 2025 Nieman Fellow Ryan Kellett — took a closer look at 46 of the 238 news desert counties identified in this year’s State of Local News report from Medill. RELATED ARTICLEMany people who live in “local news deserts” don’t feel deprived of local news, study findsLaura Hazard OwenFebruary 10, 2026“Look at the ground and news moves like water,” writes Bank. “It doesn’t stop at a county line. It runs off the surface, sinks underground and comes up wherever someone digs.” The team found that “in more places than the desert map shows, someone has picked up a shovel.” (That might help explain why people who live in news deserts don’t feel deprived of local news.) The team identifies a few patterns in how information looks and travels in news deserts, including “surface” information, wells, and springs. Posts from the local sheriff, weather alerts, and obituaries from the funeral home are all examples of “surface” information that “runs off,” Bank writes, typically telling you what happened without telling you why. Wells are newsrooms that form when a local paper shutters. The team points to the Anaconda Weekly Review in Deer Lodge County, Montana, as an example of a well appearing in a county Medill identified as a news desert. Springs, meanwhile, are “harder to spot” than wells because they’re smaller and more ad hoc. The Independent Journalism Atlas applies this label to efforts like the Gallatin County Board Illinois Unofficial Facebook page, which livestreams the board’s public meetings and posts its agendas. The team also paid attention to coverage of news deserts by outlets in neighboring counties. They found high school sports are often a gateway to coverage, pointing to a channel covering southern Illinois high school sports that interviewed the principal in Harrisburg, the seat of Saline County, another news desert county. RELATED ARTICLEUniversities are mapping where local news outlets are still thriving — and where gaps persistCorey HutchinsJanuary 16, 2025In recent years, efforts to “map” local news through different lenses have proliferated. The Independent Journalism Atlas is one such effort, focused on news creators. A better understanding of information sources in news deserts matters, Bank argues, because “you can’t tend a basin you haven’t mapped.” Read the full essay here.

Creative enhancements are now on by default in ChatGPT Ads. Here's what they can change, how to opt out, and the tracking questions still open.

OpenAI is activating creative enhancements, a feature that allows its advertising system to automatically change ads based on the conversation they appear in, by default for new and existing ChatGPT Ads campaigns starting Friday, Oct. 30, according to OpenAI’s help page.

With this setting on, the advertising system can change the copy of an ad to fit the conversation it appears in and choose which pages on the advertiser’s website the ad will direct users to after clicking the ad. These variations of the same ad can run without the need for each one to be reviewed or approved by the advertiser, and Ads Manager doesn’t display a preview for every version of the ad.

Any opt-outs saved at either the account level or campaign level stay intact.

OpenAI’s ad system may rewrite headlines and descriptions or write new ones, translate ad text into another language, resize images to fit the ad format, and optimize the destination URL to send people to a relevant page on the advertiser’s website.

To create the variations, the system relies on the subject matter of the conversation or the user’s interests, what exists (the advertisement), and what is on the landing page of the advertisement. It may create versions ahead of time or create them during a conversation.

On September 16th, OpenAI introduced the AI-powered text customization feature in an optional feature set-up process. This was defined by OpenAI as adjusting current titles and descriptions to match the conversation flow and translating the advertisement copy into the preferred language of the user. The Creative Enhancements Page also includes other adjustments to the ad including text and translations, as well as resizing images and changing destination URLs. As of October 30th, this page does not specify how these options relate to the previous September option.

According to an October 21st engineering post by OpenAI that SEJ covered last week, the company already writes a brief intro for every ad. These introductions exist separately from the advertisers’ title, description, destination link and call-to-action. Unless you opt out of creative enhancements, you can have your title, description and destination link modified to fit the conversation.

Advertisers may opt out of creative enhancements by changing the settings at any time through Ads Manager (Manage settings). Account-level settings are used as the default, while campaign-level settings take precedence over those settings.

The help page, as of October 30th, describes enhancements as one setting. It does not describe additional options to control text, translations, images, or destination URLs.

OpenAI’s ad creation guide tells advertisers to add tracking parameters, such as UTM tags, directly to each ad’s destination URL. Its ChatGPT Ads basics page says static parameters added that way persist on ad clicks. Ads Manager also lets advertisers append landing page query parameters at the campaign, ad group, and ad levels, with parameters on the ad URL taking precedence, according to the Measure Results page.

The Creative Enhancements page indicates that the system may modify the destination URL to direct users to a relevant page on the advertiser’s website. As of October 30th, this page does not discuss how tracking parameters are passed forward when the destination is changed, or whether advertisers have the capability to exclude certain pages.

Ads Manager provides reporting for campaigns, ad groups and ads. Neither the Measure Results page nor the creative enhancements page as of October 30th detail a specific report that will show you each enhanced version individually. On the creative enhancements page, OpenAI states:

“Changes over time do not, on their own, establish the effect of creative enhancements.”

OpenAI introduced a multi-image format in Ads Manager on Oct. 26 as an open beta. Advertisers choose Multiple images under Ad format, and the option is available for standard campaigns with Reach, Clicks, or Conversions objectives. Single-image ads are still available.

A multi-image advertisement utilizes 4-6 square format images (aspect ratio of 1:1). Each one will link to an identical destination URL. Currently, Learn more is the only call to action (CTA) that can be applied to these types of advertisements.

SEJ reported OpenAI’s Oct. 5 announcement of a separate test for visual ads displayed while generating an image within ChatGPT. The ad creation guide and creative enhancements page, both of which were reviewed on October 30th, give no indication if creative enhancements are applicable to multi-image ads.

With creative enhancements on, the ad that a person views may differ from the one you created. Additionally, you will not see all of the different versions of the ads prior to them running. Since the system uses your ad and landing page as its base, pricing, promotions, product information and availability on your landing page must be current.

Check where you set up your analytics for the changes to the destination URL, since what happens to your tracking parameters isn’t something indicated by the creative enhancements page. Verify that ChatGPT clicks continue to include your UTM tags and land on pages which are acceptable to receive paid traffic.

On iOS, according to the ad creation guide published by OpenAI (the company behind ChatGPT), using Share to copy the link allows users to access the full URL of an ad due to the fact that ChatGPT’s in-app browser only shows the hostname.

OpenAI describes Ads Manager as a beta and plans to add more metrics, reporting views, and insights over time. You can change the creative enhancements setting whenever you like, so turning it off for now still leaves you free to try it later.

#7256. “A gross abuse of Meta’s power”: California senator Adam Schiff tells Meta to scrap its new terms of service

All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

Democratic Senator Adam Schiff of California is urging Meta not to implement its forthcoming commercial terms on November 20, his office announced Tuesday.

In a letter sent to Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg, Schiff called on the company to respond by Monday, November 2 with the specific steps it will take to address user concerns.

“Forcing publishers to choose between surrendering their off-platform IP or forfeiting a primary channel of public communication is a gross abuse of Meta’s power as a powerful platform with critical access to consumers,” Schiff wrote. “Meta must not nullify federal IP protections and fair market competition through the unilateral insertion of fine print into terms of service contracts.”

Specifically, Schiff told Meta that it should “provide explicit guarantees that external technical boundaries like paywalls and robots.txt protocols will be fully respected.”

RELATED ARTICLEMeta delays rollout of terms that would allow broad scraping of news sites. Legal experts are still skeptical.Hanaa' TameezOctober 26, 2026“Meta’s verbal assurances that it will not supersede robots.txt files, which are voluntary server flags, do not appear to constitute enforceable legal protections,” Schiff wrote. “Without the insertion of specific language codifying Meta’s policy to respect robots.txt signals into the latest contractual terms, users lack any reliable means by which to protect their content.”

Schiff’s office did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Schiff is the latest elected official in the United States to raise concerns about Meta’s commercial terms, which have now drawn bipartisan criticism. On Friday, Republican Senator Marsha Blackburn of Tennessee said that the terms “indicate Meta is attempting to exploit American creators and businesses by granting itself sweeping authority to scrape content from any website associated with Facebook and Instagram business accounts.”

The terms were previously set to take effect on October 30. Because the terms offered no way to opt out, news of them set off an outcry from news publishers, politicians, and press associations on both sides of the Atlantic. Meta then delayed the effective date of its new terms of service for business accounts to November 20.

On Tuesday, a coalition of Norwegian news publishers sued Meta over the terms and is asking the Oslo District Court to block the terms from going into effect. The legal action, led by the Norwegian Media Companies Association, is the first known lawsuit filed against Meta over its commercial terms.

“We are extending the effective date of our updated Commercial Terms and Self-Serve Ad Terms to November 20 to allow more time for us to explain to our partners and stakeholders what’s changing and what’s not — including how Meta uses web crawlers and the fact that content owners will still be able to use robots.txt to signal preferences,” a Meta spokesperson told Nieman Lab in a statement Friday.

A Meta spokesperson said on October 17 that the company revised the language because it “wasn’t clear in the initial consolidation of terms that robots.txt preferences are respected. News sites, like all other content owners, still have the ability to disable the crawler via robots.txt flags. That has been the case, and it has not changed.”

As of October 27, Meta has made no other changes to the terms aside from the implementation date. No version of the terms includes language about respecting robots.txt preferences.

#7255. Revenue Accounting Manager at LiveKit

LiveKit is building the infrastructure layer for the voice-driven era of computing. Our platform gives developers everything they need to build, test, deploy, scale, and observe agents in production. Founded in 2021, LiveKit powers voice AI applications for OpenAI, xAI, Salesforce, Coursera, Spotify, and thousands of others, collectively facilitating billions of calls each year.

Our revenue is credit-denominated and consumption-based — usage billing, prepaid credit drawdown, and concurrency pricing across a growing enterprise base — which is close to the most complex revenue profile in infrastructure software. The load-bearing questions are open and there are few set policies and processes.

You will be the technical authority on revenue. Resolve's Michael Johnson explained which link building tactics to retire, how to earn relevant coverage, and how to plan off-page SEO and AI visibility work.

A link report can look healthy while the outreach behind it gives publishers little reason to care. For marketers planning next year’s off-page work, the useful question is not just how many links a campaign produced, but why those placements deserved to exist.

In The Link Building Graveyard: What To Bury & What Still Wins, Michael Johnson, CEO and founder of Resolve, explained which tactics he would leave behind and which he would fund heading into 2027. Loren Baker hosted the October 21 webinar, including a Q&A on publisher quality, listicles, and digital PR.

Johnson’s central test was practical: a worthwhile link should benefit the brand, the publisher, and the publisher’s audience. His keep-or-cut framework applied that test to both search rankings and AI visibility, without treating a higher link count as the goal.

Johnson argued against making Domain Authority or Domain Rating the primary measure of a placement. A high score did not establish topical expertise, a useful audience, or a sensible reason for the publisher to link to a brand.

Discussing those scores, Michael Johnson said:

“These are third-party metrics. They’re not Google signals, and they’re easy to inflate.”

During the Q&A, Johnson made the qualification process more concrete. He recommended checking topical relevance first, then looking beyond an estimated traffic total to the keywords a site actually ranked for. A supposed technology publication attracting unrelated celebrity searches would deserve a closer look, regardless of its domain score.

His point was not to discard metrics entirely. It was to use them after judging whether a site had real subject expertise and an audience the brand wanted to reach.

Johnson’s cut list included private blog networks, link-swap schemes, forced commercial anchors, and generic requests to be added to roundups. He also challenged the habit of directing most outreach toward product pages when a guide, dataset, or tool would give an editor a stronger reason to cite the site.

That distinction mattered. He did not argue that genuine partners should never link to each other, or that a product page could never earn a useful backlink. He objected to making an artificial pattern the foundation of the program.

Several familiar approaches remained on his keep list when the execution served readers:

In one client example, Johnson described converting existing product-related brand mentions into links to the relevant product page. The opportunity came from the context of the coverage, not from forcing a product URL into unrelated content.

See Johnson’s product-link example in the full on-demand webinar at 27:54.

Johnson drew a sharp line between asking for a placement and improving a publisher’s list. A generic request to add another brand did neither the editor nor the audience a favor.

His approach to earning inclusion in listicles began with studying the companies already featured. What qualified them? What useful distinction could the missing brand contribute? A relevant feature, fresh data, or a helpful tool could create a case for inclusion; wanting the backlink was not that case.

Baker also asked whether a roundup could still offer AI-search value when its links pointed through an affiliate program or to an Amazon product page. Johnson’s view was that the brand mention could still matter. He emphasized earning a legitimate recommendation rather than treating every roundup as an equally valuable target.

See why Johnson counted branded mentions as an AI visibility win in the full on-demand webinar at 8:57.

For digital PR, Johnson favored original research that gave journalists a story they could not obtain elsewhere. He walked through campaigns built around workplace AI concerns and travel costs to illustrate how a dataset could become a timely headline.

He also demonstrated an interactive news-desert map built from public data and paired with an explanatory guide. The asset gave journalism programs a relevant educational resource to consider linking to. The full session covered how he connected the tool to suitable resource pages, including why AI-generated prospect lists still needed human qualification.

See Johnson’s advice on writing guest posts around audience problems in the full on-demand webinar at 57:17.

In response to a question about inconsistent newsjacking returns, Johnson contrasted reacting to someone else’s news cycle with developing a proactive research program. He acknowledged that earned campaigns were not guaranteed to succeed. The case for repeating them rested on building a useful system, not promising that every pitch would land.

Johnson organized the work into a sequence: audit the existing program, establish a baseline for relevant AI buying prompts, identify worthwhile publishers and resource pages, create the assets those audiences needed, and pitch them.

The 90-day execution walkthrough showed how those activities could build on each other instead of becoming disconnected campaigns. The first phase focused on current spending and opportunities; the next on research, asset creation, and outreach; the final phase on reviewing placements and developing the next useful asset.

To put that approach into practice, start with a small set of decisions:

#7252. Creators who show their sources build trust, survey finds

All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

Journalist-led research found audiences increased trust when news videos identified their sources, such as government documents and interviews.

RELATED ARTICLETwo-thirds of news influencers are men — and most have never worked for a news organizationSarah ScireNovember 18, 2024About one in five U.S. adults regularly gets their news from news creators on social media platforms, but it can be difficult for audiences to suss out which personalities to trust amid an avalanche of misinformation, hot takes, and polarizing content.

New research spearheaded by a team of journalists and political scientists shows that giving audiences a peek into the reporting process can help bolster their trust in the news.

Proof News, a nonprofit newsroom focused on tech accountability, in collaboration with researchers at the French university Sciences Po, shared social news videos with 2,000 U.S. adults to measure their perceptions of trustworthiness. Participants were randomly assigned one of Proof’s yet-to-be-published short-form news videos.

Some participants viewed videos with labels describing the sources, others saw videos with labels describing the newsroom’s ethical standards, and some saw videos without a label. The Sources labels appeared on cards embedded at the end of the video, like a credits reel, or were placed into the video description, the text accompanying the video.

Participants then rated the videos on various trust metrics. We found that labeling videos did increase trust — particularly a label that described the video sources in the description and, to a slightly lesser extent, a label describing newsroom standards in the credits.

This effect was particularly prominent among survey respondents who identified as Democrats or reported having high trust in science. Those groups, when shown the sourcing label in the description of a general news video, reported higher assessments of transparency and trust in the journalist.

There were fewer statistically significant increases in trust metrics with labels for text articles, but Sally Lehrman, founder of The Trust Project, said the findings were still intriguing.

“I’m excited to see the results,” Lehrman said. “Methods and references really do resonate…People are asking, where did the journalist get this information, and how can I trust it.”

As audiences increasingly turn to social media for news, there is a growing public discussion about how trustworthy creators are, especially when it comes to disclosing their funding and relationships. In January, The Wall Street Journal wrote about corporate and foreign interests using influencers to push agendas. In August, The Washington Post reported that the Pentagon secretly hired conservative military veterans with large online audiences to amplify Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s messaging, and a New York Times investigation revealed online influencers received funding from political campaigns without disclosing the connection in their videos.

Some creators have begun trying to distinguish themselves from this type of behavior through their own disclosure efforts.

RELATED ARTICLEWith Local News International, Dave Jorgenson becomes his own TikTok guyNeel DhaneshaSeptember 9, 2025Journalist and creator Dave Jorgenson, who has nearly 1 million followers across TikTok, YouTube, and Instagram, has started publishing a transparency report on his website, Local News International, revealing his sources of funding alongside his editorial standards.

Ultimately, he thinks disclosures of political funding should no longer be voluntary but mandatory. “Platforms should be regulating themselves,” Jorgenson said in an interview. “You can’t really force that unless there are laws.”

Proof used Jorgenson’s ethics and transparency statement as a model for the newsroom standards label in video testing and found that it increased viewers’ trust in the news outlet and the likelihood that they would share a general news story.

New York City is already considering disclosure requirements in the wake of revelations in the Columbia Journalism Review that exposed the inner workings of New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s connections with influencers. The author of the article, Anya Schiffrin, a senior lecturer at Columbia University’s School of International and Public Affairs, testified at a September city council meeting that creator relationships — both paid and unpaid — should be disclosed to viewers.

“It’s important for democracy that we have standards,” Schiffrin said.

RELATED ARTICLEProof News is Julia Angwin’s attempt to bring the scientific method to investigative journalismNeel DhaneshaMarch 21, 2024Proof News, which launched in 2024, pioneered an Ingredients label that takes cues from the scientific method and names the journalists’ hypothesis, sources, limitations, and the story’s findings.

To test whether the label worked to increase viewer trust for short-form vertical videos, we stripped down the Ingredients label to a bullet list of sources followed by an asterisk denoting the reporting limitations. The survey showed the label had a consistent positive effect when placed in the video description, the text box that is often located under the video.

The team also tested how labels performed on online text news articles. The survey showed 1,600 U.S. participants original, unpublished Proof News stories without a label, with a Proof Ingredients label, a label modeled after the Trust Project that described the reporting process, and a label describing newsroom standards.

There were fewer statistically significant increases in trust metrics with the print labels. The most significant findings were an increase in perception of transparency when the reporting process label was used on a polarizing story and an investigative story.

One possible explanation for the differing results between labeling video and text articles is the “ergonomics” of the medium, said Damien Bol, a professor at the Center for Political Research at Sciences Po who helped lead the survey design and data analysis.

“When reading a text, for example, people can quickly skim through it or skip parts of it, whereas a video forces them to follow the story second by second, even when watching at double speed,” Bol said. Different formats, Bol said, shape the “experience of consuming a news story.”

Earlier this month, Julia Angwin, an author of this article, hosted a private convening of creators at Harvard Kennedy School’s Shorenstein Center on Media, Politics and Public Policy to discuss creating shared standards that could be conveyed through a label or other public statement.

The group of 30 leading content creators from news, science communication, education, history, and other evidence-based fields discussed how they could distinguish their work by signaling to viewers their commitment to standards that could include disclosing funding sources and the use of artificial intelligence. Creator-led efforts to bring this to fruition are ongoing.

San Diego-based journalist Lisa Remillard, who has more than 4 million followers on her TikTok channel “The News Girl,” said that making videos with verified facts can feel like a small club. But if she can’t independently confirm something, she’s “not putting that out there.”

Remillard’s audience appears to appreciate transparency. Earlier this year, she published a video describing her editorial standards — and was richly rewarded for it. “I think clearly defining those ethics and standards resonated with my audience and gave them a reason to want to financially support my work,” Remillard said.

Jessica Yellin, the founder of the political podcast, YouTube channel, and social media brand “News Not Noise,” has also called for news creators to voluntarily sign a Creator Constitution, agreeing to journalistic standards such as citing sources, fixing errors, and disclosing financial relationships.

She said labeling sources is about the “signal.” Even if audiences don’t take the time to digest every word, Yellin observed, “It’s the act of showing it that matters.”

Julia Angwin is the founder of Proof News and the founding director of the Independent Media + Audience Project at the Shorenstein Center on Media, Politics and Public Policy at Harvard Kennedy School. Annie Gilbertson is managing editor of Proof News. Rina Palta is editor-at-large at Proof News and senior data scientist at the Independent Media + Audience Project.

#7251. Shopify Now Lets Stores Pay The Company Behind Your AI Shopping Agent via @sejournal, @slobodanmanic

Ask the SEJ experts you already read what AI, agents, and algorithm changes mean for your traffic. Private, human to human. $97/mo.

Shopify pays the company behind an AI agent 0.3% of promoted-product orders, and stores can add more. Here is what that commission changes.

If I send an agent to buy something for me from the Shopify catalog, is it finding the best possible product for me, or the product that will make whoever is behind the agent the most money? As of Oct. 27, 2026, Shopify’s documentation gives the agent a reason to work for two others besides me: the company that built it, and Shop, Shopify’s app and website.

Shopify mixes products that pay a commission into the search results its catalog gives AI agents. It calls them promoted placements. When a shopper buys one, Shopify pays the company behind the agent (Shopify calls it the developer) 0.3% of the order.

Stores can pay more. If a store runs Shop Campaigns, Shopify’s paid promotion program, and turns on external platforms, Shopify turns the store’s campaign “into a commission” on top of the 0.3%. In search results, the total comes back with the product, next to its price, rating, and review count. Shopify’s example shows 1.5% on one product.

Shopify pays the store’s extra commission “only when the buyer completes the purchase in Shop, either in the Shop mobile app or on shop.com.” For those products, the links the agent gets point to shop.com, not to the store’s website. A sale on the store’s website earns only the 0.3%.

So the agent has a reason to pick the product that pays its developer more, and a reason to send me to Shop to buy it. Shopify’s documentation doesn’t say whether a bigger commission also moves a product up the list.

In my test, two Claude models went with the numbers they were given: at their default settings they picked a water bottle listed with 447,221 reviews 84 times out of 100, when the store’s product page showed 6,537. I haven’t tested a commission number. What an agent does with one depends on its model and on what its developer tells it.

Shopify asks developers to label promoted products, to say they may earn a commission, and to make that clear “before buyers act on a promoted result.” It points to US FTC rules on paid relationships and to EU and UK rules on ads and sponsored content, and leaves the exact wording to the developer.

The FTC, EU, and U.K. rules were written for ads and paid recommendations. The FTC’s endorsement guides say a paid connection behind a recommendation has to be disclosed when people wouldn’t expect it. The closest EU rule I found bans search results that hide “payment specifically for achieving higher ranking” (Directive 2019/2161). An agent picking one product isn’t clearly a recommendation in the FTC’s sense or a search result in the EU’s, and a commission on a sale isn’t clearly payment for a higher ranking. I’m not a lawyer, and I know of no ruling either way.

Shopify calls promoted placements a Developer Preview, which developers join from a waitlist, by invitation. The extra commission applies only to products in an active U.S. campaign, in USD. Shopify’s documentation doesn’t name any developer that has joined. Developers outside the program get ordinary results, so I can’t see promoted products from the outside either. Shopify says the details “are not final and might change”.

What I’d watch is whether Shopify says a bigger commission moves a product up the list, and whether any agent tells the shopper what it earns and where it is sending them to buy.

This post was originally published on No Hacks.
