#7234. Threads tests smaller group sharing option

Threads Friends is similar to Instagram’s Close Friends feature and allows users to add up to 50 connections.

Threads is testing a new group engagement option with Threads Friends, which enables users to create a smaller sub-community of chosen connections.

Threads Friends is essentially the same as Instagram’s Close Friends feature, providing a more private engagement and sharing space where users can display their posts only to a select group of connections instead of broadcasting every update to everyone in the app.

Threads users will be able to create a list of up to 50 Threads connections to include in their group.

As explained by Threads: “People you add will see Threads Friends on your posts, so they’ll know they're part of your list. If someone on your list likes or replies to your post, others on your Threads Friends list will be able to see their username and how they interact with your post.”

Once a user has created a Threads Friends list, they’ll have an option to only post updates to their Threads Friends.

This could be another way to drive engagement in the app, by leaning into the broader trend away from public posting and toward more curated group sharing.

Threads said that it’s testing the feature with users in Ireland, Italy and Japan, but that anyone can be added to a Friends group, no matter where they are in the world.

Shopify's performance reviews asked how staff used AI. Its CEO says the answers didn't matter, and the question can give a company a reputation to live up to.

Shopify CEO Tobi Lütke says it didn’t matter how employees answered the AI question his company added to its performance reviews. Having the question there, he said on the Sources podcast, can “give a company a reputation to live up to.”

The question came out of an April 2025 memo in which he told employees “reflexive AI usage is now a baseline expectation at Shopify.” The memo said, “We will add AI usage questions to our performance and peer review questionnaire.” It also said teams would have to show why AI couldn’t do the work before asking for more headcount and resources.

He made the comments to Alex Heath in an episode published Oct. 28 and recorded at Shopify’s Toronto office. He also said an AI skeptic who keeps their head down won’t become a top performer at a company where everyone around them works with AI agents.

Heath asked whether Shopify still had the AI review question and the headcount rule in place. Lütke said both now happen on their own. “I don’t have to enforce these kind of things,” he said.

He said the memo was seen as controversial outside Shopify but “really not inside of a firm.” More people there paid attention to it, he said, after the press “made a big deal out of it.” He took that as a sign Shopify had already made the transition.

He said he doesn’t know whether the AI question is in Shopify’s current review. He described it as a peer-rating question about how reflexively a colleague shows up with an AI prototype, and said “sometimes you play a little bit of tricks there.” The answer didn’t matter, he said.

Shopify’s CEO moved from the review question to people who resist AI. He pointed to open-source projects that have banned AI contributions and said he’s entertained by debates over whether code was “hand chiseled by humans or somehow computed by math.” His view was that good code should be accepted either way.

He said a company should decide who it’s for and who it isn’t, and that “heightening the misalignment with the people you don’t want is actually almost more important than having a good careers page.”

An AI skeptic who is “just kind of trying to lay low,” he said, will never be a top performer in a company where everyone around them uses AI agents to do their work.

He said companies should make that explicit, because everyone deserves to work somewhere they “either are or have a really good shot at becoming one of the top performers.” Once it’s clear that isn’t possible for someone, Shopify also wants to help them look for that kind of place elsewhere, he said.

In a Knowledge Project episode released Sept. 15, Lütke said AI had made one kind of lazy work worse at Shopify. Staff have a name for AI output that gets handed to a colleague without being read. They call it a slop grenade, and I covered those comments last month.

Shopify’s CEO says the AI question in its reviews was there to give the company a reputation to live up to. The question he described is about how readily someone turns to AI. The slop grenades he talked about in September come after that, when AI output reaches a coworker unread.

A review question about adoption won’t tell a team lead whether anyone checks AI drafts before they go to an editor or a client.

Earlier in the interview, Shopify’s CEO said he doesn’t expect public pessimism about AI to last long, because more people will use it themselves. He said the stories from that use will wash it away.

He didn’t say in the interview whether the AI question will be in Shopify’s next review cycle.

#7232. SDK Engineer - Python at Supabase

Supabase is the Postgres development platform, built by developers for developers. We provide a complete backend solution including Database, Auth, Storage, Edge Functions, Realtime, and Vector Search. All services are deeply integrated and designed for growth.

We're looking for a SDK Engineer - Python to join our SDK team and own how developers talk to Supabase from Python. You'll work closely with the rest of the SDK team, our Auth, Realtime, Storage, PostgREST, Functions, CLI and Docs teams, and the open-source community, helping us make the Python SDK a library Python developers genuinely enjoy using.

Python developers reach Supabase from backend services, data pipelines, notebooks, and a growing number of AI agents and agent frameworks. The Python SDK is how all of them talk to the platform: database queries, auth, storage, realtime and edge functions, in both sync and async flavors.

This is a library-authoring role, and the work happens in the open: public repos, public issue trackers, and API decisions whose consequences last for years. If you get satisfaction from a type checker that catches the bug before your users do, from an async client that cleans up after itself, and from an issue tracker that isn't a graveyard, you'll like it here.

This role is ideal for someone who thrives in async, fast-paced environments and is excited about building developer tools that scale to millions.

Build and evolve our Python SDK across database, auth, storage, realtime and functions, with both sync and async APIs that feel natural in Python.

Start new things. Alongside the maintenance work, find what's missing, make the case for it, and build it. Nobody will hand you the list.

Work in the open. Triage inbound issues, review and shepherd outside contributions, keep CI and release automation healthy, and hold a clear, kind line on scope.

Own the typing experience. Make the SDK fully typed and checker-friendly, so autocomplete and static analysis stay correct in real codebases.

Keep us honest across environments. Multiple Python versions, sync and async frameworks, workers, serverless and notebooks — with dependency ranges that don't fight our users' projects. Test it, don't assume it.

Work on realtime. Long-lived websocket connections, reconnection, and subscription and presence semantics.

Track the platform. When auth, realtime, storage, postgrest or edge functions ship a change, make sure the SDK reflects it, and that we say so in the changelog.

Design in public. Write the RFCs, migration guides, release notes and docs. Treat a breaking change as a deprecation path plus a migration story, not a version bump.

Make our SDK legible to AI coding agents, which are now a major consumer of it.

Know modern Python typing deeply. You use generics, protocols, overloads and TypedDict as design tools, run strict type checking, and fix type errors without reaching for Any.

Have authored or maintained a published library with a public API and users outside your own company. You know what it costs to change something people depend on.

Know the maintainer side of open source. Issue triage at volume, reviewing outside PRs, release automation, changelogs and semver, security reports, and saying no to a feature request without losing the person who asked.

Are fluent in asyncio and have opinions on how a library should serve both sync and async callers.

Know Python packaging for libraries: pyproject.toml, wheels, modern tooling, version support policy, and why libraries shouldn't pin their dependencies tightly.

Test as a habit: unit, type-level and end-to-end against a real stack. Every fix comes with a regression test.

Write well. Design docs, changelogs and issue replies are a large part of the output here, much of it public, and we're async by default.

Have real autonomy: you find the important work, scope it, ship it, and say what you didn't do.

Communicate clearly across both technical and non-technical audiences

Have experience in async or globally distributed teams

Are energized by solving real-world problems for developers

Are comfortable navigating ambiguity and moving quickly

Bonus points if you: have run a major-version migration for a public package, know your way around JWT/OAuth, have built integrations for AI agent frameworks, or have generated idiomatic clients from a schema.

Every team member receives ESOP (equity ownership) in the company. We want everyone to share in the upside of what we’re building together.

Use this budget to set up your ideal work environment—laptop, monitor, headphones, or whatever helps you do your best work.

Supabase covers 100% of health insurance for employees and 80% for dependents, wherever you are. Your wellbeing and your family’s health are important to us.

Once a year, the entire company gathers in a new city for a week of connection, collaboration, and fun. It’s a highlight of our year.

We operate asynchronously and trust you to manage your own time. You know what needs to be done and when.

Every team member receives an annual education allowance to spend on learning—courses, books, conferences, or anything that supports your growth.

Supabase was born-remote and open-source-first. We believe our globally distributed team is our secret weapon in building tools developers love.

Over $1B raised (including our $500M Series F)

We move fast, build in public, and use what we ship. If it’s in your project, we probably use it in ours too. We believe deeply in the open-source ecosystem and strive to support—not replace—existing tools and communities.

#7229. YouTube subscriptions are rising as more users turn to CTV

Ad growth slowed in the third quarter of 2026 but still brought in more than $11 billion in revenue, according to parent company Alphabet.

YouTube’s ad growth slowed in the third quarter of 2026, with parent company Alphabet reporting that YouTube ads brought in $11.2 billion in revenue for the period. At the same time, YouTube’s subscription revenue is rising and the company is also developing more ways to build on creator revenue opportunities and drive more momentum in take-up.

First, YouTube’s Q3 ad revenue in 2026 grew 9% year over year, which is a slight slowdown from the 13% growth reported in Q2.

In Alphabet’s second-quarter earnings call in July, the company said that YouTube saw significant momentum in Premium sign-ups among connected TV viewers for that period as more people watched YouTube content as an alternative to traditional TV.

YouTube is now the top streaming platform in the U.S., according to Nielsen’s The Gauge report from Aug. 2026, which looks at U.S. TV viewing behaviors.

In an accompanying Q3 earnings call, Google Chief Business Officer Philipp Schindler said Living Room, YouTube’s connected TV experience, is becoming a bigger factor for YouTube revenue beyond just direct subscriptions, and accounted for more than one-third of total YouTube ads revenue.

Schindler also said that it continues to see strong SMB adoption of its Demand Gen products. Meanwhile, more than three million creators are now available as part of YouTube’s partnership program.

Schindler also highlighted the platform’s increasing momentum in e-commerce, with more than 1.3 million channels now enrolled in YouTube’s shopping program. YouTube recently announced a new affiliate partnership with Amazon, which will let U.S.-based creators tag Amazon products in their videos, Shorts and livestreams, significantly expanding promotional and creator monetization opportunities.

Finally, Alphabet also discussed the increasing use of AI to improve YouTube ad targeting and increase creative output among users.

“Every day, more than 20 million videos are being uploaded,” Schindler said. “We're making creation easier with new generative AI tools in YouTube Studio, plus a conversational editing assistant in Shorts and YouTube Create.”

On that front, YouTube added an AI-powered reimagine option for Shorts in March, which enables viewers to generate an alternative video based on another creator’s clip. YouTube also tested an Extend with AI option that allowed creators to generate alternative video endings.

That is seemingly driving more AI adoption. Last week, YouTube published a report that found that 61% of people who have posted videos in the app over the past 12 months said they were interested in using AI to insert themselves into video content.

As with all platforms, YouTube will have to contend with AI slop, but the data suggests that YouTube’s AI-powered creative additions are resonating with users.

Google's spam guide adds indexing advice for pages made for sharing. Other updates cover restaurant ordering controls, report dates and AI Mode revenue.

Welcome to the week’s Pulse: updates have an impact on which user-created pages are meant for Search, who is able to turn off ordering links on restaurant profiles, and just how much to read into a page-indexing report that appears to no longer update.

Google added information about indexing shareable pages to its spam guide and provided restaurants with direct control over ordering providers. In response to a user’s report that their page-indexing data was no longer updating, John Mueller at Google referred to the date on the reports. New citation data and Alphabet’s earnings round out the week.

Here’s what matters for you and your work.

In a section added Oct. 26, Google’s guide to preventing user-generated spam now recommends that platforms, by default, apply noindex or block crawling on pages created for direct sharing.

The new part, “Only index content meant for Search,” is concerned with webpages that were designed “for direct sharing, collaboration, or utility rather than public search discovery.” There are two options for this type of webpage; using the noindex (via a robots meta tag or an X-Robots-Tag HTTP header), or adding a crawl-block in your robots.txt file. Google now recommends you confirm your website in Search Console to receive notifications of manual actions and security issues, and also check your Page Indexing and Search performance reports to see if there have been “unexpected spikes.” Neither the guide nor the changelog mentions any changes in how Google will enforce these guidelines.

Robots.txt will stop Google from crawling the pages it blocks, however according to Google’s introduction to robots.txt, the file “is not a mechanism for keeping a web page out of Google.” Even though a URL has been disallowed in robots.txt, that does not mean Google cannot find it; as long as another site links to your URL it may appear in search results. A noindex rule will prevent share link URLs or generated page URLs you wish to remove from appearing in search engine results only if Googlebot can crawl and read them.

Read our full coverage: Google Updates Spam Guide For Shared Pages, Generated Content & Apps and Google Signals A Wider Crackdown On SEO Spam

Restaurants can now turn off specific third-party ordering providers directly from their Google Business Profile dashboard, Google’s Lisa Landsman wrote on LinkedIn on Oct. 28.

The post included a screenshot of the individual pickup and delivery buttons under “Show provider to customers.” When asked about which countries allow the feature, product manager at Google, Michael G. stated that all do. Prior to this, restaurants were able to submit a removal request on a provider through their Business Profile; however, the provider was required to complete the action, and Google’s help page gives providers up to 5 business days after a request to remove the link.

Google’s policy page for ordering providers says “All partner integrations are enabled by default.” It’s worth checking the ordering list on each restaurant profile you manage to make sure it doesn’t include providers the restaurant doesn’t use.

Read our full coverage: Google Gives Restaurants Direct Control Over Ordering Providers

A user on a social media site, Reddit, stated they had not received an update of their Page indexing report since Oct. 16 and questioned if this was due to some type of stall in the data pipeline. In response to this question, John Mueller from Google said, “I don’t think it makes sense for me / us to comment on the data freshness for all reports all the time, this is why we put dates in there.”

Mueller stated that this user’s website appeared to be fairly recent and had steady numbers; he added “Indexing doesn’t change quickly, and when it does, you see that reflected in the performance reports first.” Mueller told the user to “save your energy,” and that Google focuses on faster updates “where we think it’s actually useful for folks.” Mueller did not indicate if the report was late. On Oct. 29, I checked SEJ’s property in the page indexing report, which indicated the most recent data update was Oct. 22.

Before interpreting a drop or rise in indexed pages, it’s worth checking the Page indexing report’s last-update date, as the chart may lag behind what’s happening on your site. Mueller’s reply points to the Performance report as the first place to look for indexing changes.

Read our full coverage: Google Responds To Concern Over Search Console Indexing Reports

TJ Robertson analyzed 193,507 AI answers from ChatGPT, Google AI Mode, and AI Overviews. In two rounds of blind ratings, the analysis found that cited pages more often opened with a direct answer to the question than the comparison pages did.

In comparison to pages that came up for the same answer to users’ questions but were not cited, cited pages directly answered user queries in their opening lines in 23%, while the uncited pages did so in 14%. In comparison to Google’s top 10 results that the AI never pulled up, the split was 20% for cited pages versus 5% for those top 10 pages on all 195 rated pairs. These statistics were taken from questions tracked by Robertson’s agency TJ Digital for their clients, and TJ Digital sells both SEO and generative engine optimization services. Robertson states that he has identified association (not causation), not proof that a particular feature of a webpage causes it to be referenced.

When the pages that were not referenced had also come up in the AI’s search, this gap in opening answers given on a page (both for reference and non-reference pages) was smaller. Seeing if the key pages answer the question in the first line will give you a good fast check, and you can compare these patterns with those of the questions you are tracking.

Read our full coverage: AI-Cited Pages More Often Got Straight To The Answer

Alphabet’s third-quarter results show Google Search & other revenue rising 12% year over year to $63.35 billion, following growth of 19% in Q1 and 17% in Q2.

Asked on the earnings call whether fewer ads in AI Overviews and AI Mode explained slower Search growth, Chief Business Officer Philipp Schindler named currency as the biggest factor in the slowdown from Q2, then developments in retail and media. He then said “the strong growth in AI Mode queries had an impact because of the lower monetization we were seeing in AI Mode,” and added, “To be clear, we feel very good about our trajectory here.” The same day, Google expanded ads in AI Mode to 10 more countries and said it’s launching multiturn ads in the U.S.

Schindler didn’t say what AI Mode monetization was lower than, or by how much. Neither Pichai’s published Q3 remarks nor the call included a figure for clicks sent to websites, which he gave in Q2, so the quarter adds detail on AI Mode revenue and none on that traffic.

Read our full coverage: Google Says Lower AI Mode Monetization Weighed On Search Growth

This week’s updates include defaults, date stamps, and caveats. Defaults shape what people see until someone chooses to change them, from the indexing setting on a share page to the ordering providers on a restaurant profile. The date stamps and caveats, on a Search Console report, a set of citation data and Alphabet’s earnings, mark the limit of what each source told you. What happened on your own sites is the check left for you to run.

DebugBear, a Real User Monitoring tool widely used by SEO experts, reported an attack. Site owners must remove its script and check for unauthorized access.

Who this affects: This security alert concerns website owners using DebugBear’s Real User Monitoring script.

DebugBear told customers to remove its Core Web Vitals monitoring script. Site owners should also check exposed accounts and unauthorized changes.

If your website uses DebugBear’s Real User Monitoring script to track Core Web Vitals, remove it now. The company issued that instruction on October 29 after reporting a security incident involving its infrastructure.

Example of the embed code to remove. The script ID varies by site:

SEO teams should flag this to their development and security teams, who should remove the script and investigate any unauthorized access or changes made while it was active.

In a follow-up update, DebugBear said attackers compromised its DNS records through its domain registrar. DebugBear said its initial investigation showed that the attack targeted one customer’s website. It reported no indication that its internal systems had been compromised.

In the same update, DebugBear said it could not receive email sent to its domain. Customers can follow updates on DebugBear’s X account.

Cybersecurity firm Hudson Rock’s analysis found malicious JavaScript at a DebugBear script URL used by Polymarket on October 29. The code sought the trading client already available in a logged-in browser. Polymarket’s October 30 incident report confirmed that the script sold positions and moved funds from some users’ wallets. It used the access a signed-in visitor already had and did not need the user’s password.

That is the concern for other site owners: what could malicious code do with the permissions of a visitor who is already signed in?

I would have the development and security teams take these steps:

The retrieved payload targeted Polymarket’s trading accounts. Attackers used the compromised DebugBear script to reach this high-value target and stole funds. Other high-value websites may have been targeted as well. It is not yet clear whether other DebugBear customers also received malicious code.

Removing the monitoring tag prevents new loads. It does not reverse unauthorized actions or remove anything an attacker may already have planted.

#7225. Pinterest reports solid user growth in Q3

The company’s third-quarter earnings report showed more than 20 million new users since Q2, including 17 million in regions outside its core markets.

Pinterest published its third-quarter 2026 results on Oct. 29, which showed that the platform saw a significant boost in user growth in the period.

Indeed, Pinterest added 21 million global monthly active users versus Q2, with the platform now up to 661 million MAU.

A major positive for Pinterest this time around is that its European user growth is trending back up, after stagnating, and even declining over the past year.

That’s particularly relevant for at least in the immediate term, because Pinterest still generates a lot more revenue from its users in the U.S. and Europe, as opposed to the “Rest of World” segment.

Though the majority of Pinterest’s user growth is still happening in the Rest of the World category, with Pinterest adding 17 million more users in markets outside the U.S. and Europe.

In its accompanying notes, Pinterest said that Gen Z now represents 57% of its audience. It also reported that in-app engagement is rising among users in the U.S. and Canada, with more activity across search, board creation and outbound clicks.

In order to capitalize on its rising user growth, Pinterest said that it hopes to implement a similar business growth strategy to what led to its re-accelerated growth in the U.S. and Canada. Meanwhile, it also launched its programmatic buying solution in all regions.

In terms of Q3 revenue, Pinterest posted $1.17 billion, representing a 12% year-over-year increase.

Pinterest said that revenue in the U.S. and Canada increased 14% year over year, while international revenue growth was primarily impacted by regulatory changes in Europe that impacted cross-border selling.

Pinterest also highlighted its continued improvement in ad relevance, with its expanding array of signals now being integrated into its broader AI-powered targeting process.

The company is also seeking out more opportunities to build on its revenue options through the aforementioned programmatic solution and more partnerships.

On that front,  Pinterest has been developing more ways to help creators make money from their content in the app, while also leaning into creator-driven recommendations to drive brand promotion opportunities.

Brands can now sponsor creator Pins related to their products, and Pinterest also has its own TV show on Roku TV, in which creators showcase products listed in the app.

Last month, Pinterest also launched visual search ads, which let advertisers place promotions in Pinterest search results and Pin close-ups.

These tools should help advertisers tap into the high shopping intent of Pinterest users, with the platform now facilitating more than 80 billion searches per month.

Pinterest also continues to lean into AI-powered discovery, while also promoting its value as a complement to real-world experiences, as opposed to trying to keep people scrolling.

Strategically, Pinterest’s approach is well-aligned with its use case, and it’s seemingly not stepping out of its lane with radical AI updates that don’t align with discovery.

Yet, the platform is also contending with an influx of AI-generated content in Pins, which many users have cited as a concern.

It’s a balance that all platforms are working to get right, in providing new AI-powered tools to drive engagement while also limiting overuse and misuse of AI.

That’s especially relevant on a visual discovery platform, and it will be interesting to see if Pinterest looks to take a bigger stand against AI content in future.

A shared robots.txt line could let sites opt out of AI training with several providers at once, but companies involved are handling it differently.

Google, Microsoft, and OpenAI announced plans on Friday to honor a shared robots.txt line for AI training preferences. A site could use it to state one training preference to every provider that takes part, instead of writing rules for each company’s crawler.

The line is from an Internet Draft that Anthropic’s Kevin Kelley submitted to the AI Preferences working group at the IETF (same date). This is listed in the IETF’s document tracker as an individual draft, which does not represent official IETF standardization activity. In a post to the working group’s email list, Kelley indicated that Anthropic has started development to provide this feature.

Based on their provided timelines, none of the three companies currently supports the line. Google and Microsoft described how each would handle it differently. According to Google, if a site sets up a shared opt-out line, Google plans to treat it like a Google-Extended block when a website doesn’t specify Google-Extended, and this control also applies to grounding within Gemini Apps. Microsoft wants sites that use its NoArchive and NoCache tags to switch to new preferences by March 1, 2027.

Kelley’s draft adds no new directive to robots.txt. An ordinary rule group, that a site might write under what the draft calls a policy token, __usage_ai-training, would be written like it always has been, using Allow and Disallow. The draft provides an example of how one might opt out of AI training on the entire site, except for the /press-kit/ folder.

The token itself has its meaning based upon the working group’s vocabulary draft, specifically defining AI Training as using content to modify a generative AI model’s learned parameters. Those models that do nothing but non-generative tasks like classification or ranking are exempted from this definition.

Rules that have already been put into robots.txt files will not be considered as part of any shared training preference. In the draft, a wildcard group (User-Agent: *) can never match the token, and a file without a __usage_ai-training group indicates no preference, which Kelley states is true of every robots.txt file currently published. The token doesn’t control crawling either.

On Oct. 22, I covered a different working group draft, co-written by Google’s Gary Illyes, that would add a Content-Usage rule to robots.txt. Kelley wrote that the group set that draft aside to make progress on the vocabulary.

Google’s post, by John Mueller, says that when a site opts out of training with the shared line and doesn’t specify Google-Extended, Google plans to interpret that “as if the publisher had disallowed Google-Extended.” Google aims to support the control in 2027, according to the post, and its crawler documentation says early 2027.

The documentation says Google-Extended controls whether content can be used to train future Gemini models and whether it can be used for grounding in Gemini Apps and on Vertex AI. Grounding, in Google’s description, means supplying content from the search index to the model when it answers. The post adds that sites that specifically allow Google-Extended are eligible to appear in Gemini Apps responses through grounding.

The documentation also says Google-Extended doesn’t affect a site’s inclusion in Google Search. AI Overviews and AI Mode have a separate opt-out, the Search generative AI control in Search Console, which I covered when it rolled out worldwide in August.

Microsoft’s post, by Bing principal product manager Krishna Madhavan, adopts the shared line for training and adds a separate AI Grounding preference. That one is set only at the page level and governs whether content can help inform AI-generated answers. Microsoft also lets a meta tag or HTTP header set the training preference for a single page, overriding robots.txt for that page.

A default of Allow is what happens with grounding, and keeping a page out is how Disallow works. The new option called DisallowExtended allows grounding in Microsoft created tools like Copilot and Bing’s AI Mode but does not allow grounding through Microsoft provided grounding services that are used by other businesses (Web IQ). Microsoft said either restriction will limit visibility of your brand in answers using Artificial Intelligence (AI) and will have no effect on your ability to be listed in search results from Bing.

Microsoft is replacing NoArchive and NoCache for training and grounding with these two new options. They will begin honoring the new options on February 1, 2027, as they crawl, and they will stop recognizing the older tags as training or grounding options after March 1, 2027.

Sites that use the old tags and want to stay out of grounding also need to record a temporary preference in Bing Webmaster Tools. The setting opens Dec. 15 and is available only to sites still using those tags on that date. Microsoft’s FAQ says pages without one by March 1 default to allowing grounding until Microsoft recrawls them. Microsoft also says that once it detects either new preference on a site, it will disregard any NoArchive or NoCache tags still on that site.

OpenAI aims to honor the signal in the next few months, though its current robots.txt policy will still be in effect.

Neither OpenAI’s blog post nor its crawler documentation (checked Oct. 30) states what would happen when a website has both a shared line rule and GPTBot rule that conflict with each other.

As of Oct. 30, there was no posting in Anthropic’s newsroom regarding the signal. According to Kelley’s mailing list message, implementing support for this feature across all of Anthropic’s services will take some time.

According to Anthropic’s crawler-help webpage (checked Oct. 30), they have only three crawl control options available, which are ClaudeBot, Claude-User, and Claude-SearchBot.

One robots.txt group could replace a stack of per-company training rules once each company reads it; however, an opt-out through the shared line won’t reach the same uses at Google and Microsoft. For example, at Microsoft, training and grounding are separate settings. In contrast, both sit under Google-Extended at Google, and there is no way described in the crawler documentation to keep content out of Gemini training while still letting Gemini Apps use it for grounding.

Microsoft’s is the only announcement that replaces controls sites already use. According to Google, OpenAI, and Anthropic’s Kelley, existing controls will continue to work, so sites that use NoArchive or NoCache to limit how Copilot uses their content have things they need to do first.

OpenAI’s post encourages other AI providers to honor the signal, and Kelley wrote that he hopes others will join. Google and OpenAI say they’ll share more details as their support arrives. Kelley’s draft expires May 3, 2027, unless a new version replaces it, and he plans to propose his design as a change to the Content-Usage draft.
